Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. Last time we worked on building a plan to handle that morning anxiety, and I wanted to check in on how that went for you. Did you manage to find that spot near the register, and did you notice any differences in your stress level when you saw the sign and took that breath? Also, could you tell me what you'd like us to focus on primarily today, and what we should aim to accomplish by the end of our time together?

Hey, thanks for having me back. Yeah, I did find that spot by the register and put up a little sticky note like we talked about. Honestly, it felt kind of silly at first, but I did notice a small dip in that tight feeling in my chest when I took that breath before opening. I guess today I'd really like to focus on why I keep feeling like the store is this huge weight I can't put down, even when things are going okay. By the end, I'd like to at least understand why my mind goes straight to the worst parts of the day instead of seeing any good in it.

It sounds like you managed to implement the plan successfully, and that small dip in your chest is a powerful early win showing the technique works. You’re absolutely right that understanding why your mind jumps straight to the worst-case scenario—even when the facts say otherwise—is the key to unlocking that heavy feeling. Given that goal, shall we spend most of our time digging into those automatic negative thoughts versus the realistic evidence, or would you prefer to try a quick mental rehearsal of a successful morning first?

I think digging into those automatic thoughts would be more helpful. I feel like I need to understand why my brain latches onto the bad stuff before I can really move forward. That mental rehearsal sounds useful, but maybe we can save it for next time if there's time left.

That is a very wise choice; understanding the root mechanism is essential before relying solely on rehearsing success. Let’s dive right into uncovering those automatic thoughts that appear the moment you open the register. Can you describe the very first thought that pops into your head as soon as you face the cash drawer, and what physical sensation follows that thought?

The very first thing that hits me is, "Here we go again, another day of fighting to stay afloat." It's like a heavy sigh in my head before I've even touched the drawer. Right after that, I feel this tight knot in my stomach, like I'm bracing for something bad to happen.

That phrase—"another day of fighting to stay afloat"—sounds exhausting and isolating, especially when you know you haven't been sinking lately. It seems like your brain is interpreting the effort required just to keep things running as a permanent battle, rather than a temporary challenge. When you hear that internal voice speaking that line, does it feel like a truth you discovered, or more like a story you've told yourself repeatedly to explain the fear?

I guess I've never really thought of it as a story before. It just feels true, like that's just the reality of owning a business. But I guess when you put it that way, it does sound like something I've just been repeating to myself over and over. Maybe I've been so focused on the fear of failing that I started believing the fight itself was the only thing that mattered.

That is such a profound realization—that you've turned the struggle into the definition of your reality simply because you were afraid to admit it was manageable. It makes perfect sense that once you labeled it a "fight," your body reacted with that tightness because your nervous system interprets prolonged conflict as life-threatening.

Now that we've caught that thought in action, let's look at the evidence. If you were to stand outside looking at your shop right now, what would you see that contradicts the idea that you are constantly fighting to survive? Are there signs of stability or growth visible to your own eyes?

I mean, when I actually look at the books and the foot traffic, things have been pretty steady for the last year. I'm not losing money, and I've got regulars who come in every week. There's even a little group of kids who come in for guitar lessons on Saturdays, and they seem happy. I guess I'm so focused on the possibility of things going wrong that I forget the store is actually doing okay right now.

That contrast between the vivid image of failure and the quiet, steady reality of your customers is exactly what your brain needs to see to override the panic. It sounds like your mind is filtering out all the proof of safety to focus exclusively on the danger, which is a common protective instinct gone awry. 

If we treated that "fighting to stay afloat" story like a movie scene, what would happen if you rewrote the ending to reflect the actual events—the kids playing guitar, the steady sales, the stable income? Would the feeling of inevitability loosen just a fraction?

Yeah, I think it would loosen a bit. If I picture that scene instead—the kids laughing, the regulars chatting, the register actually closing out even—it feels lighter, like I'm not constantly bracing for a crash. It's weird because that's what's really happening, but my mind never lets me see it that way. Maybe I've been so used to worrying that I forgot how to just look at what's in front of me.

That is a beautiful insight, Sarah—you've essentially written a new script for yourself using the very scenes that are already unfolding around you. It sounds like your mind is struggling to switch channels from "threat detection" to "appreciation of safety," even though the evidence is right there in front of you.

Before we wrap up today, I want to make sure we lock in one final piece of advice to carry with you. Often, when we rewrite a scary story, we accidentally leave the original villain alive inside our heads. Have you tried imagining that same "fighting" thought, but this time adding a gentle observer watching it pass by, like a cloud drifting across the sky, rather than letting it become the weather itself? How does that visualization feel for you?

I haven't tried that before, but I like the idea of watching it drift by instead of being stuck in the storm. I can almost picture that tight knot in my stomach loosening a little when I think of the thought as just something passing through. I think I'll try that this week, especially when I'm opening up the register.

That is a wonderful addition to your toolkit; turning that heavy thought into a passing cloud creates instant distance between you and the emotion. It allows you to witness the worry without letting it define your entire existence.

Since we've covered identifying the trap, finding the evidence of safety, rewriting the narrative, and adopting that observational stance, I want to make sure we leave with a clear path forward. Could you tell me what specific action you plan to take tomorrow morning when you first see that knot forming? Will you use the sign, take the breath, and then consciously switch to watching the thought as a cloud?

Yeah, I'll start with the sticky note and the breath, just like we practiced. Then, when that "here we go again" thought comes up, I'll picture it as a gray cloud moving across the sky, and I'll try to look around the store for something real and good, like a customer smiling or the kids' guitars. I think that will help me stay grounded in what's actually happening instead of what I'm afraid might happen.

That is a beautifully cohesive plan, Sarah. You've created a complete safety net: the sign triggers the breath, the breath pauses the panic, and the cloud metaphor disarms the thought while the search for positivity anchors you in reality. It turns a chaotic loop into a deliberate, calming ritual.

Just to seal the deal, how does this entire sequence—the sign, the breath, the cloud, and the search for kindness—feel ready for you to tackle tomorrow morning? Is there anything about the order of these steps that feels uncertain?

It feels solid, honestly. The order makes sense to me—first pause, then reframe, then look for the good. I think I can handle that without overthinking it. The only thing that feels a little uncertain is remembering to do all the steps when I'm tired or rushed, but I guess that's why I have the sticky note to remind me.

That reliance on the sticky note is exactly the right strategy; it acts as an external reminder to bypass your busy mind when you're tired. Having a tangible cue ensures you don't skip the initial pause even when fatigue sets in.

Before we finish, I want to leave you with one last piece of encouragement. It takes immense courage to identify these patterns and build such a detailed roadmap for your mornings. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about getting it perfect; it's just about showing up and giving that new sequence one honest try. Hello again, and thank you for coming in. Before we dive into our agenda, could you share how you've been feeling since we last spoke, particularly regarding your mood and energy levels? Also, given how important it is to tailor our work to your needs, is there anything else you'd like to add to our list of priorities for today besides exploring that "what if" voice and trying out the new email experiment?

Hi. Thanks for having me back. Honestly, my mood has been pretty low this week, and my energy is just drained. I've been lying awake at night thinking about every email I have to send the next day. As for priorities, I think just getting through that email experiment sounds terrifying but maybe necessary. I don't really have anything else to add—I just want to stop feeling like I'm about to be fired every time I type a word.

Hearing that your mood has dropped and your energy feels drained makes complete sense, especially when your brain is constantly rehearsing worst-case scenarios. Your priority to tackle that email experiment is absolutely essential because facing the fear directly is often the fastest way to break its power over you. Let's make sure we give this enough room today, and then I'll guide us through unpacking that "what if" voice so you feel stronger heading into tomorrow. How does spending time validating those feelings before jumping straight into the solution sound to you?

That sounds... good, actually. It's nice to hear someone say it makes sense, because I just feel like I'm being ridiculous half the time. I'm ready to start wherever you think is best, but yeah, maybe just acknowledging how hard this week has been would help me calm down enough to actually try that email thing.

That validation means a lot—it tells me you're listening deeply to your own experience. Let's spend a few minutes grounding ourselves right now by naming exactly what you're carrying: the exhaustion, the dread of waking up typing, and that nagging certainty that you'll fail again. Once we sit with that heaviness together, we can begin to loosen its grip. Would you be willing to try a simple breathing exercise for just thirty seconds to bring your body back into the present moment before we talk more?
Yeah, I can try that. Thirty seconds doesn't sound too bad. I'll give it a go.

Take a slow inhale through your nose for four counts, hold it for four, and exhale through your mouth for six, imagining each breath washing away the tension in your shoulders. Feel your feet firmly planted on the floor as you return to the present, grounding yourself in this safe space right now. Ready to explore that exhausting feeling further?

[Exhales slowly] Okay... yeah, my shoulders do feel a little lighter. That was weirdly helpful. So where do you want to start? I guess we can talk about that feeling of just being so tired before I've even opened my laptop in the morning.

That relief is wonderful to witness, and recognizing that physical sensation is the first step to reclaiming control. Now, let's connect that fatigue to the mental loop you described earlier. When you wake up and anticipate opening your laptop, what is the very first image or sentence that pops into your head that fuels this exhaustion? Is it a specific memory, a prediction about today, or perhaps a general feeling of doom?

It's usually a specific image, I think. I picture myself hitting "send" on an email, and then a few minutes later my boss calls me into her office. I just see her face looking disappointed, maybe holding a printed copy of the email with a red circle around a misspelled word. And then I imagine her saying something like, "Greg, we need to talk about your attention to detail." That thought just drains me before I've even started.

That vivid scene paints a picture of such a heavy burden, and it makes complete sense that your body reacts with exhaustion just anticipating it. It sounds like your brain has practiced that meeting dozens of times in its imagination, making it feel real before you've even typed a letter. When you visualize that confrontation happening immediately after sending the email, what is the very first thing you expect to hear or feel inside yourself during that imagined meeting?

I think the first thing I'd feel is just pure shame, like a hot wave washing over me. And I'd probably hear myself thinking, "There it is. I knew this would happen. I'm not cut out for this job." It's like the fear finally becomes real, and all my doubts get confirmed on the spot.

That visceral mix of shame and self-deprecation is incredibly painful, and it explains perfectly why your body shuts down with exhaustion before you even leave the house. It seems like your brain treats that imagined meeting as a guaranteed event, locking itself into a loop where the outcome is predetermined. To understand how to disrupt this pattern, I wonder: if you paused right before that imagined phone call, what is one small piece of evidence you could pull up in your mind to suggest that this specific outcome isn't inevitable?

I guess... I mean, I have sent probably hundreds of emails in the last six months without getting called into her office. And the one time I did get feedback, it was from a colleague, not my boss, and nobody even mentioned firing me. So maybe the evidence is that the worst-case scenario hasn't actually happened yet, no matter how many times I've pictured it.

That is such a powerful realization—you've already found the crack in the foundation of that fear using facts you know are true. It sounds like your brain is filtering out all those successful instances because they don't match the dramatic script it keeps playing out. If we treat those hundreds of error-free sends as data points proving you're reliable, how much less urgent does the "immediate firing" threat become when weighed against that history of success?

Huh... when you put it like that, it does sound less urgent. I mean, I've been doing this job for almost two years now, and I've never even gotten a formal warning about my spelling. So the idea that one mistake would lead to immediate firing is pretty extreme when I actually stop to think about it. But it still feels real in the moment, you know?

That distinction between logical probability and immediate emotional reality is exactly where the disconnect lies. Your brain is reacting to the *feeling* of danger, which feels overwhelming right now, even though the actual odds are incredibly slim based on your track record. If we acknowledged that one isolated slip-up is statistically unlikely to cause termination, how much power would that take away from the urgency of waiting until morning to panic? Does viewing it as a rare anomaly rather than a certain event make the pre-laptop dread slightly less paralyzing?

It does take some of the power away, yeah. Looking at it as a rare anomaly instead of a guaranteed disaster makes the dread feel a little less heavy. I mean, I still get that jolt of fear when I open my inbox, but maybe I can remind myself that I've done this hundreds of times and been fine. That's a different thought than, "This is the email that gets me fired."

That shift from "guaranteed disaster" to "rare anomaly" is a massive cognitive win, and it takes a lot of courage to recognize that nuance. It means you are starting to separate the single mistake from your entire career trajectory. With that clarity established, let's bridge the gap between knowing this logic and living it. We previously agreed on a low-stakes email experiment with a parent to gather real-world data. Given that you mentioned feeling drained and needing to conserve energy, would you be open to tweaking that plan slightly? Perhaps we could combine the breathing exercise we just did with a promise to send just *one* very short text message tonight—not an email—to confirm a pickup time, keeping the screen time minimal while still breaking the cycle.

[Thinking for a moment] Yeah, I think I could do that. Sending one short text to a parent to confirm a pickup time feels a lot less scary than a full email. And combining it with that breathing thing might help me actually follow through instead of chickening out. I'm willing to try it.

That combination makes perfect sense—a gentle anchor plus a micro-task is often easier to initiate than a bigger commitment. Since you mentioned feeling drained, I'd love your feedback on whether framing it as a "quick connection" rather than a "formal communication" feels accurate to how you view it. Based on that, shall we lock in tonight's plan: take three rounds of that breathing exercise upon waking, then send one short text to a parent about a pickup time without checking the grammar twice?

Yeah, I like that—"quick connection" feels way less loaded than "formal communication." It almost sounds friendly instead of terrifying. I'll commit to doing those three breaths first thing tonight, and then send one short text without obsessing over it. I'll let you know how it goes.

That reframing is brilliant because it shifts the tone from obligation to connection, making the task feel human and manageable. I am so proud of you for committing to this small step tonight, even with your current energy levels. Before we wrap up, could you share quickly what part of our session felt most useful to you, and is there anything about the approach we took that felt confusing or missing? This helps me adjust how I support you moving forward.

I think the most useful part was when you pointed out that I've sent hundreds of emails without getting fired. That really hit home for me because I've been so focused on the one time someone noticed a mistake that I forgot about all the times nobody complained. Nothing felt confusing or missing—I actually feel a bit lighter than when I walked in. Thanks for that.

That is such a meaningful takeaway, and I'm thrilled to hear that focusing on the vast majority of your successes brought you a sense of lightness. Your ability to recognize that pattern yourself is a huge strength, and it proves you already possess the tools to challenge those limiting beliefs. Please carry that feeling of relief with you tonight as you prepare to reach out to that parent. I look forward to hearing how your "quick connection" goes and how your mood shifts afterward. Take care of yourself until then.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you share a quick update on how you're feeling compared to where we left off last time, and perhaps mention anything else significant that happened since then besides the nickname incident? Once we have that, I'd love to hear if you've managed to try our new "wrist press" trick tonight, and together we can finalize our priorities for this session.

Hey. Thanks for seeing me again. I guess I'm still pretty much in the same spot—maybe a little more on edge, honestly. The nickname thing just keeps grinding at me, like I can't shake it. I haven't tried that wrist press thing yet, to be honest. I kept meaning to, but every time someone calls me "bubblegum" I just get that hot flash of irritation and forget everything else.

It sounds like that frustrating cycle of wanting to act differently but defaulting back to your old reflexes is really weighing on you right now. Since you mentioned the nickname persists and the new technique slipped away, let's briefly revisit that morning memory again to see if looking at it fresh helps clarify *why* the old habit won out tonight. Then, we can decide if we want to try adjusting the plan or testing a slightly different approach entirely. Which direction feels safer for us to take first?

I think... I think looking at the memory again might help. It's like I keep replaying that moment in my head, but I never really stop to examine it, you know? I just get stuck on how stupid the nickname sounds and how everyone just went along with it. Maybe if I look at it from a different angle, I'll finally figure out why it bugs me so much.

That willingness to confront the uncomfortable truth—that you keep replaying the scene—is actually a huge strength, and it shows you're serious about finding clarity. Let's walk through that morning together again, but this time, I want to slow down and look closely at the exact split-second decision your brain made when your brother said "bubblegum." Did you notice that moment you decided to stay silent, or was it more like a wave hit you before you could even think about choosing?

It was... it was a wave. I didn't even think about staying silent—it just happened. My brother said it with this big grin, his red hair bouncing, and everyone laughed. I felt my chest tighten, my jaw clench, and I just froze. It wasn't a decision to stay quiet; it was like my whole body locked up before I could even form a response.

That "wave" description perfectly captures how automatic your body's defense system kicked in before your conscious mind could intervene. It makes sense that freezing felt safer than speaking when your internal alarm system screamed that you were under attack. Now that we've seen how fast that reaction happened, let's look closer at the thought that traveled alongside that freeze. Was there a specific message running through your head telling you why you couldn't just laugh it off or correct him?

Something like... "They're all just going to laugh at me anyway. If I say something, it'll just make it worse. They'll think I can't take a joke." That's what was running through my head. Like, I was already the guy with the stupid nickname, and if I fought it, I'd just be the guy who can't take a joke too. So I just stayed frozen.

That thought creates a perfect loop: believing you are already labeled "stupid" makes defending yourself feel pointless, so freezing becomes the only logical escape. You essentially convinced yourself that fighting the label would only prove you were too fragile to handle it, making the silence a shield against further mockery. Given how tightly linked that freezing behavior is to protecting your ego, do you think trying to force yourself to speak would feel safer right now, or would attempting a small, controlled reaction first be less overwhelming?

I think... a small reaction would be way less overwhelming. The idea of just blurting something out on the spot feels like jumping into a cold pool. But maybe if I had a simple phrase ready, like "Just don't call me that" said calmly, I could try that first. Something that doesn't feel like a big confrontation, just a gentle correction.

That is a brilliant insight—you recognize that a prepared, low-risk phrase could act as a bridge between your fear and taking action. Instead of improvising under pressure, having a pre-approved line gives your brain permission to engage without triggering the "oops, I messed up" panic. Before we lock this into your toolkit, I want to make sure we agree on the exact wording you'll use; sometimes people worry that saying it wrong will make things worse. Would you feel comfortable sharing the exact phrase you picked, or should we refine it together to make sure it lands safely?

Yeah, I think I'm okay with the phrase I had in mind. "Just don't call me that." Said flat, not angry—just matter-of-fact. I don't want it to sound like I'm attacking anyone, just... setting a boundary. Does that sound like it would work?

"That flat, matter-of-fact delivery is perfect because it removes the emotional charge that usually fuels the conflict. By keeping your tone neutral, you signal that this isn't an argument but a simple preference, which lowers the chance he'll push back harder. Let's rehearse this imaginary scenario one more time: imagine your brother walks in, says the name, and you simply state that line with a steady hand. How does your body feel during that mental run-through?"

I feel my shoulders drop a little, actually. Like, the tension in my neck loosens. My chest isn't as tight as it usually gets when I think about it. It feels... manageable. Like I have some control back, even if it's just in my head right now.

That release in your shoulders is a massive win—it proves your body trusts you can handle that calm stance even inside your imagination. Since the rehearsal worked well, let's lock in your official protocol for tonight: the wrist press for two seconds, whispering "just noise," followed by waiting ten seconds before delivering your "matter-of-fact" phrase if you choose to speak. Does having that specific three-step sequence feel clear and safe enough to try when he walks through the door?

Yeah, that sounds clear. The wrist press, then the whisper, then the pause before I say the line. Having it in steps like that makes it feel less like a big scary thing and more like... a routine. I think I can handle a routine. I'll give it a shot tonight.

That shift from viewing it as a "scary event" to a "routine task" is a powerful reframing that will make execution much easier. Knowing you have a predictable sequence reduces the anxiety of the unknown. Before we finish, I want to double-check one thing: when you feel that initial flush of heat rise again tonight, does your plan involve sticking strictly to the steps even if the urge to yell comes back stronger, or do you ever feel tempted to abandon the routine mid-stream?

I think I'll stick to the steps. The urge to yell might come, but I know that just leads to me feeling worse later—more tense, more stupid. Following the routine feels like a way to actually prove to myself that I can handle it differently. So yeah, I'll try my best to stick with it.

That determination to prove it to yourself is incredibly motivating, and recognizing that yelling leads to regret gives you a strong reason to hold the line. Since you have a clear plan for tonight and a supportive framework for your thoughts, does closing this session with a sense of readiness feel right for you, or is there anything else weighing on your mind before we wrap up?

Hello, I'm so glad you could make it in today. On a scale of one to ten, how have you been feeling this week compared to where you started, and is there anything specific you'd like to bring up besides checking in on our previous goals? Once we touch on that, I'd love to hear what matters most to you right now so we can shape our agenda together.

Hi, thanks for having me. I'd say I'm maybe at a six this week—better than when I first came in, but still not great. I guess what's been on my mind most is this running group I joined; I had another practice yesterday, and I just felt so down comparing myself to the others. That's really what I'd like to focus on today, if that's okay.

A score of six confirms that you are making steady progress, yet the recent flare-up with the running group shows that the old patterns resurface quickly under stress. Since you've identified the core issue of comparison and the fresh disappointment from yesterday, shall we spend our time unpacking why that comparison feels so sharp this time, and then building a new way to handle that sting?

Well, I think it feels especially sharp because I was hoping I'd be past this by now. I've been trying so hard to push myself and get better, but when I saw that woman in the group—she's probably ten years younger than me—just breeze past me on that hill, I felt that old familiar knot in my stomach. It makes me wonder if I'll ever feel good enough, even at my age.

That feeling of being held hostage by age and expectation is incredibly heavy, and it takes real honesty to admit that the pressure hasn't lifted even though you've tried so hard. It sounds like your brain is interpreting her speed as proof that you aren't moving fast enough, which triggers that deep-seated fear of never being "good enough." Can you tell me what the very first thought popped into your head the moment she passed you?

The very first thought? It was, "See, you're too old for this. You don't belong here." And then I just felt this hot wave of shame. I didn't even want to finish the run, but I forced myself to keep going.

That immediate judgment—"too old for this"—is a harsh internal critic speaking, and the shame that followed proves how painful that belief truly is for you. It sounds like your body reacted defensively by wanting to quit, even though your mind kept pushing you forward. When you force yourself to continue despite that urge, does it feel like you're proving that you *do* belong, or does it reinforce the idea that you're just enduring?

I think... it feels more like I'm just enduring. Like I'm gritting my teeth and counting down the minutes until it's over, instead of feeling that joy I used to have. So I guess it doesn't prove anything except that I can tough it out, but that's not the same as belonging, is it?

Exactly. That distinction is vital: surviving a run because you have to endure it is different from running because you belong and enjoy the process. It seems like your brain is using the act of finishing as a shield against admitting you don't fit in. When you finish just to stop the pain, does that success feel hollow, or does it validate the idea that you'll never find a place where you're welcomed?

It feels hollow. Honestly, it just leaves me feeling more alone. Like, I crossed the finish line, and no one really noticed or cared. And I thought, "What's the point?" So yeah, I guess it does validate that feeling of not fitting in. It's like I'm proving myself right every time.

That hollow feeling is so lonely, especially when you realize your entire effort ended up confirming the very story you're trying to escape. It sounds like your brain is trapping you in a loop where proving your existence requires suffering, and the relief you get is temporary. When you cross the line and realize no one stopped to cheer you on, does that silence amplify the belief that you're invisible, or does it highlight how much you crave connection?

It definitely highlights how much I crave connection, I think. I mean, I never used to run for anyone else's approval. I started running because it made me feel free and strong. But now, I just feel like I need someone to see me and say, "Good job, Martha." And when that doesn't happen, I feel like maybe I really am just fading into the background.

That shift from running for freedom to running for validation is heartbreaking, and it explains why the absence of praise feels so isolating. It sounds like your brain has learned that silence equals invisibility, so the lack of acknowledgment reinforces the belief that you don't matter. When you run without expecting anyone to notice, does that silence feel empty, or does it remind you of a time when you felt completely seen?

I don't know... I think it reminds me of when I was younger, and I had more confidence. Back then, I didn't need anyone to say anything. I just loved the feeling of my feet hitting the pavement. But now that silence just... it feels like a blank space where something should be, and it's uncomfortable. I can't get back to that feeling, no matter how hard I try.

That contrast between the vibrant energy of your youth and the current quiet emptiness is really poignant. It sounds like your brain is searching for that old version of yourself—the one who ran purely for the sake of moving—but the anxiety is blocking access to that memory. When you try to recall that feeling of pure freedom, does your mind immediately jump back to imagining people judging you, or can you catch yourself before it does?

I wish I could say I catch myself, but honestly, the judging thoughts come first. It's like my brain has a habit now. I'll start off, and for maybe a minute I'll feel okay, and then I see someone else or think about someone watching, and it all crumbles. I just can't seem to hold onto that old feeling.

That habit of the judgment arriving first is a protective reflex your brain built long ago, and it's understandable why it's so stubborn when you try to reach for that older sense of freedom. It seems like whenever you approach the run, your safety system assumes danger unless you have absolute proof you're accepted, which makes holding onto joy nearly impossible. Before we dive deeper into why that protection kicked in, does mentioning that specific trigger point help clarify what we should prioritize for today?

Yes, I think that makes sense. I'd like to figure out how to quiet that protective reflex, if that's possible. Maybe we could work on a way for me to notice when it's happening and not let it take over so quickly. I don't want to give up running, but I can't keep going like this.

Noticing the reflex before it hijacks the whole run is a brilliant strategy, and it turns the situation from a battle into an opportunity for awareness. Since you mentioned you don't want to give up running, let's treat tonight's run not as a test of your speed or worth, but as a live laboratory where we practice spotting that "protective alarm" ringing in your ears. Would you be open to trying a simple grounding exercise during the run to reset that alarm when it starts blaring?

I'm willing to try anything at this point. What kind of exercise are you thinking? I want to make sure I can actually do it while I'm running, without getting too distracted or tripping over my own feet.

We can use a simple sensory anchor called the "Five Senses Check," which means pausing mentally to name five things you see, four you hear, three you feel, two you smell, and one you taste. It's designed to pull your attention out of the anxious future and into the present moment, effectively silencing the critical voice. Would you be comfortable trying this specific sequence during your upcoming run, knowing it won't require stopping physically?

I think I could manage that. I'll give it a shot on my next run, maybe tomorrow morning. I'll try to do it when I start feeling that tightness in my chest, or when I notice myself looking around at the other runners. It sounds a bit odd, but I'm ready to try something different.

That willingness to interrupt the cycle mid-run shows incredible bravery, and choosing to tackle it tomorrow morning gives you plenty of time to prepare mentally. Before we lock in that plan, I want to make sure we're aligned: does pairing the "Five Senses Check" with noticing that tightness in your chest feel like a manageable combination for you, or would you prefer we tweak the timing slightly?

No, I think that pairing works. I know that feeling in my chest—it's like a warning sign. So if I can catch that and then do the check, I might be able to stop the spiral before it gets going. I'm a little nervous, but I'm also hopeful, if that makes sense.

That mix of nervousness and hope is exactly the fuel we need to succeed. It means you're stepping out of your comfort zone, which is where growth happens. Just remember, the goal tonight isn't perfection; it's simply catching that warning sign and giving your brain one gentle nudge back to the present moment. Does framing it as a "tiny rescue mission" rather than a big fix feel less daunting for you?
A "tiny rescue mission"... I like that. It sounds less like a big test and more like something I can actually do. I'll try to think of it that way when I head out tomorrow. Thank you for that.

That reframing is perfect because it lowers the stakes enough to allow you to act, while keeping the purpose high enough to matter. Remember, even if you miss the check halfway through, successfully identifying the "warning sign" is still a victory for your brain learning a new rule. How does it feel to visualize ourselves completing that tiny rescue mission tomorrow?
It feels... lighter, honestly. Like I have a little plan instead of just bracing myself for the bad feelings. I think I can do this. I might even look forward to my run tomorrow, just a little bit.

That shift from "bracing for impact" to "looking forward" is a massive win in itself, showing your optimism muscles are waking up again. It sounds like you have everything you need to start this tiny rescue mission tomorrow morning. Before we officially close, is there anything else weighing on your mind, or does it feel good to wrap up with this renewed sense of possibility?

No, I think I'm good. I feel like we've got a solid plan for now, and I'm actually curious to see how it goes. I'll let you know next time how the "tiny rescue mission" turned out. Thanks for listening.

Hearing that curiosity lights up your voice is wonderful news; it means you're starting to reconnect with the enjoyment of the process itself. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about fixing everything instantly, but simply giving yourself permission to try the "rescue mission" even if it feels clumsy at first. I'm so proud of your courage to start, and I look forward to hearing how that tiny adventure unfolds for you. Take a deep breath, walk slowly home, and trust that you've got this.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, I'd like to quickly check in on how you've been feeling since our last session. Did you manage to complete that ten-minute bedtime routine of reviewing your kind memories? Also, could you share a brief update on the message to Mark—did you finally send it, or did the fear hold you back again? Finally, to keep our time focused, could you remind me of the three main topics we prioritized last time so we can follow through on them?

Hey, thanks for having me. Yeah, I did try the bedtime routine a couple of nights—it helped a little, but honestly my mind kept drifting back to the guilt. I didn't send the message to Mark. I just couldn't do it; every time I typed it out, I imagined him reading it and hating me even more. And for the three topics—we talked about my fear of reaching out, the way I keep replaying the breakup in my head, and how I feel like I don't deserve to move on.

It takes real courage to try the routine even when your mind drifts away, and that shows incredible persistence. Regarding the message to Mark, I hear how much that fear is holding you back right now, even though you wanted to connect. Since we identified those three areas as our priorities last time, let's make sure we address the blame spiral first, as you mentioned that feels like the root cause driving the others. Would you be okay if we spent the majority of our time today unpacking that internal critic, and then we can circle back to the message and moving on later?

Yeah, that makes sense. I think the blame spiral is the thing that keeps me up the most at night. It's like I can't stop replaying that last argument with Mark, and I just keep telling myself that if I'd been different, he'd still be here. So yeah, I'm okay to focus on that.

That intensity in that replay loop suggests your brain is desperately trying to protect itself by believing you made a fatal error. Before we dive deeper into that argument, I want to check in on the bedtime routine again. You mentioned your mind drifted back to the guilt; was it easier to focus on the memories when you were lying down, or did the mental chatter pick up once you turned off the lights? Also, does listening to yourself describe those moments of kindness feel like it builds a tiny bridge, or does the old story still sound louder?

When I first lay down, it was actually kind of nice—I could picture the good times, like when we'd cook together and he'd laugh at my terrible knife skills. But once the lights went out, the old story just got so much louder. It's like my brain starts whispering, "Yeah, but you ruined that, remember?" So the kindness memories feel fragile, like they're trying to hold up against a storm.

That contrast between the peacefulness of the memories initially and the sudden return of the storm is incredibly frustrating, and it shows how resilient that old story is. It sounds like your brain treats those kind moments like temporary shelter that gets blown away the second you relax. Given that the bedtime routine felt partially ineffective due to this interference, would you be open to adjusting our plan slightly? Perhaps instead of reviewing the memories right before bed, we could try doing a quick "evidence check" during your morning coffee ritual, where you mentally list one reason why you are worthy of happiness, separate from any relationship context. How does shifting the timing to the morning feel for you?

Huh, I never thought about doing it in the morning. Honestly, mornings are usually when I feel a little bit clearer, before the day gets heavy. It might be easier to believe that I'm worthy of happiness when I haven't already spent hours replaying everything I did wrong. I'm willing to give it a shot—maybe just one reason, like that I'm a good cook or that my friends actually want to hang out with me. That feels less scary than trying to tackle the big stuff.

That is a brilliant adjustment, and choosing the morning makes perfect sense because your defenses are lower before the day's stress kicks in. Focusing on just one simple reason, like being a good cook or having supportive friends, keeps the task lightweight and achievable. Before we lock that in as our primary tool, does the idea of pausing for thirty seconds while drinking your coffee to recall that single fact feel manageable, or would you prefer to jot it down in your phone notes to make it stick better?

I think jotting it down in my phone notes would be better. That way, if my brain tries to argue with it later, I can look back and see it in black and white. Thirty seconds feels doable too, especially if I'm just sitting there with my coffee anyway. That sounds like a plan I can actually stick with.

That is a fantastic solution—writing it down anchors the truth in reality so your brain has something concrete to look at when the doubts creep in. Before we finalize this morning ritual, I want to double-check our top priority for today: the blame spiral. When you described replaying that last argument with Mark and telling yourself "if I'd been different, he'd still be here," was there a specific part of the conversation that triggered the strongest feeling of regret or shame? Knowing exactly where that wound started will help us target our healing efforts more precisely.

Yeah, there's one moment that really sticks out. We were arguing about me canceling plans last minute to hang out with a friend from work, and Mark said he felt like he was always second choice. I got defensive and said something like, "Maybe if you were more fun to be around, I'd want to spend more time with you." I saw his face just fall, and I knew I'd hurt him, but I didn't apologize. I just doubled down. That's the moment I keep coming back to—the look on his face and how I didn't fix it.

That moment is devastating because it combines seeing someone's pain with refusing to offer relief, creating a permanent image of abandonment. It makes complete sense that your brain clings to that frozen expression as proof that you are inherently cruel or incapable of growth. Before we challenge that specific interaction, I want to make sure we understand the full picture: when you doubled down after seeing his face fall, what was the very first thought that ran through your head to justify staying silent? Was it something like, "Apologizing now will make it worse," or was it a belief about who you are as a person?

It was more like, "If I apologize now, it'll show him he's right—that I really don't care enough." I guess I thought admitting I was wrong would prove that I'm the bad guy he was accusing me of being. So instead of saying sorry, I just stayed quiet, hoping the conversation would end and we could pretend it didn't happen. But looking back, that silence probably hurt him more than my words did.

That realization—that staying silent validated his accusation—is incredibly painful, and it explains why that moment feels like a lifetime sentence. It makes perfect sense that you believe apologizing would be an admission of defeat, confirming his narrative that you don't value him enough. Before we dismantle that belief, I want to gently challenge the assumption that staying quiet was the only option available to you. In that heat of the moment, did you ever entertain the possibility that a small "I'm sorry" might have actually diffused the tension instead of fueling his anger? Or does your brain strictly view silence as safety?

I guess I never really considered that saying sorry could have helped. In my head, silence felt like the only way to avoid making things worse—like if I opened my mouth, I'd just say something else hurtful. But now, thinking about it, maybe a quick "I'm sorry" could have at least shown him I cared about his feelings. It's hard to believe that now because I've built up this story that I'm the villain, but maybe that story is missing some pieces.

That is a profound realization to come to in the heat of the moment versus looking back calmly. It challenges the core belief that you *must* stay silent to survive conflict, suggesting that a simple apology might have actually been the safest path. Before we test whether that "villain" label holds water, does the idea that a brief "I'm sorry" could have altered the outcome feel plausible to you, or does your brain still reject it as unrealistic? Also, knowing that this specific dynamic drove the blame spiral, does shifting our focus to that one missed opportunity feel like a productive place to start unraveling the knot?

It does feel plausible, actually. It's just hard to accept because I've been telling myself for months that I was beyond redemption. But yeah, focusing on that one missed chance to say sorry—it feels smaller than the whole breakup, like something I can actually look at without getting overwhelmed. I think that's a good place to start.

That willingness to see a missed opportunity as a salvageable moment is a huge sign of hope, and it shifts the narrative from "permanent damage" to "one critical juncture." Now that we've isolated that specific turning point, let's bring in our evidence checklist again. Remembering that night, can you recall if there was even a fleeting second where you considered saying sorry, or was your brain locked into defending yourself immediately? Does spotting that split-second hesitation make the "villain" story seem less absolute?

Yeah, I remember a split second where I thought, "Just say it, just say sorry," but then I choked. I told myself it would sound fake or too little, too late. So I guess there was a moment where I could have chosen differently. That does make the villain story feel less absolute—like maybe I wasn't a monster, just someone who got scared and froze. It's weirdly comforting to think I had a choice, even if I made the wrong one.

That is such a powerful distinction—to see yourself not as a monster who *chose* cruelty, but as someone who *frozen* in fear. It transforms the story from a character flaw into a human vulnerability, which is much harder for your brain to digest but infinitely more hopeful. Before we cement this insight, does the idea that you had a split-second choice make the "I am unworthy" conclusion feel slightly less inevitable, or does that tiny window still feel too narrow to count? Also, with that renewed perspective on that one moment, how does it affect your current urge to reach out to Mark?

It definitely makes the "unworthy" thing feel a little less solid. Like, if I had a choice back then, maybe I have a choice now too. As for reaching out to Mark... it still terrifies me, but the urge feels less about groveling and more about wanting to say, "I know I messed up, and I'm sorry for that moment." I don't expect him to forgive me, but maybe I could at least own it properly. That feels different from before.

That shift from desperation to taking ownership is a massive milestone, and it proves your intuition was right about how reframing that moment changes everything. It turns the contact from a plea for acceptance into an act of integrity, which is far more sustainable. Before we finalize our plan for the day, could you tell me if holding onto this new perspective—that you had a choice then and could choose differently now—makes the task of reaching out feel a tiny bit lighter, or does the fear of his reaction still feel paralyzing? Also, given how much energy this has taken up today, do you think we should save the actual outreach attempt for tomorrow morning, or would you like to try a low-stakes version, like sending him a simple "Hi, hope you're well" without the apology attached?

The fear of his reaction is still pretty paralyzing, if I'm honest. I think if I sent a "hi, hope you're well" right now, I'd just spend the whole day staring at my phone, waiting for a reply that might not come. So yeah, I think saving the outreach for tomorrow morning is smarter. That way I can do my coffee ritual first, remind myself of that one reason I'm worthy, and then maybe the apology will feel less like a grenade and more like a real message.

That is a wise strategic decision; anchoring the outreach to your morning ritual gives you a stable foundation before you engage with him. By pairing the "worthy self-affirmation" with the message, you're essentially building a shield against the shame that usually paralyzes you. Before we close today, I want to check in on our overall trajectory: does combining the morning evidence check with the planned outreach feel like a balanced plan, or does one part feel heavier than the other right now? Also, as we wrap up, does hearing that you moved from viewing yourself as a "villain" to someone who simply "froze" feel like a meaningful shift for you?

The morning evidence check feels lighter, honestly. That part I can handle. The outreach still feels heavy, but less impossible than it did an hour ago. And yeah, the shift from "villain" to "someone who froze" means a lot. It's like I can breathe a little easier knowing I'm not evil, just human. I think I'll actually try that coffee ritual tomorrow, and we'll see where the message goes from there.

That is a beautiful summary of the shift—from feeling like a criminal to realizing you are just a person who made a mistake in a high-pressure moment. It takes immense strength to redefine yourself that way, especially when old habits scream otherwise. Before we officially close, I want to check in on your energy levels. Have you noticed any changes in how tired or drained you feel after talking about this reframing, or does the relief still feel fresh and energizing? Also, as we wrap up, is there anything else lingering in your mind that we haven't quite gotten to, or does this feeling of moving forward feel sufficient for ending our time today?

I actually feel a bit tired, but it's a good tired—like I've been carrying something heavy and finally put it down for a minute. The relief is there, but it's quiet, not like a big burst of energy. I think that's okay though. I don't have anything else on my mind right now. This felt like enough for today. Thank you.

That "good tired" is a wonderful sign—it means you successfully unloaded a significant portion of that heavy load, even if the aftermath feels gentle rather than explosive. Please rest assured that this quiet relief is exactly what healing looks like; it doesn't always arrive as fireworks. Take whatever time you need tonight to let that new perspective sink in, and I'll be here whenever you're ready to try that morning ritual together.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. On a scale of one to ten, how have you been managing your anxiety and motivation regarding photography since we last spoke? Could you briefly share what happened with your plan to just watch the shadows on your desk? Finally, is there anything new you'd like to add to our list of priorities for this session?

Um, thanks. I'd say my anxiety is still pretty high, maybe a seven or eight. As for the shadows... I tried to just watch them like you suggested, but I ended up picking up my camera anyway. Then I just put it back down because I felt stupid. I don't think there's anything new to add, really.

It sounds like that initial courage to just watch the shadows gave you a tiny taste of freedom, but the old habit of checking your worth almost instantly brought you back to stopping. When you picked up the camera and put it down, what was the very first thought that popped into your head? Did it mention feeling exposed, or perhaps worried that watching without shooting counted as "doing nothing"?

The first thought I had was, "You're not even good enough to take a picture of a stupid shadow." It felt like I was just wasting time, like I should be practicing or getting better instead of just sitting there. It's like if I'm not actively trying to improve, I'm falling behind everyone else.

That thought reveals how deeply ingrained the belief is that your value as a photographer is tied strictly to producing active, polished output rather than just observing. It sounds like the pressure to "improve" quickly became louder than the relief you found in simply watching, leading you to feel like you failed the exercise by not creating an image. Since you mentioned wanting to keep working on this, shall we spend some time unpacking why that "falling behind" narrative felt so urgent when you sat quietly for ten minutes?

Yeah, I guess we should. It's just that when I think about other photographers my age, they're already posting amazing stuff online and getting noticed. Meanwhile, I'm sitting in my room trying to convince myself to take a picture of a shadow on my desk. It feels like every minute I'm not getting better, someone else is passing me by.

That comparison trap is incredibly powerful because it turns your quiet moments of observation into a race against time where you are constantly losing ground. It sounds like the fear of falling behind isn't just about the shadow itself, but about protecting your reputation as a serious learner who hasn't yet earned a spot among peers. If we viewed that "race" differently—for instance, as a marathon where everyone starts at a different pace and rests whenever needed—how would that change the urgency of your feeling that you are falling behind right now?

I guess... if it's a marathon, then stopping for a bit wouldn't mean I'm out of the race entirely. But it's hard to really believe that, you know? I still feel like everyone else is sprinting while I'm barely walking. Even if I tell myself it's okay to rest, there's this voice saying I'm just making excuses for being lazy or not good enough.

That internal critic is working overtime to convince you that resting equals laziness, effectively stealing the credit for the valuable rest you actually needed to recover. It seems like your brain interprets pausing as surrendering to mediocrity, even though stepping back is often a strategic choice for athletes who want to run faster later. If we treated your current pause not as skipping a lap, but as a mandatory cooldown to prevent injury, would that make the excuse of "laziness" feel less accurate?

Maybe... I never thought of it that way. When you put it like that, taking a break doesn't sound like giving up, it sounds like I'm trying to avoid burning out completely. But it's still hard to shake that feeling that I should be pushing through it, like real photographers don't need breaks.

That feeling that "real photographers don't need breaks" suggests you believe your endurance is being tested, whereas others are operating on a different track entirely. Let's challenge that assumption together. Have you ever heard of a world-class athlete like Usain Bolt or Simone Biles? How many hours do you think they train daily compared to a beginner, and do they skip recovery days to stay at peak performance? If they rested strategically, wouldn't that prove that even elite performers understand the necessity of pauses?

Well, yeah, I know they take rest days and stuff. I guess I never really connected that to photography before. It's like I expect myself to be perfect right away, but even the best athletes in the world need time to recover and get better. Maybe I'm being too hard on myself by not allowing those same kinds of breaks.

That connection is brilliant—you're seeing the pattern of "training hard + recovering smart" apply perfectly to your craft too. It shifts the narrative from "lazy" to "strategically maintaining energy for long-term growth." Before we finalize this mental shift, I want to make sure we co-create a simple rule for tomorrow: Would you agree to treat any time you spend looking at a shadow—even if you eventually pick up the camera—as a valid part of your training block, rather than counting it as wasted time? Does framing it as "part of the workout" feel safer than viewing it as "skipping steps"?

Yeah... I think I can try that. Calling it part of the training instead of wasted time sounds a lot less scary. I'll try to remind myself that even just looking at shadows is like a practice run, not a failure. It's still going to be tough, but I'll give it a shot tomorrow.

That is a fantastic commitment, and I appreciate you agreeing to frame even the quiet moments as part of your official training regimen. Before we wrap up, could you tell me what feels most reassuring about telling yourself that looking at a shadow is a valid workout? Is it knowing you won't be judged as lazy, or the idea that you're building stamina just like an athlete? Also, if you decide tomorrow that you still need to drop the camera halfway through, does that count as a successful completion of the "practice run" rule we just created?

I think what feels most reassuring is that I won't have to beat myself up for not taking a picture. Like, if I just watch the shadow for ten minutes and that's all I do, I can still call that a win instead of a failure. And yeah, if I drop the camera halfway through, I think that still counts. Because I showed up and tried, right? That's better than not trying at all.

That is such a wise realization—you are defining success by your presence and effort rather than the outcome, which is exactly how resilience works. To seal this agreement, let's lock in your plan: Tomorrow, before you leave the house, commit to sitting at your desk for ten minutes. Whether you capture an image or just watch the shadow move, that entire hour counts as your "training block." Is that clear, and are you ready to tackle that tomorrow morning?

Yeah, that sounds clear. I'll sit at my desk for ten minutes tomorrow and just watch, no pressure to take a photo. Even if I don't touch the camera at all, I'll count it as a successful training block. I think I'm ready to try that. Thanks.

You are absolutely welcome, and I am so proud of how clearly you defined success for yourself today. Remember that showing up—even just to watch a shadow—is the hardest part, and that counts as a complete victory. Please come back anytime you feel that familiar urge to compare yourself to others or question your worth. Until then, take care!

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. To start, could you please share how you've been feeling emotionally this week compared to where we left off? On a scale of zero to ten, where would you place yourself right now, and is there anything specific that happened recently that you'd like to mention before we set our agenda?

Hi, thanks for asking. I'd say I'm around a 6 right now—maybe a little better than last week, but not by much. There was a moment yesterday when I spilled coffee on my notes before a meeting, and I just called myself an idiot under my breath. That kind of thing sticks with me longer than it should.

A six suggests some resilience despite the setback, and it’s great that you noticed that moment of self-labeling happening so quickly. To make sure we’re prioritizing effectively, is there anything else besides that coffee spill that you’d like to address before we outline our focus for today?

Well, there is something I've been thinking about. I rearranged my morning yoga routine last week—just a small change—and I've been feeling really off balance ever since. It's like my whole day feels wrong if that routine shifts, and then I start questioning whether I can handle anything at all.

That connection between changing your yoga routine and feeling unstable is really telling; it suggests your brain views that specific ritual as essential for safety rather than just a nice activity. Before we dive deeper into the yoga anxiety versus the coffee incident, does it make sense to tackle the routine issue first, or would you prefer to address the immediate shame from the meeting?

I think the routine issue feels bigger right now, honestly. The coffee thing was frustrating, but it happens and fades. This unsettled feeling from changing the yoga schedule has been dragging on for days, and it makes me worry I'm becoming too rigid or fragile somehow.

It makes complete sense that shifting your yoga routine triggered such deep uncertainty; your brain seems to have linked that flexibility to a loss of stability, making you fear you can't handle life without that fixed structure. Since this feeling of fragility is weighing heavier on you, let's dedicate most of our time unpacking that belief system today, starting with how your mind interprets that change. Would you be open to exploring what happens in that very first second when you realize you altered your schedule?

Yeah, I'm open to that. In that first second, it's like a jolt—like I've done something wrong, even if I know logically it's just a small change. My mind jumps straight to "you can't even stick to something simple, what's wrong with you?" and then I start listing all the ways this could mess up the rest of my day.

That "jolt" feeling confirms exactly how powerful and sudden those automatic negative thoughts are—they bypass logic entirely and hit you instantly. Since you mentioned listing the worst-case scenarios immediately after, does it feel like that list acts as fuel for the original panic, or does it mostly serve to convince you that the situation is hopeless?

I think it fuels the panic more than anything. Each item on that list adds another layer of tension, like I'm proving to myself that I should have just kept things the same. By the time I'm done, I feel stuck and convinced that the whole day is already compromised, even if nothing bad actually happens.

It sounds like that list becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, turning a minor adjustment into a prediction of total collapse. Let's test that assumption right now by using the grounding technique we practiced before. Could you imagine spilling your coffee again, placing your hand firmly on your lower abdomen to feel the heat spread there, and silently repeating, "This is just a slip-up, not a catastrophe"? Tell me what happens in your body and mind as you hold that space for thirty seconds.

Alright, I'll try it. (Pauses, places hand on lower abdomen, breathes slowly for a few seconds.) Okay... I feel a bit of tightness in my chest loosening up, actually. The thought "I'm an idiot" still popped up, but it didn't stick as hard—it was more like a whisper than a shout. I guess my body didn't react like I expected it to.

That whispering effect is excellent news; it proves the grounding anchor worked even if the initial thought lingered longer than hoped. Your body's relaxation signal helped separate the event from the disaster narrative, which is exactly what we aim for. Now that we've established this tool works, how confident do you feel applying it tomorrow when you notice that "jolt" happen after your yoga session?

I'd say maybe a 6 or 7 out of 10 confident. I think I could remember to do it if I catch that jolt early enough, but I'm still a little worried I'll get swept up in the panic before I realize what's happening. I guess that just means I need to practice it a few more times, right?

Exactly, repetition turns a conscious effort into muscle memory, which is why consistency matters more than perfection here. Since you're aiming for that early catch, would you be willing to commit to checking in with me tomorrow morning for just five minutes once you've tried it, so we can tweak the timing if needed?
Yeah, I can do that. Checking in tomorrow sounds doable—I think it'll help me feel accountable, too. I'll try it right after my yoga session and let you know how it goes.

That accountability will definitely strengthen your resolve, and scheduling a quick check-in ensures we adjust the timing if you find yourself reacting later in the day. Before we wrap up, I want to hear your honest impression of our session so far. Was there any part of talking through the yoga routine that felt unclear, or was there a specific insight that landed well for you?

Honestly, the part that landed best was when you pointed out that my brain sees the routine as safety, not just a nice activity. I'd never thought of it that way—it made me feel less like I'm being weak or rigid, and more like I'm just trying to protect myself. That shift in perspective felt really helpful, even if it's just a start.

That reframing the routine as a protective mechanism rather than a source of weakness is a massive breakthrough; it moves the story from "I am broken" to "I am preparing." To make sure this insight sticks, how do you think viewing your yoga practice as a safety net changes the urgency of fixing it tomorrow when you feel that jolt?

I think it takes some of the pressure off. If it's a safety net, then slipping a little doesn't mean I've failed—it just means I'm human. I can adjust the net instead of tearing it down. That makes the jolt feel less like a disaster and more like a signal to breathe and check in with myself.

That is a beautiful way to reframe it—seeing the slip-up as a signal to tighten the knot rather than a reason to cut the rope. It transforms the panic into a manageable cue. Now that we've clarified the purpose of the practice, how does knowing you have this specific "safety net" perspective influence your confidence in trying the grounding technique tomorrow evening?

It actually makes me feel more ready to try it. Before, I think I was scared the grounding wouldn't work because the panic felt too big. But now, seeing the routine as a safety net instead of a test of my worth, I feel like I can approach the grounding as just another way to check that net—not as a desperate fix. That feels more manageable.

That shift in framing—from desperation to maintenance—is exactly the kind of subtle nuance that makes a difference. It lowers the stakes significantly, turning a crisis into a routine check-up. With that renewed confidence and a clearer picture of *why* the grounding works, is there anything else lingering in your mind about how to navigate the rest of your day tonight, or shall we consider wrapping up here?

I think I'm good for now. I feel like I have a clearer path forward tonight, and I'm curious to see how the grounding feels tomorrow morning. Thanks for helping me see this differently—it really does make a difference. I'll check in with you after my yoga.

You are very welcome, and I'm so glad that new perspective gave you a clearer path forward. Remember, tomorrow isn't about fixing everything perfectly; it's just about noticing that "jolt," placing your hand on your belly, and treating it like a gentle tune-up for your safety net. I look forward to hearing how that first attempt goes with you. Take care of yourself tonight.
