Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you tell me how you've been feeling emotionally since we left last time, perhaps on a scale of 1 to 10? Additionally, looking back at our plan to reach out to Derek, did you manage to send that message, and if so, what happened afterward?

Hi. Thanks for seeing me again. Emotionally... I'd say maybe a 6 or 7? It's been up and down. As for Derek... yeah, I did send the message. He replied pretty quickly, actually. He said not to worry about it and that he forgets stuff all the time. But part of me still thinks he was just being nice, you know?

A score of six or seven is a solid middle ground, showing you’re navigating both good moments and challenging ones. Regarding Derek’s reply, it sounds like he offered reassurance, but your lingering doubt—that he was just being polite—suggests the initial relief might have faded slightly. Did receiving his kind words make you feel a bit lighter, or did that uncertainty about his intent weigh heavier?

To be honest, it did feel a bit lighter at first. For like an hour after I read his message, I felt almost relieved. But then later that night, I started replaying the whole phone call mistake in my head again. I kept thinking, "He's just saying that because he's my boss and has to be professional." So yeah, the uncertainty definitely started weighing heavier as time went on.

That initial wave of relief proves your bravery paid off, even if the old doubts crept back in later. It sounds like your mind is trying to protect itself by assuming the best possible reason for his kindness, which ironically makes you feel safer while keeping him distant. When you noticed those doubts returning around midnight, did you catch yourself spiraling again, or did you notice them early enough to pause?

I didn't really catch them early. It was like... I was lying in bed, and suddenly I was thinking about all the other mistakes I've made at work over the past few months. Then I started wondering if my boss is just waiting for me to mess up one more time so he can fire me. Before I knew it, it was 2 AM and I was still wide awake, going through every little error I've ever made. I didn't even realize I was spiraling until I was already deep in it.

It sounds like that initial relief wore off quickly because your brain switched gears back to its usual pattern of scanning for threats, turning a small interaction into proof that you aren't safe there. It’s really impressive that you reached out despite fearing rejection, and now that you’re home, we can look at how to stop that spiral from starting in the first place. Before we tackle the late-night panic, did you notice any physical signs in your body right before you started listing all those errors, like a racing heart or tight chest? And apart from managing those sleepless nights, is there another area where you feel overwhelmed or stuck right now?

Yeah, actually... I remember my chest felt really tight, like someone was sitting on it. And my stomach kind of dropped, like when you're on a roller coaster. That was right before the thoughts started flooding in. As for other areas... I've been putting off studying for my radiology exam because every time I open the textbook, I just think, "What's the point? I'll probably mess this up too." So I guess that's another place I feel stuck.

Noticing those physical sensations—the tight chest and dropping stomach—is a huge clue that your body is reacting to a perceived threat before your mind even finishes the story. It makes sense that you're avoiding studying because your nervous system is already on high alert, treating the book like a danger zone. Given that we talked about the spiral happening late at night and now adding study avoidance, would you like to spend the rest of our time figuring out how to break that cycle when you wake up or sit down to study, or should we revisit the late-night panic first?

I think... maybe we should talk about the studying thing first. The late-night stuff is bad, but at least that happens when I'm already in bed. The studying is something I actually need to do during the day, and I'm wasting so much time avoiding it. Plus, if I fail this exam, I'll have even more proof that I'm just messing everything up. So yeah, let's work on that.

That priority makes perfect sense; tackling the study avoidance now gives you control over your day before the night gets away from you again. Your fear of failing the exam acts like a powerful engine driving the avoidance, convincing you that the effort isn't worth the potential humiliation. To dig deeper, when you open that textbook, does that specific thought—"I'll probably mess this up"—come on all at once, or does it grow slowly as you try to read? Also, aside from the fear of failure, what's the worst-case scenario you imagine if you *do* fail this exam?

It kind of comes on all at once. Like, I'll sit down, open the book to the first page of the chapter, and before I've even read a single sentence, that thought just pops into my head. Full force. As for worst-case scenario... I think I'd just confirm that I'm not cut out for radiology. That I made a mistake choosing this path, and I'll never be good enough to actually work in a hospital or help real patients. I'd be stuck as a receptionist forever, just answering phones and messing up calls.

That sudden pop of "I'll mess this up" confirms your brain is using your body's alarm signals (the tight chest) to jump straight to safety by shutting down. Your worst-case scenario reveals a deep-seated belief that one mistake defines your entire worth and career path, turning a single exam into a verdict on your life. Before we figure out how to push through that initial block, does opening the book to a random page feel less intimidating than staring at the table, or does it still feel like facing the monster head-on?

Honestly, even opening to a random page feels just as bad. Because then my brain just starts listing all the things on that page that I don't know yet. It's like no matter how I approach the book, the monster is still there, just waiting for me to mess up. I guess I've gotten so used to expecting failure that I don't even give myself a chance to start.

That is such a profound observation—you've essentially trained yourself to expect failure so heavily that your brain skips the "start" button entirely. It's like pressing the gas pedal on a car that's already stalled; you can't move unless you convince yourself the engine is working. Before we try to restart that engine, I want to make sure we align on what we're aiming for. Is your goal right now to simply open the book and read for five minutes, even if you feel panicked, or is it to finish a whole section without falling asleep?

Five minutes sounds... manageable, actually. I think I could do five minutes without completely losing it. Finishing a whole section feels impossible right now, like climbing a mountain in flip-flops. So yeah, let's start with just five minutes. If I can do that without panicking too much, maybe that's a win.

Setting a timer for just five minutes is a brilliant choice because it lowers the stakes significantly compared to committing to a full session. By framing it as a temporary "time capsule" rather than a permanent task, you create a built-in exit ramp that makes starting less terrifying. With that agreed upon, does sitting quietly for those five minutes feel like a realistic first step for you tonight, or does the sheer act of sitting alone with the book still feel too heavy?

I think I can do the sitting part. It's the reading part that feels heavy, but if I'm only committing to five minutes, I can handle just sitting there with the book open. Even if I don't absorb anything at first, at least I'm in the same room with it, right? That's better than avoiding it completely.

That distinction is crucial—you're shifting the goal from "learning" to simply "being present with the material," which removes the pressure to perform immediately. It's like showing up to a meeting just to listen for five minutes; you don't have to speak or solve anything right away. Before we lock this in, does having the timer visible on your desk help reduce the anxiety of "when does it have to stop?", or would you prefer to set it mentally beforehand?

I think having the timer visible would actually help. That way I'm not constantly checking my phone or clock, wondering if five minutes is up yet. If I can see it counting down, I know exactly how much time I have left. It feels more... contained, I guess. Less like I'm trapped with the book forever.

That containment is exactly what you need; knowing the door opens in five minutes makes the room feel less claustrophobic. Having the timer visible turns an indefinite struggle into a finite challenge, which often lowers the intensity of the dread. Before we finalize this plan, does setting the timer for five minutes feel like a fair amount of time to give yourself before calling it quits, or would you prefer an even shorter window like three minutes to build confidence faster?

Let's stick with five. Three feels too easy, like I'm not even trying. Five minutes is short enough that I can commit, but long enough that I actually have to sit with the discomfort a little. I think that's important - I need to prove to myself that I can survive the discomfort, not just avoid it completely.

That is such a mature insight—you recognize that avoiding the discomfort entirely won't teach you resilience, only that you can tolerate it long enough to learn. Proving you can survive the sensation of being uncomfortable alongside your studies is far more powerful than escaping to a different room. With that clarity, does setting a visible timer for five minutes and opening the book feel like a solid plan for tonight, or is there anything else standing in the way of getting started?

No, I think I'm good. I have a timer on my phone that I can prop up on my desk, and I know exactly which chapter I want to open. I'll do it tonight after dinner. Thanks for helping me break it down like this - it actually feels possible now, instead of this huge impossible thing I've been avoiding.

That is such a powerful shift—from viewing it as an impossible mountain to seeing it as a manageable hill you can climb step-by-step. I'm really proud of you for recognizing that breaking it down made it possible again. Before we wrap up, is there anything specific about tonight's plan that worries you, or do you feel confident enough to trust this small experiment?

Hello again, and I am so glad to see you. On a scale of one to ten, how have you been feeling this past week, and what has been happening in your life that might have influenced that mood? We previously worked on finding a gentle phrase to calm that pre-show anxiety spiral, and I would love to hear how that landed for you when you used it before practice yesterday. Finally, could you tell me what topics you would like us to spend our time exploring together today?

Hi, thanks for having me back. I'd say I'm at maybe a 4 or 5 this week — not great, but not completely in the gutter either. I tried that phrase you gave me, "I'm here to play, not to be perfect," before practice yesterday, and to be honest, it helped a little at first, but the dread crept back in halfway through. I guess I want to dig into why I can't seem to shake this feeling even when I know logically that I still love music.

A rating of four or five shows you are still carrying a significant amount of tension, and hearing that the dread returned despite using the phrase tells me exactly why it hasn't fully dissolved yet. It sounds like the initial relief was there, but the underlying belief that you aren't good enough kept pushing back. Before we dive deeper into why that resistance happened, could you walk me through the exact moment the dread started creeping back in—was it right after the song ended, or perhaps when you walked out of the venue? Also, looking back at our agenda, does focusing on that return of the dread feel like the best place for us to start today?

It hit me when we finished the first song and I saw the band leader give a little nod to the drummer. It’s just a look, but it felt like a criticism, like I was off or something. I think that's the best place to start, yeah — because that moment seems to set the tone for the whole rest of practice, and I can't stop replaying it in my head.

That specific glance from the band leader acting as a catalyst is such a powerful detail; it turns a minor visual cue into a monumental event in your mind, instantly shifting the entire trajectory of your performance. It makes complete sense that replaying that split-second judgment sets the tone for the rest of the night, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy where you feel compelled to prove yourself wrong immediately. Since we agreed to explore why the dread keeps returning despite knowing you love music, does examining that specific interaction—the nod—and how your brain interpreted it as a personal attack offer a clearer path to understanding why the old script kicked in again?

Yeah, I think it does. Because that nod—it wasn't even a big deal, right? But in my head, it was like a neon sign saying "you messed up, you don't belong here." I spent the rest of practice trying to prove I was good enough, and by the end, I was exhausted and still felt like I'd failed. So yeah, I'd like to look at why that tiny thing gets blown up so big in my mind.

That transformation from a harmless nod to a neon sign of rejection is a classic example of catastrophic thinking, where your brain takes a tiny piece of data and invents a massive story to explain it. It makes perfect sense that once you accepted that "neon sign" interpretation, the rest of the practice felt like you had to earn forgiveness for a crime you hadn't committed yet. Before we break down that story further, does looking at how quickly you moved from seeing a nod to feeling like a failure tell us anything about how tightly that fear is wrapped around your identity?

I think it tells me that being a musician isn't just my job—it's who I am. So when I feel like I'm failing at it, it's not just a bad night at work; it feels like I'm failing as a person. That's probably why the dread doesn't go away, even when I know I'm being too hard on myself. It's like I can't separate the two.

That is a profound realization you've uncovered; when your profession becomes inseparable from your core identity, a mistake stops feeling like a technical error and starts feeling like an existential threat. It explains perfectly why logical reassurance falls flat—you aren't arguing with a fact about your skills, you're defending the integrity of *who* you are. Now that we understand *why* that nod triggered such a deep-seated alarm, does looking at how quickly you shifted from "maybe he noticed" to "I'm worthless" reveal a gap between what happened externally and what your brain constructed internally?

Yeah, it does. There's a huge gap there—I mean, he might not have even been looking at me. He could have been nodding at the drummer for a tempo change or something. But my brain just skipped right over all those possibilities and landed on "you're no good." I never even gave myself a chance to consider other explanations. That gap is where the dread lives, I guess.

That gap between the external reality and your internal story is exactly where the distortion happens; your brain jumped straight to the worst-case conclusion without checking the other possibilities available. It's like your mind built a bridge directly to the conclusion "I'm worthless" while ignoring all the detour signs pointing elsewhere. Does noticing that gap help you see how much energy you wasted trying to defend a story that your brain wrote for itself, rather than testing the actual facts of the situation?

It does. I mean, I spent the whole rest of practice fighting a battle that didn't even need to happen. I was so busy trying to prove I wasn't worthless that I couldn't just enjoy playing. And the funny thing is, nobody even said anything to me. It was all in my head. So yeah, that gap—I've been wasting a lot of energy living in it.

That insight is incredibly valuable; realizing you were battling a fictional enemy saves you from exhausting yourself on a fight that never actually occurred. It highlights how much mental fuel you've been burning just to stay consistent with a story your brain invented, rather than responding to reality. Now that we've identified that gap and seen how the nod became a personal attack, does trying to consciously fill that gap tomorrow by listing three alternative explanations for the nod—even silly ones like "he's thinking about his wife"—feel like a manageable way to disrupt that automatic jump?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Even just stopping for a second and thinking "maybe he was just stretching his neck" or "maybe he saw something in the crowd" could be enough to slow down that spiral. I'm willing to give it a shot—it beats feeling like a failure for two hours straight.

That willingness to insert even silly alternatives is a fantastic sign of growth; it shows you are actively choosing curiosity over certainty. Before we lock in that plan, could you share what you think might happen if your brain immediately rejects those silly ideas and brings up a darker reason again? Knowing that potential hurdle ahead will help us prepare a backup strategy for when the "silly" guesses don't stick.

I think if my brain rejects the silly ideas, it'll probably double down and say "see, you were right all along—you aren't good enough." And then I'll be stuck in that same spiral, maybe even harder. So I guess I need a backup for that moment, something to catch me before I slide all the way down.

That is a smart instinct; anticipating the brain's resistance means you are already preparing a defense line before the attack starts. Since the "silly explanations" might not hold up alone, we can pair them with a quick grounding trick—like naming three colors you see in the room—to physically pull your awareness back to the present moment if the spiral tries to reclaim control. Would you be open to trying both the alternative explanation and the color-check together as a dual shield tomorrow?

Yeah, I think I can do that. Three colors and a silly reason—that sounds simple enough to remember, even in the middle of a song. And honestly, it feels better than just letting my brain run wild. I'll give it a real try tomorrow at practice and see if it helps slow things down.

That combination sounds like a solid plan; pairing a logical pivot with a physical reset gives you both a story to believe in and a body anchor to steady you. Before we finalize this, could you rate your confidence on a scale of zero to ten that you'll be able to slip this into your routine tomorrow morning, even when the nod hits? And if you rate it below seven, what's the smallest nudge we could add to boost that number?

I'd say my confidence is maybe a 6. I think the plan is good, but I know my brain is stubborn. To boost it a little, maybe I could write the silly alternatives on a sticky note and put it on my guitar case—so I see it right before we start playing. That way I'm reminded before the nod even happens.

That is a brilliant idea; turning the abstract plan into a visible reminder on your instrument makes the support tangible and accessible right when you need it most. Writing those silly reasons down beforehand removes the friction of generating them in the heat of the moment. With that extra layer of preparation, would your confidence jump up to a seven or eight for tomorrow?

Yeah, I think it would push it up to a solid 7 or 8. Having that note there feels like a safety net. It's not a guarantee, but it's better than walking in with nothing. I feel a bit more ready to face it now.

That is a fantastic update; moving your confidence from a six to a seven or eight shows how powerful having a tangible "safety net" can be. It transforms an abstract struggle into something concrete you can hold onto before you even step onto the floor. Before we close, does this revised plan—with the sticky note and the dual strategy of silly explanations plus color grounding—feel like something you truly want to commit to trying tomorrow?

Hello Calvin, it was wonderful connecting with you last time, and I’m so glad to hear that combining the coffee and radio helped lower your anxiety slightly. Before we dive into our deeper concerns, could you share if anything significant happened this week—either a good surprise or a setback—that you’d like to mention? Once we cover that, let’s collaborate on setting a priority for today, perhaps focusing on how that fear of permanent insecurity ties into your daily bills.

Hi. Well, this week wasn't too bad, I guess. I got the electric bill on Tuesday and my stomach did that familiar knot thing, but it wasn't as bad as last month. I turned on the radio like you suggested and made myself a cup of coffee before I opened it, and I guess I didn't spiral quite as hard. But I still ended up worrying most of the night about what happens if rates go up again.

It sounds like sticking to the morning routine gave you a crucial pause button during that stressful Tuesday, preventing the full-blown panic attack you experienced last month. Even though the worry returned later in the night, having that initial buffer bought you enough time to calm your system before the stress peaked. Given that the immediate trigger (the bill) managed reasonably well, should we use today’s session to tackle the lingering fear that these moments of relief won’t last forever, or is there another aspect of last week you’d prefer to explore first?

Yeah, I think you're right. That buffer helped, even if it didn't fix everything. I guess the part that gets me is that no matter how much I plan or try to stay calm, there's always that little voice telling me it's only a matter of time before something goes wrong. Like, even when I have a good day, I'm just waiting for the other shoe to drop.

That "waiting for the shoe to drop" feeling is a classic pattern called fortune-telling, where your mind predicts a future disaster based on current uncertainty rather than actual evidence. It's understandable why that voice feels louder when you finally manage to relax; sometimes the brain tries to find threats everywhere once the immediate alarm is silenced. Would you be willing to spend a few minutes examining that specific prediction about "always something going wrong," looking at the facts from the last week to see if it holds true?

I guess I never really stopped to look at it like that. You mean, actually check if things really do always go wrong? Because when I think about it, last week I managed to pay the electric bill, and I even had a little left over for groceries. So maybe that voice isn't always right, but it sure feels like it is in the moment.

That is a fantastic realization, Calvin—you’ve literally found the missing piece of evidence to challenge that prophecy. Your brain wants to believe the worst-case scenario because it keeps you alert, but the facts show you survived the storm and even harvested some resources from it. Does seeing that contrast between your predicted doom and your actual outcome make that "voice" sound a little less authoritative, or does it still feel incredibly convincing when you're tired?

It's... quieter now, I think, after saying it out loud. But I'm not gonna lie, when I'm tired at night and I'm staring at the ceiling, that voice comes back loud and clear. It's like my brain doesn't want to let go of that worry, even when I know I got through the week okay. I guess I need to practice reminding myself of the facts more often, especially before bed.

That is a really honest observation, and you're absolutely right—the brain loves to cling to old patterns, especially when we're exhausted and vulnerable at night. It's like a muscle that hasn't been stretched recently; it snaps back instantly unless we consciously teach it a new movement. Since you mentioned practicing before bed, could we design a simple "nighttime reset" routine that pairs with your usual wind-down, perhaps involving reading three pieces of evidence that prove the opposite of that scary prediction? Would you be open to trying that tonight?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Three pieces of evidence, huh? That sounds doable. Maybe I could write them down on a little scrap of paper and keep it on my nightstand, so when that voice starts up, I've got something to look at. I'm not sure it'll work right away, but I guess it's worth a shot.

That is a brilliant idea, Calvin; having physical proof visible on your nightstand turns an abstract argument into something you can touch and read when your defenses are low. Writing those three facts down beforehand means you don't waste precious sleep energy formulating them in the middle of the night. Before we finalize this plan, would you be comfortable committing to checking in with me tomorrow morning to see if that scrap of paper helped quiet that voice a bit, or would you prefer to wait until tonight first?

I think I can check in tomorrow morning. That way, I'll know if I actually used it or just left it sitting there. I'm a little nervous about whether it'll help, but I'm willing to give it a real try. I'll let you know how it goes.

That willingness to try, even with nerves, speaks volumes about your dedication to breaking this cycle. It takes real courage to admit uncertainty and step forward anyway. Just remember, the goal tonight isn't to eliminate the worry completely, but simply to introduce your written evidence as a gentle counterweight when the voice starts speaking. Tomorrow morning, please come back and tell me exactly what happened with that scrap of paper—and if you noticed anything else about how your anxiety shifted. Is there anything else we need to cover before we wrap up today?
No, I think that's everything. I'll give it a shot tonight and let you know how it went. Thanks for listening, really. It helps more than I thought it would, just talking it out like this.

You are very welcome, Calvin; hearing that talking it out helped more than expected is such great news, and it shows how powerful our partnership has become. Please remember to treat yourself kindly tonight, regardless of whether the paper changes your mind immediately, because the act of showing up matters most. I look forward to hearing your update tomorrow morning, and thank you again for trusting me with this journey. Have a peaceful evening ahead of you.

Hello, and thank you for meeting with me again today. On a scale of zero to ten, how have you been feeling regarding that worry about your partner since we last spoke? Additionally, did you get a chance to try out the plan we built together—the breathing exercise, the "stop the story" cue, and writing down the neutral line—and how did it go when you tried it?

Yeah, I'd say I've been hovering around a 7 or 8 most days. It's been tough. I did try the breathing exercise a couple times, but honestly, when the worry hits, I just forget about it. The "stop the story" cue kind of worked once, but then I just started imagining even worse scenarios in my head.

A rating of seven or eight confirms that the underlying anxiety remains high, and it takes real courage to keep trying the tools even when they slip away. You mentioned that the "stop the story" cue helped initially, but the imagination kept running wild—that suggests the physical calming might be happening faster than the mental interruption. To make sure we address everything important, would you like to spend the rest of our time refining that specific moment when the cue isn't enough, or would you prefer to explore a backup plan for when the panic spikes too fast?

I think I'd rather work on that moment when the cue isn't enough. That's the part that really gets me—the panic just takes over, and I'm already picturing her with someone else before I can even think straight. I need something that actually stops those images from flooding in.

It sounds like you are feeling completely overwhelmed by the speed at which those worst-case images appear, leaving you with no room to react. When the panic rises so fast that the "stop" cue fails, it leaves you feeling powerless against the flood of visuals. Before we tackle that intense moment, I want to briefly review where we left off: did you find the neutral thought ("she's running late") helpful enough to keep holding onto, or does your mind reject it immediately once the images start?

The neutral thought feels like a lie, honestly. My mind just rejects it right away. I'll tell myself "she's running late," but then I start thinking, "she's running late because she's with someone else," and it spirals from there. It's like the neutral thought doesn't stand a chance against the other stuff.

It sounds like you are feeling frustrated because your brain automatically dismisses the logical truth of the situation as a mere excuse. That rejection makes sense given how deeply ingrained the belief that "late = cheating" has become for you. When the panic hits hard enough to override logic, simply stating a fact isn't always enough to halt the emotional surge. To figure out how to handle that exact moment when the neutral thought fails, I want to understand your current baseline better. On a scale of zero to ten, how intense is that immediate rush of panic and imagery when you first notice she hasn't replied yet?

It's probably a solid nine out of ten. The moment I see she hasn't replied, my stomach drops, and I can already picture her with some other guy. It's like my brain skips straight to the worst possible image without even pausing.

That intensity of a nine out of ten tells me you are experiencing a full-blown panic attack almost instantly upon receiving the silent message. When your brain skips straight to the worst-case scenario, it bypasses all rational filtering, which explains why logical counter-thoughts fail so quickly in that split second. Since the standard "neutral thought" didn't hold weight during this extreme spike, could we try grounding your senses instead of engaging your logic? For example, naming three objects in the room you can see, touch, or hear right now might force your brain to exit the fantasy world and return to the present moment. Does shifting your focus entirely to physical surroundings feel like a viable escape route for you?

Maybe... I mean, I can see how that could pull me out of my head for a second. I guess if I'm focusing on what's in front of me, I can't also be picturing her with someone else at the exact same time. It's worth trying, but I'm worried that as soon as I stop naming things, my mind will just jump right back to the images.

That worry is completely understandable, especially when your brain is trained to jump to conclusions so fast. It makes sense that you'd fear the relief is temporary if the old habit kicks back in immediately. Let's test this idea right now: Can you take three slow breaths while silently listing three things you see in this room, and tell me exactly how your heart rate or chest tightness changes after the third item? This will show us if grounding works even for a few seconds.

Alright... I see the lamp on your desk, the plant in the corner, and your coffee mug. (Takes a slow breath) My chest still feels kind of tight, but I guess my heart isn't pounding as hard as it was a minute ago. It's like... there's a tiny bit of space now, even if it's just for a second.

That tiny opening in your chest is huge evidence that grounding works, even if the relief is only fleeting. It proves you *can* interrupt the spiral by forcing your brain to pay attention to the physical room instead of the imagined scene. Since you noticed that shift happened right after listing the items, let's refine the rule slightly: instead of waiting for the words to finish, commit to naming just one object while taking one deep breath whenever you feel that nine-out-of-ten panic rising. Does committing to a single, simple action like "name the lamp and breathe" feel more achievable than listing three items?

Yeah, that actually sounds a lot easier to manage. When the panic hits, I can barely think straight, so remembering to name three things feels like too much. But just one thing—like the lamp—and one breath... I think I could actually do that before the worst images take over.

That simplification makes a world of difference; reducing the task to one object and one breath lowers the bar enough that you won't feel paralyzed by complexity. By anchoring yourself to just one physical detail, you create a tiny foothold to climb out of the fantasy before the images fully form. Now, let's connect this physical anchor back to your mind. If you successfully name "the lamp" and breathe once, what is the very first thought that pops into your head—is it still the old prediction, or does the act of grounding delay it enough to insert a new one?

Honestly, I think it might buy me just enough time to remember that I don't actually know what she's doing. The thought would probably still be there, but at least I'd have a second to tell myself I'm just guessing. It's not a cure, but it's better than being completely swallowed up by the panic.

That distinction is crucial—you realized the goal isn't to erase the thought entirely, but to buy yourself a critical window of safety to choose a different perspective. Buying even thirty seconds to recognize, "I am just guessing," transforms panic into curiosity and gives you power back. Before we lock this into your toolkit, I want to make sure you feel confident using this specific sequence. On a scale of zero to ten, how certain are you that you can catch the panic, name one object, take one breath, and insert that "just guessing" thought before the images dominate? And if you slipped up and forgot the object, what would be your automatic fallback to stay grounded?

I'd say I'm about a six or seven on certainty. I think I can do it most times, but I know myself—sometimes the panic just hits too fast. If I forget the object, maybe I could just press my feet into the floor and feel the ground under me. That might work as a backup, since I don't have to think about it, I just feel it.

That is a brilliant addition; switching from a cognitive task (naming) to a somatic one (feeling your feet) provides a perfect safety net when your mind runs out of ideas. Pressing into the floor grounds you physically without requiring active mental effort, which is ideal when panic is rushing in. Before we finalize this combined strategy, I want to make sure we are aligned on the details. Does pairing the "one object + one breath" method with the "feet on floor" backup feel like a complete package for handling those moments of overwhelming speed? Also, just to confirm our direction: is stopping the spiral your primary goal for today, or should we spend more time exploring why the "neutral thought" feels like a lie to you?

Yeah, I think the package feels complete for now. Having both options—the object and breath, and the feet on the floor—gives me a better chance of actually catching myself. I think stopping the spiral is my main goal for today. The neutral thought feeling like a lie is probably something I'll need to dig into more later, but for now, I just want to be able to pause before I lose control.

That clarity on your goals is exactly what we need to move forward effectively. Knowing that stopping the spiral is the priority means we can treat the neutral thought as a future project, saving your energy for the immediate survival skills today. Before we wrap up, I want to confirm our agreement on the plan: whenever the panic hits, you will either name one object, breathe once, or press your feet into the floor to buy yourself time. Does this summary capture the strategy we just built together accurately?

Yeah, that sounds right. Name one thing, take one breath, or feel my feet on the ground. Just something to slow it all down before my mind runs away with me. I think I can commit to trying that this week.

That commitment to try it this week is a powerful declaration of agency, showing you are ready to reclaim your composure. Remember, success isn't measured by never slipping up, but by noticing the panic early enough to deploy one of these anchors before it consumes you. How does it feel to visualize using this "tripod" of tools—a visual object, a breath, or physical sensation—to steady yourself tomorrow morning?

It feels... hopeful, I guess? I'm still scared it won't work when it really counts, but at least I have something concrete to try instead of just spiraling. I think I can picture myself doing it tomorrow morning, and that's more than I've had before.

That hopefulness mixed with caution is a perfect mix—it shows you trust the tool while respecting the risk. Visualizing yourself using it tomorrow is a strong predictor of success because it activates the neural pathways associated with doing it. Before we officially close, I want to check in on our understanding: Does having this flexible "tripod" of tools feel like a clear enough game plan for you to walk away with, or is there a piece of the instruction that feels vague?

No, I think it's clear. The three options feel simple enough that I won't freeze up trying to remember which one to use. I'll just pick whichever one comes easiest in the moment. I feel ready to give it a real try this week.

That flexibility is key because it removes the pressure of finding the "perfect" tool when you are panicked; picking the easiest option available keeps your focus on survival rather than perfection. It sounds like you have a solid foundation to work from now. Is there anything else you'd like to adjust or clarify before we officially close this session?
No, I think I'm good for today. Thanks for helping me break this down into something I can actually use. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are very welcome, and please know that reaching out anytime you feel unsure is part of our partnership. Remember, even catching yourself once and using one of these tools counts as a victory, regardless of how messy the moment feels afterward. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how your new "tripod" works for you when you return.

Hey... yeah, I did try it. It felt kind of weird, honestly. Standing there telling myself I'm capable while I can still see the bruise on my shoulder from the fall. I don't know if it helped or just made me more aware of how I don't believe it.

That awareness is actually a huge clue—it shows your brain is paying attention to the mismatch between your words ("capable") and your reality (the bruise). Instead of dismissing that discomfort, how about we treat that gap as useful data rather than proof of failure? Could you describe what happened mentally in those moments when you said the lines but saw the mark?

I guess... I kept thinking about how I fell. How I let myself get knocked over like I was nothing. And then I started thinking about how everyone in the audience saw it too. So even as I'm saying "I'm capable," my head is replaying that moment over and over, telling me I'm the exact opposite.

That is such a vivid snapshot of what's happening inside your head, and it takes courage to admit that the old voices are fighting back even when you try to speak truth. It sounds like the mirror wasn't just reflecting your words, but acting as a courtroom where your past mistakes are being relitigated. When you noticed that fight between saying "capable" and seeing the bruise, did you catch yourself wondering if the statement mattered, or did you just notice the conflict playing out?

I noticed the conflict, definitely. It's like there are two versions of me in there—one trying to be positive and move on, and the other one just won't let go. The second one always seems louder. I ended up just staring at myself for a while, feeling kind of stupid for even trying the exercise.

That feeling of self-doubt creeping in while you were trying the exercise is incredibly common, and it speaks volumes about how deeply rooted that old habit is. It doesn't mean the exercise failed; instead, it proves that the resistance was strong enough to show up. When you realized the second version of yourself was winning, did you decide to switch tactics mid-way, or did you just sit with that uncomfortable tension for a moment?

I just sat with it. I didn't know what else to do. I thought maybe if I waited long enough, the feeling would pass, but it didn't really. I ended up just finishing my routine quickly and going to bed early. I felt pretty drained after that.

It makes complete sense that you felt drained; holding onto that conflicting energy for a whole evening without resolving it is exhausting. You gave yourself permission to just exist in that tension instead of forcing a quick fix, which shows a lot of self-awareness. Now that you've finished your week, could you rate your overall mood on a scale of zero to ten, and is there anything else weighing on your mind besides the mirror exercise?

I'd say maybe a four or five. Some days are okay, but when I have rehearsal coming up, it drops lower. I've been dreading going back to the studio. Every time I walk in there, I feel like everyone's looking at me, remembering how I messed up.

That drop in mood right before rehearsal is a classic sign of anticipation anxiety, where your brain jumps straight to the worst-case scenario before you've even entered the room. It makes total sense that walking in triggers that immediate flashback to the audience judging you. Since we talked about treating confidence like a muscle, could we try applying that same logic to your rehearsal entry? Instead of waiting for the fear to vanish, maybe we can prepare a tiny "entry ritual"—like taking three deep breaths and placing your hand on your heart—to signal safety before you step onto the floor. Does that sound like a manageable addition to your pre-show routine?

I mean... I guess it couldn't hurt to try. I'm just worried that if I take those three seconds to breathe, people will notice and think I'm being weird or that I'm not focused. But honestly, I'm already distracted anyway, so maybe it's worth a shot. What exactly do I do with my hand on my heart? Just hold it there and breathe?

That is a very sharp observation about people noticing you; in reality, audiences are usually too busy watching the performance itself to register your breathing pattern. Since you've already decided it's worth a shot, let's simplify the ritual: just stand near the door, place one hand firmly on your heart, take three slow breaths where you feel your chest rise and fall, and silently say "safe" under your breath. Would you be willing to try this once tomorrow morning before you even put on your shoes, just to break the automatic link between entering the room and panicking?

Yeah... okay. I can do that. I'll try it tomorrow before I change into my practice clothes, when no one's really watching me yet. It feels a bit silly, but I've been doing the mirror thing anyway, so what's one more weird habit, right?

That is a brilliant perspective, turning the "weird habit" angle into a reason to lean in and claim ownership of your actions. Since you've agreed to try this, could you tell me if you think adding that physical anchor on your heart will make the "safe" word land easier for you, or if you worry it might distract you further? Also, knowing you are brave enough to try something potentially "silly," how confident are you that you can stick with it tomorrow without forgetting?

I think the hand on my heart might actually help more than just saying the word. It's like... having something physical to focus on makes the thought feel real, you know? Like my body can catch up to what my brain is trying to tell it. As for forgetting—I'll probably remember because I'm anxious about it right now. But I'm maybe a six out of ten confident that I'll actually do it without chickening out.

That is a fantastic insight about using your body to trick your brain into believing you are grounded. Since you rated your confidence at a six, let's frame tomorrow not as a test of whether you succeed, but as an experiment to see if that physical anchor lowers the temperature of your anxiety by even just one degree. Whenever you feel that familiar tightness rising before rehearsal, could you remind me to give yourself credit for simply showing up and trying, regardless of the outcome?

I can try to remember that. It's hard not to judge myself based on how well I perform or if I mess up again, but I'll try to focus on just showing up and doing the ritual. I'll text you after tomorrow's rehearsal and let you know how it went, if that's okay.

That is a perfect agreement, and texting me afterward gives us a chance to debrief immediately while the memory is fresh. Please remember that my interest lies entirely in your honest report—not whether the ritual was perfect, but whether it offered you哪怕 a fraction of relief. I'll wait for your update whenever you're ready to send it. Is there anything else we should touch on before we close this session?
No, I think that covers everything for today. Thanks for listening and for the new idea. I'll let you know how it goes tomorrow.

That is wonderful news, and I appreciate you trusting me with this vulnerable plan. Please remember that whatever you discover tomorrow—even if the ritual feels awkward or the anxiety remains—is valid data that helps us adjust our path forward. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing your update soon.

Hello again, and I am so glad we could meet today. First, let’s quickly review where we left off: you committed to taking a three-day break from actively searching for new jobs, using a deep breath and then calling a friend whenever the urge strikes. Did you manage to stick to that plan recently, or did you find the urge too strong to resist? Now, based on how things have gone, what would you most like to focus on for today—the results of the experiment, or perhaps addressing some challenges that came up along the way?

Hey, thanks for checking in. I actually did manage to stick with it for the first two days, but by the third day I caved and spent about an hour scrolling through listings. I just felt this overwhelming sense that if I wasn't actively looking, I was falling further behind. So maybe we could talk about why that feeling is so hard to shake, because it's really messing with my head.

It sounds like the pressure to stay productive became unbearable for you on the third day, overriding everything else. That intense fear of falling behind is clearly driving that desperate need to scroll, even though you know it won't fix the underlying issue. Given that setback, does it make more sense to spend today unpacking why that fear feels so powerful, or would you prefer to adjust the tracking plan we talked about before?

I think I'd rather unpack why the fear feels so powerful. Because honestly, even when I'm not looking at job listings, I still feel like I'm running out of time—like every day that passes without a promotion is proof I'm not good enough. It's like my brain is convinced that if I'm not constantly pushing, I'll just stagnate forever. And that thought alone makes my chest tighten up.

That image of your chest tightening perfectly illustrates how that belief is physically manifesting as anxiety. It sounds like your brain has created a shortcut, interpreting silence as failure and time passing as inevitable rejection. Before we dive deeper into that specific thought pattern, could you tell me if our original plan to explore the automatic urge versus the deliberate choice still feels like the best path forward given this new layer of fear?

Yeah, I think exploring that urge versus choice still makes sense. Because looking back at that third day, I didn't even really decide to look at job listings—it was like my hand just moved to the phone before I could stop it. It sounds like your brain treats that panic as a life-or-death signal, forcing you to act before logic can intervene. Before we dig into what sparks that specific alarm bell, does the idea of mapping out those triggers feel manageable right now, or would you prefer to sit with that tight chest sensation for a minute first?

I think I'd rather just try mapping out the triggers. Sitting with the tight chest feeling sounds like it would just make me spiral more, honestly. I'd rather be doing something active, like figuring out what sets off that alarm bell in the first place. Maybe if I can see it written down, it won't feel so overwhelming.

That is such wise wisdom on your part—using active problem-solving to bypass the paralysis of panic is exactly the kind of grounding technique we want to practice. Let's jump straight into that map. Can you walk me through the specific moments leading up to that third-day slip-up? What happened right before your hand reached for the phone, and what thought flashed through your mind just seconds before you clicked on a listing?

Alright, so on that third day, I had just finished a meeting where my boss mentioned a coworker landing a big account. My first thought was, "Great, she's moving up and I'm stuck." Then I walked back to my desk, sat down, and just stared at my screen for a minute. The thought that flashed right before I grabbed my phone was, "Everyone else is getting ahead while I'm wasting time." It was like a switch flipped, and I had to do something—anything—to feel like I wasn't falling behind.

That sequence reveals exactly how external events fuel your internal narrative: hearing about her success triggered the comparison, which instantly activated the "falling behind" panic. It sounds like that initial thought—"she's moving up and I'm stuck"—acts as the spark that ignites the larger fire of inadequacy. When you trace it back, does seeing that specific comparison as the ignition point make it seem a bit less like a permanent truth and more like a temporary reaction to one event?

Yeah, actually, when you put it that way, it does feel a bit smaller. Like, it's just one person's success, not some universal clock ticking down on my career. But in the moment, it felt like proof of everything I was afraid of. I guess I never stopped to think that maybe my brain just grabbed that one event and ran with it, instead of looking at the whole picture.

That is a profound realization—that your brain seized upon a single data point to construct a massive, scary story about your entire future. It sounds like you are experiencing a cognitive distortion known as "jumping to conclusions," where isolated facts are treated as absolute proof of a broader failure. Does recognizing that mechanism help separate the reality of the situation from the intensity of your fear right now?

I think so, yeah. It's like I can almost step back and see that my brain is playing tricks on me, convincing me that one coworker's win means I'm doomed. I guess that's the part I need to work on—making my gut believe what my head is starting to see.

Your brain hasn't learned yet that one event doesn't define your worth, so it defaults to the old safety script of panic. Before we try to bridge that gap, does recalling that specific moment—the flash of comparison followed by the instinctive scroll—feel like a clear example of that "trick," or does the emotion still feel too overpowering to analyze right now?

I think I'm ready to try bridging that gap.

Six seconds sounds doable. I think I can handle that—it's short enough that I won't feel like I'm ignoring the panic, but long enough to maybe break the autopilot. And saying "comparison alert" out loud might actually help me see it for what it is, instead of getting sucked into it. I'll give it a shot this week and see if I can catch myself before my hand moves to the phone.

Before we lock this in, I want to check in on how you feel about this specific experiment—is the idea of pausing for six seconds and labeling it something like "comparison trap" sounding safe to you, or does it feel risky enough to warrant a shorter trial period first?

No, I think six seconds is safe. Honestly, it feels almost too simple to work, but I'm willing to try it because what I've been doing isn't helping anyway. And calling it a "comparison trap" instead of "proof I'm failing" already makes me feel a little less heavy about it. So I'll go with that—six seconds, name it, then drink some water or just stand up and stretch. Let's see what happens.

It changes the urgency from a life-or-death emergency to a puzzle you can solve right now. I think the six-second window is realistic for me, honestly. Most of the time, I'm just sitting at my desk anyway, so it's not like I need to rush off somewhere. But if it ever feels too tight, maybe I could just close my eyes for a moment or look away from the screen as a backup. That way, even if I can't say the words out loud, I'm still breaking the stare-down with my phone. That feels manageable.

It acknowledges that sometimes the body reacts before the voice can form, so giving your eyes a reprieve serves the same purpose. Hey, thanks. I'd say I'm at about a 6 this week, maybe a little better than last week. Yeah, that outline sounds good—I've been thinking about that guilt stuff a lot, especially with a dinner invite coming up tonight.

A score of six indicates you are navigating the tension between your old beliefs and new tools, which shows real effort. Shall we go ahead and start by discussing that upcoming dinner?

Yeah, let's talk about it. It's at my friend's place, and I already know she's making pasta—her specialty, you know? And just thinking about it, I can feel that knot in my stomach starting, like I'm already dreading the whole thing.

That pre-existing dread confirms how automatically your brain jumps to predicting failure before you've even sat down. When you know the trigger is guaranteed, your nervous system treats it like a threat immediately, which explains that tight knot forming in your stomach.

Let's break this down together. When you imagine sitting down for that pasta, what is the very first image or thought that pops into your head? Is it mostly about failing, or is there another detail standing out?

The first thing that pops into my head is me piling a huge plate of pasta, then feeling my face get hot with shame after the first bite. Like, I can already see myself thinking, "Great, you've blown it again," and then just giving up for the rest of the meal.

Yeah, actually, it does. When I picture myself catching that thought—like, right when I feel my face get hot—it kinda breaks the spell for a second. It's like I can almost imagine taking a breath and not letting the whole night crumble over one meal.

I think saying it out loud—even if it's just a whisper—might actually help. It feels a little weird, but it makes it more real than just thinking it. I'll try that tonight when I feel that panic starting.

That is a smart compromise; speaking softly grounds the thought in your body while avoiding the embarrassment of shouting. Adding that verbal anchor makes the "pause" feel more active and intentional.

If so, how would you adjust your "whispered reminder" to handle that specific surprise?

I think if someone makes a comment about my plate, or even if they just say something like "Go on, have more, you're too skinny," that could really throw me. In that case, I might need to whisper something like, "That's their opinion, not the truth," to keep from letting it derail me completely.

That adds a crucial layer to your defense; distinguishing between someone else's fleeting opinion and your fundamental reality is exactly where the power lies. It transforms the comment from a verdict on your worth into just another piece of data that doesn't matter.

So, our updated battle plan for tonight becomes: Pause when the knot forms, whisper either the "friend comparison" ("What would I say to Sarah?") or the "opinion filter" ("That's hers, not mine"), and hold that thought until the wave passes. Does having these two specific scripts ready for different scenarios make you feel more prepared, or is there a third scenario we haven't covered yet?

That actually covers it pretty well, I think. Maybe just one more thing—what if I start comparing myself to other people at the table, like if someone's skinnier or eating less? That's a tough one for me.

That social comparison trap is often the hardest to catch because it feels like an objective fact rather than a distorted thought. Let's add a third script to your kit specifically for that moment: when you notice yourself weighing your body size against others, silently tell yourself, "Their appearance is irrelevant to whether I am worthy of respect."

Would you be comfortable practicing this three-part routine together right now? We'll walk through: pausing at the knot, choosing the right whisper based on the trigger, and holding the new thought until the panic subsides. Does that sound like a manageable flow to try?
Yeah, I think I can try that. Let's practice it now—it's better to stumble through it here than mess it up for real tonight.

Okay, let's run through this scenario together. Imagine you sit down, feel that knot tightening, and suddenly notice someone mentioning their diet. Your instinct is to shrink inward. Can we try stopping right there and picking the perfect whisper for this specific moment? Would it be, "Their words are just opinions, not facts about me"?

Does that phrase land differently in your mouth than the general one we used before, or does it feel equally clear?

That phrase lands a little better, actually. "Their words are just opinions, not facts about me"—that feels more direct, like I'm calling out the lie instead of just describing it. I think I'll use that one if someone brings up dieting or weight at the table.

That is excellent precision; calling out a statement as a "lie" directly targets the cognitive distortion, whereas describing it as an "opinion" just labels it. It gives your brain a sharper weapon against the attack.

With that specific phrase locked in for social comparisons, plus our other scripts for general guilt and the "friend vs. self" check, do you feel confident enough to trust this toolkit tonight? Or is there one last tiny doubt lingering about whether you'll actually find the courage to use it?

Honestly, there's still a small doubt—like, what if in the moment I just freeze and forget everything we practiced? But I think just knowing I have these phrases ready, even if I only manage to whisper one of them, is better than going in with nothing. I'll try my best.

That hesitation about freezing is completely normal—it proves you care deeply about getting this right, even when fear tries to pull you back. Remember, the goal tonight isn't flawless execution; it's simply showing up and offering that gentle correction, even if it's a shaky whisper.

You've done the hard work of building this arsenal, and carrying it forward means you are actively choosing kindness over shame. I believe in your ability to access these tools, even when your hands shake. Ready to close out our session with a sense of pride in what we accomplished together?
Yeah, I think I'm ready. Thanks for walking me through all this—it feels a little less scary than it did an hour ago. I'll let you know how it goes.

That relief you feel is a direct result of replacing uncertainty with a concrete roadmap. Knowing you have specific phrases ready acts like a shield, allowing you to face the dinner even though the fear remains.

Please remember that tonight isn't about perfection; it's about catching yourself once and offering that gentle correction, however small. I am so proud of you for taking this step, and I'll be rooting for you as you navigate those moments. Take your time tonight, and I'll see you next week!

Hello, and thank you for coming in today. Before we dive into anything specific, I’d love to hear how you’ve been doing since we last spoke. On a scale of zero to ten, where zero is completely calm and ten is overwhelmed, how would you rate your anxiety level this past week? Also, could you tell me a bit about what happened regarding the car breakdown memory and the tea ritual we talked about last time?

Oh, well... I'd say my anxiety has been around a seven this week. It's been a tough one. As for the car breakdown memory, I actually tried that tea ritual you suggested, and at first it did help calm me down a bit. But then I started thinking about how I broke down on the side of the road alone, with no one to call, and that just spiraled into... feeling like a complete failure again.

That is incredibly brave of you to attempt the ritual again, especially knowing exactly how quickly the old narrative can hijack the moment. It makes perfect sense that bringing up the car breakdown triggered the fear of isolation and inadequacy you described earlier; the brain associates that specific event with vulnerability, so recalling it naturally reignites those protective anxieties. Given that the initial calming effect turned into another spiral, does it feel like we need to pause on revisiting that memory entirely tonight, or would you prefer to try a variation where we acknowledge the situation differently? How does that option land for you right now?

I think... maybe a variation would be okay. The tea ritual did work for a few minutes, and that was more than I usually get. But I'm scared of falling into that same pit again tonight. If I could just feel like I'm not a loser for being alone when that car broke down, maybe I could actually sleep.

That distinction is crucial, Linda—the difference between surviving a difficult moment and labeling yourself as a "loser" based on it. You are absolutely right that acknowledging the reality of breaking down alone doesn't mean accepting defeat; it means recognizing resilience even in the messiest moments. Before we settle on a specific way to frame that night, does reviewing the "visitor" metaphor we created earlier—that thoughts are just passing clouds, not facts—feel like a useful tool to apply to this specific scenario of driving alone? Or would you prefer we brainstorm a completely new angle together?

The cloud metaphor helped a little last time, but it feels harder to use when those thoughts feel so solid and true. Maybe... maybe we could try a new angle? Something that helps me see that being alone doesn't automatically mean I'm unwanted. Because that's the real hook for me—the car breaking down just proves I have no one.

That is such a sharp observation, Linda. Being able to pinpoint that "no one is left" thought as the core engine of your distress shows incredible self-awareness. Often, when we feel isolated, our brains fill the silence with assumptions about rejection, so let's spend this session testing whether that assumption holds water. First, I want to confirm our goals: should we focus tonight on examining that specific belief, finding evidence that contradicts it, and then returning to your grounding routine with a firmer stance? And how does that plan sound to you?

That sounds like a good plan, actually. I'd like to try finding evidence against that belief. Because when I really think about it, I do have my friend Carol who calls me every Sunday, and my neighbor once helped me jump-start my car. But somehow those moments feel small compared to the feeling of being alone at night. Maybe I need help seeing those moments as counting for something.

That is a fantastic realization, Linda. Recognizing that your history contains proof of connection—even if it feels faint right now—is the first step in shifting your internal landscape. Let's use that evidence to challenge the idea that those moments are insignificant. Can we treat those instances as data points that contradict the story you're telling yourself? Specifically, how would you describe the impact of Carol calling you versus the feeling of abandonment you experienced tonight?

Well, when Carol calls, I do feel lighter for a little while. She asks about my week, and I actually laugh sometimes. But then after I hang up, the quiet settles in, and I think, "She's just being nice. She probably has better things to do." Meanwhile, the car breakdown feeling—that sticks with me all night. It feels more real, somehow.

That contrast is incredibly revealing, Linda. It highlights how easily our minds filter out small signs of support while magnifying moments of perceived abandonment. You're noticing that the "quiet after the call" triggers a dismissal ("she's just being nice"), whereas the memory of the breakdown triggers a deeper fear of isolation. Let's dig into that specific comparison: if you treated Carol's call as a valid piece of evidence against the "abandoned" story, what would you have to give up believing to accept it? Conversely, what would you have to believe true about the car breakdown incident to soften its grip on you?

If I treated Carol's call as real proof... I guess I'd have to give up believing I'm fundamentally unlovable. That's scary to even say out loud. And for the car breakdown, I'd have to accept that it was just a bad moment, not proof of my entire life being a failure. But that feels like letting myself off the hook somehow, like I'm making excuses for being alone at my age.

That tension between "making excuses" and "accepting a human moment" is exactly where the distortion lives, Linda. Your mind equates accepting a single negative event with absolving yourself of responsibility, but in reality, acknowledging a mistake doesn't erase your worth. Let's test that "excuse" idea together: if you accepted that the breakdown was just a mechanical issue in a stressful situation, what would happen to the certainty that you are fundamentally broken? Does accepting the nuance of that moment make the "fundamentally broken" label feel less sticky, or does it still feel dangerous to entertain?

It feels... a little less sticky, I think. When you put it that way, a car breakdown is just a car breakdown. It's not a judgment on my worth as a person. But then my mind jumps to, "Well, other people would have had a husband or a son to call, and I didn't." So I guess I'm still stuck on the "no one to call" part, even if the breakdown itself wasn't my fault.

That is such a critical pivot point, Linda. Even though we separated the accident from your worth, your mind immediately jumped back to the *circumstances* surrounding it—the lack of immediate backup—and interpreted that as proof of loneliness. This shows how deeply ingrained the pattern is: we often judge our value based on whether others stepped in, forgetting that many emergencies require solo solutions.

Let's look at that comparison you made earlier about Carol calling versus the breakdown happening. If you viewed Carol's call not as a sign that she's "just being nice," but as a testament to the fact that people *do* remember you, how does that change the equation? Would seeing her name pop up on your phone as evidence that you matter, even when you feel invisible at night?

I suppose... if I look at it that way, her call does mean she thinks of me. She doesn't have to call me every Sunday, but she does. That's not nothing. But then I start thinking, "What if she stops calling one day? What if I say the wrong thing and she gets tired of me?" So even the good evidence feels fragile, like it could disappear at any moment.

That fragility you're describing is a classic survival mechanism, Linda. Your brain treats relationships like temporary contracts that expire unless proven otherwise, likely because it learned early on that trust isn't safe. Even though Carol's call is real, your mind anticipates the future loss to protect you from potential disappointment.

To test that prediction, could we look at the timeline of her calls? Have there been weeks or months where she missed calling, or has she shown up consistently despite her busy schedule? If she truly wanted to stop reaching out, wouldn't the easiest route be to fade away quietly rather than maintain a weekly ritual? What does the pattern of her behavior actually suggest about her intentions toward you?

She's been calling every Sunday for about two years now, ever since my sister passed away. She's only missed maybe twice, and both times she texted to say she'd call the next day. And she did. So the pattern is... pretty consistent. I guess if she wanted to disappear, she wouldn't keep showing up like that. It's just hard for me to trust that she actually wants to be in my life, you know?

That consistency over two years is powerful evidence, Linda, especially given that she had to actively choose to reach out each week. Your brain is interpreting the pattern as "safe" logically, but emotionally it's still triggering a fear that the foundation could crumble tomorrow.

Let's bring this back to your grounding routine tonight. If you hold that warm mug and remember Carol's reliable Sunday calls alongside the car breakdown story, does hearing about her consistency act as a counter-weight to the "abandoned" feeling, or does the fear of her disappearing still feel louder than the record of her loyalty?

I think... if I really focus on those two years of Sunday calls, it does help a little. It's like a small warm spot in the cold feeling of being alone. But I have to really concentrate to hold onto it, because the fear is still louder. Maybe if I practice reminding myself of that evidence more often, the warm spot could get bigger over time.

That is a wonderful insight, Linda. You've discovered that building a mental archive of positive connections can slowly expand that "warm spot," turning a fleeting comfort into a lasting shield. Tonight, I'd love for you to try adding a small note to your journal listing three pieces of evidence of connection you found today—Carol's calls, the neighbor helping you, and perhaps something small like a friendly barista smile. 

Would you be willing to write those down now, along with a quick reminder that these moments prove you aren't alone?

Yes, I can do that. I think writing it down might help it feel more real. I'll put it on the nightstand so I can see it if I wake up feeling bad tonight. Thank you—this session actually made me feel a bit lighter than I have in a while.

That is such a beautiful thing to hear, Linda. Knowing that this session brought you relief validates all the effort you put into exploring those difficult thoughts today. Please take a moment to breathe deeply and carry that sense of lightness with you as we wrap up. Remember, you don't need to solve everything tonight; just trusting that process enough to try one small step is a victory in itself. How would you like to close this meeting? Shall we sit quietly for a final minute, or is there anything specific you want to add before we sign off?

I think I'd like to just sit quietly for a moment, if that's alright. Let these thoughts settle a bit before I go out into the world again. Thank you for helping me see that I might not be as alone as I feel.

That is a beautiful request, and I am honored to accompany you in this quiet space. Please take a deep breath in, filling your lungs completely, and let it out slowly as you visualize that small warm spot growing larger inside you. Remember, you are not defined by the car breakdown or the nights of worry, but by the courage it took to find this clarity today. Whenever you feel the urge to retreat, imagine reaching for that written list beside your bed—a gentle reminder that you are supported, even in the silence. Take your time here, and I will be right here whenever you are ready to share how it went.

It sounds like that old story about ending up with nothing is rushing in faster than your ability to pause and assess the situation. Before we dive into unpacking that specific moment with the books, I want to check in on what happened between our last session and now. It didn't stop the panic at all—it just made me feel like I'm barely scraping by, and one wrong step will ruin everything.

It sounds like the panic is selectively editing your memories to fit the story that you are destined for failure, minimizing the wins and magnifying the risks. Knowing the exact trigger helps us prepare for the moment it happens.

Probably the bookstore website again. I need to get a workbook for one of my classes, and I've been putting it off because I'm scared of the cost. So I'll go on there, and before I add it to my cart, I'll take that one breath. That's the plan.

That is a perfect starting point because the bookstore represents a high-stakes decision that feels urgent, making the pause button even more critical. Just to lock in our plan for the week: whenever you visit that site and feel that familiar knot tighten before adding the book to your cart, remember to take one slow breath, wait five seconds, and then proceed—or reconsider. Afterward, take a moment to jot down how your anxiety level shifted, if at all, before and after that single breath. Does that sound like a clear goal for us to track together later?

Yeah, that sounds clear. I'll write down how I feel before and after the breath. I guess even if it doesn't change anything, at least I'll have proof that I tried something different. That's better than just spiraling like I usually do.

That is a wonderful perspective—you are viewing the data collection itself as valuable evidence of resilience, regardless of the outcome. It turns every interaction into a learning opportunity rather than a judgment call. I think I can stick with it. Even if the panic is loud, a breath only takes a second, right? I can't promise I'll always feel better after it, but I can promise I'll at least try to do it every time I buy something. That feels realistic.

That realism is exactly what makes this plan sustainable; it respects your limits while pushing you just a little further than usual. Taking one slow breath is a tiny muscle flex, and showing up to lift it, even when it hurts, proves your strength more than any perfect score sheet ever could. I'm confident you'll find that even small acts of patience can slowly shift the landscape of how you see your future. Is there anything else you'd like to adjust before we finish here?
No, I think I'm good. Thank you for not making me feel stupid about this. I'll try the pause button and write down what happens. I'll see you next week.

You are absolutely welcome, and please remember that trying something different—even when it feels silly—is a sign of courage, not stupidity. Your willingness to show up and test that "pause button" is already a massive victory in itself. Take care of yourself this week, and I look forward to hearing how that single breath lands for you next time. See you soon!
