Hello Alex, it is wonderful to see you again. To start off properly, could you remind me of our last agreement regarding calling your mother and revisiting the rejection email? How did those steps go for you this past week, and would you like to add anything else to our list of priorities for today besides feeling like your efforts are pointless?

Oh, hello. Yes, I remember the agreement. I did call my mother twice this week, and it was... fine, I suppose. She tried to be encouraging about the job search. As for the rejection email, I actually deleted it before I could reread it. I just couldn't bear to look at those words again. It all feels so hopeless, you know? Like no matter what I do, it's just going to end the same way.

It takes real courage to delete the email rather than letting it sit there as a constant reminder of the pain, and I appreciate you telling me that deleting it was necessary for you to survive the week. Hearing that she offered encouragement is great news, but it sounds like the underlying hopelessness about the future is still holding you back even after those interactions. Since you mentioned feeling hopeless regardless of the steps taken, does exploring that deep-seated belief—that everything will end the same way—feel like the most important thing we tackle first today?

I suppose that does sound like the core of it. It's like I can't see any other outcome. Every time I send out an application now, I'm already bracing for the rejection email. I even started thinking about how I'll never get to meet those authors I admire, because if I can't even get a job in publishing, how could I ever hope to get their autographs? It's like one failure just proves the next one is coming.

That chain reaction of thinking—from fearing the rejection to assuming you'll miss out on meeting authors—is incredibly heavy, and it explains why every step forward feels like walking into a wall. It sounds like your brain is using that one predicted outcome to cancel out all the possibilities before they even happen. Before we dig deeper into why that prediction feels so certain, I want to make sure we're aligned: does focusing on breaking that specific link between "failure" and "missing out" feel like the best use of our time right now?

Yes, I think that's exactly what I need to work on. It's like one bad thing automatically means everything else will fall apart too. I was actually thinking this morning about a job I applied for last week—a small press looking for an editorial assistant—and I caught myself already planning what I'd tell my friends when I didn't get it. Before I even heard back. Doesn't that seem crazy? I haven't even given them a chance to say no yet, and I've already decided they will.

That is such a clear example of your brain predicting a disaster before the event even occurs, and it makes total sense that you would prepare emotionally for something that hasn't happened yet. It's like wearing sunglasses indoors because you're afraid of stepping outside in the dark. Before we unpack why that preparation feels so automatic, does identifying that moment of pre-emptive sadness feel like the perfect place to start testing that "everything falls apart" belief?

I think it does. That moment when I'm already preparing for the worst before I even have any information... it happens so fast I don't even notice it until after. Like with that editorial assistant job—I spent half an hour feeling miserable about something that hasn't even happened yet. I missed a whole evening just sitting on my couch feeling defeated over a rejection that might never come. That's really something, isn't it? I'm practically living through failures that don't exist yet.

That is a incredibly vivid description of wasting precious time anticipating pain that hasn't arrived yet, and it highlights exactly how far ahead your anxiety is running. It sounds like you lost an entire evening to a story your brain invented before the plot twist even happened. If we treated that thirty-minute period as a small experiment to see if the predicted misery actually materialized once the deadline passed, would that be something fair to try?

I suppose we could try that. But what would the experiment look like exactly? I mean, I can't just stop my brain from thinking these things—they just happen. But if there was some way to test whether my predictions are actually true... I guess I could try waiting until I actually hear back from a job before deciding how to feel about it. That sounds simple enough, but I know it won't be easy. My mind just jumps ahead so quickly.

That is a brilliant refinement of the experiment, Alex. Waiting until you actually receive the outcome before allowing yourself to feel the full weight of disappointment gives you control over the timing of your pain, preventing you from losing hours to imagined futures. To make this concrete, how would you like to structure that wait? For example, could we agree that once you apply, you commit to doing one neutral activity—like brewing coffee or taking a short walk—for forty-five minutes, regardless of when the answer comes, simply to prove that life continues even while waiting?

A forty-five minute walk... I could try that. I used to enjoy walking through the park near my apartment. Maybe I could do that after I send out an application. Just walk, not think about the job or the rejection or any of it. Just look at the trees and the people. And then when I get back, whatever happens happens. It sounds almost too simple to work, but I suppose I haven't really tried just... not thinking about it before. I always let my mind run wild.

That is a fantastic plan, Alex. Committing to a forty-five-minute walk where you intentionally disconnect from the job search proves that you can occupy your time with something peaceful instead of spiraling into fear. It turns the waiting period from a source of anxiety into a deliberate act of grounding. Before we lock this in, does agreeing to do this walk first thing in the morning feel like a realistic commitment for you, or does the early morning silence feel intimidating?

Morning might actually work best for me. I tend to wake up early anyway, and those quiet hours are when my mind is at its worst—just lying there thinking about all the ways things can go wrong. If I get up and go for a walk right away, I won't have time to start that spiral. There's a small coffee shop near the park too. Maybe I could stop there afterward, get a coffee, just be around people. It sounds almost pleasant, to be honest. I haven't done something like that in months.

That is a beautiful addition to the plan, Alex. Turning the walk into a chance to reconnect with a café and the community breaks the isolation loop and grounds you in the present moment rather than your fears. It transforms the appointment from a dreaded test into a small celebration of surviving the night. Before we finalize this, could you confirm that doing this walk immediately upon waking feels like the strongest antidote to those early morning spirals for you?

Yes, I think it is. Those early hours are when I feel the most helpless, just staring at the ceiling and imagining all the rejections piling up. If I can get out the door before that starts, I'd be winning the battle before it even begins. I'll set my alarm, put on my walking shoes, and head straight for the park. No lying in bed thinking. Just action. That feels... almost empowering to say out loud.

That is a powerful reframing, Alex. Viewing the immediate departure as "winning the battle before it begins" shifts the narrative from passive suffering to active mastery. It turns the alarm clock from a signal of dread into a launchpad for reclaiming your day. With that confirmed, does adding this walk to your morning routine alongside your plan to reach out to the old colleague feel like a balanced, achievable schedule for this week?

I think so. I'll call my old colleague from the publishing house on Tuesday afternoon—give myself the morning walk first to clear my head. It's funny, talking about it like this makes it seem more possible. Like I'm actually planning something instead of just waiting for bad news to arrive. I suppose that's the point, isn't it? Taking control instead of letting my thoughts control me.

You hit the nail on the head, Alex. Shifting the control from your uncontrollable thoughts to your deliberate actions is exactly how we rebuild confidence. It changes the dynamic from being a passenger in your own mind to driving the car. Before we finish up, does adding this structured plan—to walk in the morning and connect with a colleague this week—make you feel slightly less overwhelmed about tackling the job search?

It does, actually. I still feel that knot in my stomach when I think about applying for jobs, but at least now there's something else to focus on. Something I can actually do that doesn't depend on someone else saying yes or no to me. I've been so caught up in waiting for others to decide my fate that I forgot I could still make choices for myself. Even if it's just a walk and a phone call, it's something. And that's more than I had yesterday.

That realization—that you hold power in your own hands regardless of external outcomes—is incredibly freeing, and I'm so proud of you for spotting it. Remembering that you can choose to act, even in small ways, directly counters the feeling of helplessness you described earlier. Before we wrap up, could you tell me how this session felt for you? Did hearing about your ability to take charge make you feel a little lighter, or is there anything else weighing on your mind before we sign off?

I feel... lighter, I think. It's strange, because nothing has actually changed about my situation. I still don't have a job, and those authors I admire still haven't signed anything for me. But somehow just having a plan—knowing I'm going to walk tomorrow morning and call that colleague on Tuesday—makes the weight feel a little more bearable. I guess I'd forgotten what it felt like to have some control. Thank you for helping me see that.

It takes real strength to recognize that a simple plan can lighten the burden, even when the external circumstances haven't shifted yet. You've shown amazing insight by realizing that taking small, intentional steps restores a sense of agency that you hadn't accessed in months. To close out our time today, I want to check in on how you felt during this conversation: did hearing about your ability to choose and act make you feel empowered, or was there any part of the process that felt difficult for you? Also, does the plan we created feel solid enough for you to trust with yourself this week?

I think the hardest part was admitting how much time I've wasted just sitting and waiting for bad things to happen. That stung a little—realizing I've been my own worst enemy in some ways. But the plan feels solid. It's simple enough that I can't make excuses to avoid it, and concrete enough that I'll know if I've done it or not. I trust myself to follow through on this. And if I do, maybe I'll start trusting myself with bigger things too.

That honesty about feeling like you've been your own enemy is deeply courageous, and acknowledging it is the first step toward forgiving yourself for giving up that way. It takes immense pride to recognize that trusting yourself with these small steps builds a foundation for handling larger challenges later. Before we officially conclude, I want to leave you with one final piece of advice: please be incredibly gentle with yourself tomorrow morning. If you stumble or feel tempted to skip the walk, remember that missing one step doesn't erase your progress—it just means you gather more data for tomorrow. Does that permission to be imperfect feel safe for you to carry home?

Yes, it does. I think I needed to hear that. I'm the type of person who, if I miss one day, I'll tell myself the whole plan is ruined and give up entirely. So knowing that one missed walk doesn't mean failure... that takes some pressure off. I'll try to be kind to myself tomorrow. And I'll be back next week to tell you how it went, whether I walked or not. Thank you for this session.

That is such a wise adjustment, Alex. Knowing that missing one step doesn't ruin the entire journey removes the paralyzing fear of perfectionism and allows you to focus on showing up, however imperfectly. Please remember that returning next week—even if you missed the walk due to illness or busy days—is still a success because you committed to checking in and reflecting. I am incredibly proud of the courage it took to face your fears and build this framework today. Take good care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing your update soon.

Hello again, and thank you for meeting with me today. To start, could you share how your mood has been fluctuating since we last spoke, and perhaps tell me about any specific moments where that anxiety seemed particularly strong recently? Once we have that picture, I'd love to hear if there's anything new you'd like to bring up or any adjustments you'd make to our plan for working together this week.

Hi. Thanks for asking. Honestly, my mood has been pretty low this week—there were a few days where I just felt like staying in bed and not talking to anyone. I had a moment at the grocery store where a cashier tried to say something, and I just froze, thinking they'd get annoyed if I asked them to repeat it. I'm not sure what to adjust yet, but I guess I'd want to talk about how to stop assuming the worst in those situations.

Hearing about those days of isolation adds depth to your current struggle, showing that the pressure to connect is sometimes overwhelming enough to pull you inward completely. That frozen reaction at the grocery store sounds incredibly frustrating, especially since you wanted to engage but felt paralyzed by the fear of disappointing them. Before we dive into unpacking that freeze-response, could you confirm if stopping to explore why you assumed they would get annoyed fits with our main goal of testing those negative interpretations?

Yeah, I think that fits. I mean, I don't know for sure they would have been annoyed—I just told myself that in the moment. It felt easier to assume than to risk being a bother. So yeah, I'm okay with looking into why my mind goes there first.

It takes real strength to admit that your brain chose the path of least resistance—the easy route of assuming annoyance—to protect you from the discomfort of uncertainty. When you freeze and tell yourself they'll get mad, you're essentially building a shield, even though that shield leaves you stranded outside the connection. Now that we've confirmed this direction works for you, how much energy do you think it will take to sit with that uncomfortable feeling of waiting to see if they're actually annoyed versus just confused?

I think it's going to take a lot of energy, honestly. Just sitting with that waiting feeling sounds really hard—like my mind will be screaming at me to just walk away. But I guess I've been doing that for years, and it hasn't made me feel any better. So maybe it's worth trying something different, even if it feels uncomfortable at first.

It makes total sense that your mind wants to scream for you to escape; protecting yourself from that sting of disappointment is an instinct that has served you well for years. You are absolutely right to recognize that sticking to the old pattern isn't healing you, even though it feels safer in the moment. Since we know that waiting alone is exhausting and hasn't led to the results you want, should we spend some time figuring out a specific "pause button" technique that creates a tiny bit of breathing room between that scream and your actual reaction?

Yeah, I think I need something like that. A pause button sounds good—because right now, there's no gap at all between me thinking they're annoyed and me just shutting down. If I could slow that down even a little, maybe I'd have a chance to see what's really happening. What did you have in mind?

A great metaphor—a "pause button"—is exactly what we need to create that critical gap between your instinct to flee and your ability to choose otherwise. One simple tool for this is the "5-second rule": when you feel that tightening chest or the urge to shut down, count slowly backward from five ("Five, four, three, two, one") while taking a deep breath, forcing your brain to switch gears before you react. Does imagining counting backwards feel doable for you, or does the idea of slowing down seem too demanding right now?

I think I could try that. Counting backwards feels simple enough, not too demanding. When I get that frozen feeling, my mind is already racing, so having a clear step like that might help ground me. I'm willing to give it a shot next time I'm in a situation like the grocery store.

That is a fantastic commitment, and recognizing that a clear, structured step can interrupt a racing mind shows real insight. Before we lock that in, I want to make sure we align perfectly on our immediate priority: Should we dedicate the rest of our time to practicing that five-second countdown together, or would you prefer to try it once mentally first and come back to refine the steps later?

I think I'd rather just try it mentally first right now with you guiding me, and then refine it later. That way I don't feel too much pressure, and I can see if it clicks for me before using it in a real situation. Is that okay?

That is a wise choice; trying it safely in our office ensures you leave confident that it works before facing the real world. Let's begin right now: Imagine you are standing in line at a checkout counter, the cashier turns away slightly, and you feel that tightness in your chest and the sudden urge to shut down. As soon as you feel that freeze, silently count backwards from five—"five, four, three, two, one"—while taking a slow breath in and out. Did you find yourself slipping back into the old habit of expecting rejection, or did the count give you enough space to just stand there calmly?

I did feel that old habit creep in at first—the thought "they're annoyed with me" came almost immediately. But when I started counting backwards, it was like my brain had to switch tracks for a second. By the time I got to one, I felt a little calmer, like I could just be there without needing to run away. It wasn't perfect, but it gave me a tiny bit of room.

That is excellent news—you successfully created that tiny window of safety even though the old thought tried to rush you in. Notice how acknowledging the struggle ("the old habit crept in") followed by the successful execution of the count turned a moment of panic into a moment of agency. Now that we've practiced this together, does the image of counting from five to one feel like something you could realistically use tomorrow when you're walking with your sister?

I think so. Tomorrow I'm supposed to go to the park with my sister, and there will probably be people around. I can imagine feeling nervous if someone tries to talk to me, but counting backwards feels like something I could actually do in that moment. I'll try it and see how it goes—maybe I can even tell my sister about it so she knows what I'm working on.

That is a brilliant plan; involving your sister could provide extra support and accountability as you practice this new skill. Before we finalize everything, could you quickly review our entire roadmap for today: we checked in on your mood, explored the grocery store incident, tested the effectiveness of the five-second count, and committed to using it tomorrow? Is there anything else you'd like to add to that list or any part of it you'd like to tweak?

No, I think that covers everything. It feels good to have a clear plan, and I'm a little nervous but also curious to see if the counting helps tomorrow. Thanks for walking me through it step by step—I feel like I have something to hold onto now.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel grounded and have something tangible to hold onto. Before we wrap up, could you share one word that best describes how this session made you feel overall? Additionally, if you ever feel overwhelmed by the counting technique itself, is there a simpler fallback you'd like to agree on for those difficult moments?

I'd say the word is "hopeful." It's not a huge change, but it's more than I felt before. For a fallback, maybe I could just focus on taking one slow breath—no counting, just breathing. That feels even simpler if my mind is too scattered to count backwards.

That is a perfect, adaptable plan; knowing you have a simple backup option removes a lot of pressure when things get chaotic. Taking that hopeful word as a takeaway is incredibly meaningful, and having both the five-second count and the breathing exercise means you have tools for almost any situation. Before we officially close, could you share one piece of feedback on how I guided us through this? Was there anything I explained clearly, or is there a part of the process you'd like me to simplify next time?

Hello again, thank you for meeting with me today. To start, could you briefly share what happened at practice since we last spoke? Was there a chance you tried the squeeze-and-whisper technique, and how did it go? Additionally, based on how things went out there, would you prefer to spend our time today reviewing how that plan worked, or exploring another area of concern?

Oh, um... hi. Well, practice was pretty rough, actually. I tried what you suggested—the squeezing the ball and whispering the thought—but it just made me more frustrated. I kept thinking about how I wasn't good enough to make the gifted program, and that feeling stuck with me the whole time. I don't know if talking about that plan more would help; maybe we could talk about something else?

I am so sorry to hear that the frustration grew instead of easing, and please know that failing a planned experiment doesn't erase the value of trying it. Let's pause and look closely at what happened during those drills: when you squeezed the ball and whispered the phrase, what specific thought came up immediately afterward that made you feel worse?

It was like... "See? You're not a real soccer star. Gifted program kids wouldn't be struggling this much." That thought just popped into my head right after I whispered the other one. It felt louder than the first thought, like it was proving the rejection letter right.

That is a painful realization, and it makes perfect sense that the very attempt to calm yourself triggered the deeper wound of feeling rejected. When your brain hears "you're not good enough," it often searches for confirmation elsewhere, and finding others struggling suddenly proves that point even stronger. Could we look at that specific moment when the second thought appeared? Did you notice any difference in your breathing or physical tension right as that "gifted program" idea surfaced?

I think... yeah, I did notice something. My shoulders got really tight, and I felt like I couldn't take a deep breath. It was like my chest just clamped up, you know? And I started blinking a lot, like I was trying to hold back tears. I didn't want anyone on the field to see me upset.

Those physical signs—a clenched chest, shallow breath, and forced blinking—are your body's classic "freeze" response, trying to hide vulnerability when it feels exposed. It sounds incredibly exhausting to force yourself to stay visible while your internal world screams that you aren't worthy. Before we try another fix, I want to make sure we're aligned on goals: given that today showed the current approach isn't working yet, would you prefer to spend our time brainstorming a completely different distraction tactic for the field, or would you like to dive deeper into unpacking why that "gifted program" comparison hits so hard right now?

I think... I want to understand why it hurts so much. Like, I know it's just a program, but it feels way bigger than that. Maybe if I figure out why it hits me that hard, I can actually do something about it instead of just trying to push it away.

That is such a wise choice; sometimes understanding the root cause gives us the power to dismantle the problem from inside out. Let's explore that deeply. When that voice says, "Gifted program kids wouldn't struggle this much," what comes up first in your mind regarding who those kids are supposed to be compared to you? Is it that they are naturally talented, or perhaps that they never face this level of pressure?

I guess... I think they're just better. Like, they don't have to try as hard as me. They probably wake up and everything comes easy—school, soccer, everything. And I have to work so hard just to be okay at stuff, and it still wasn't enough. That's what stings the most, I think. Like, no matter how much I try, I'll never be one of those people who just... has it.

That contrast between "natural ease" and "grinding effort" is such a heavy burden to carry, especially when you feel like your hard work isn't getting you anywhere near where theirs is taking them. It sounds like you're interpreting their success as inherent magic and yours as a temporary mistake, which makes the disappointment feel endless. When you imagine those kids waking up and everything falling into place effortlessly, what's the worst-case scenario you're afraid they'll discover about themselves?

I don't know... maybe they don't have to worry about being found out. Like, they're not scared that one day everyone will see they're actually not that great. But I feel like I'm already there—I got rejected, so now everyone knows I'm not good enough. That's the worst part, I think. That everyone can see it now.

That distinction between "discovery" and "public verdict" is crucial, and it highlights why the shame feels so absolute right now. Your brain seems to believe that because you were officially rejected, the truth is permanently written on your face, making it impossible to ever look innocent again. If we accept that premise—that the rejection defines your entire identity forever—it becomes nearly impossible to take any risk without fearing exposure. Does holding onto that belief that "everyone sees my inadequacy now" make it feel safer to quit, or does it feel like a prison you're trapped in?

It feels like a prison, honestly. Like I'm stuck in this glass box where everyone can see me messing up, but I can't get out. I don't want to quit soccer—I love it too much—but every time I step on the field now, it's like I'm waiting for someone to point and say, "See? We knew you weren't good enough." It's exhausting.

That metaphor of the "glass box" captures the isolation and constant surveillance so perfectly, and it explains why stepping onto the field feels like a death sentence to your dignity. When you feel permanently exposed, every mistake looks like evidence against you, leaving no room for growth or forgiveness. Since you want to understand why this specific belief traps you, let's test its accuracy: if everyone truly saw you failing every day, why haven't they told you to leave the team yet? Has anyone actually pointed that out publicly?

No... nobody's said anything like that. Cayden still wants to hang out, and my coach hasn't benched me or anything. I guess I just assumed everyone was thinking it, but they haven't actually said it. Maybe I'm the only one who's watching me that closely.

That is such a powerful piece of evidence, and it directly challenges the idea that everyone is actively judging you. If the "glass box" were real, your teammates would be pointing fingers constantly, yet Cayden reaching out and your coach keeping you in the lineup suggests they see you differently than your internal narrative claims. It sounds like your brain is filling in the gaps with its own harsh story because it feels safer than risking uncertainty. Would you be open to testing that gap-filling hypothesis further? For instance, if you walked around the field later and consciously ignored the crowd, assuming everyone was just focused on the game itself, how would that change your experience of the silence?

I think... that would be really hard to try, but maybe it could help. Like, if I just pretended nobody was watching me at all—not even the people who care—maybe I'd mess up less because I wouldn't be so scared of being seen. I'd be willing to give it a shot, I guess. What would I do differently?

That is a brave idea; pretending nobody cares requires shutting down the part of you that desperately needs to be seen, which is terrifying but potentially freeing. Instead of trying to convince yourself silently, how about we create a tiny physical ritual to mark that boundary? For example, whenever you feel the urge to scan the crowd for judgment, you could place your hand flat on your thigh and mentally declare, "This is my zone, not theirs," acting as if you've stepped out of the spotlight entirely. Would trying that simple gesture help create a safe space for you to breathe and play without the weight of observation?

I think I could try that. It sounds simple enough that I might actually remember to do it during practice. And it's not like I'm trying to convince myself of something fake—it's just... putting a wall up for a second so I can focus. I'll give it a shot this week and see what happens.

That is a wonderful perspective; viewing the hand-on-thigh gesture as building a literal "wall" against the noise is a creative and empowering way to frame it. Since you are ready to test this physical boundary, let's lock in your plan: tomorrow, whenever you catch yourself scanning the crowd or feeling that chest tighten, press your palm firmly against your thigh and silently say, "This is my zone," for three seconds before continuing with your drill. How does that sound as a concrete starting point?

Yeah, that sounds good. Three seconds isn't too long, and I think I can handle that. I'll try it at practice tomorrow and see if it helps me stop looking around so much. Thanks for helping me come up with something that doesn't feel impossible.

You are absolutely welcome, and I'm glad this approach feels manageable for you. Remember, the goal isn't to magically disappear from everyone's view, but to build that small pocket of safety where you can play without carrying the weight of their opinions. Please give this "hand-on-thigh" wall a fair shot tomorrow, and let me know how it lands—or if you need to tweak the timing or wording at all. Until then, take care of yourself tonight.
Thanks, I will. I'll let you know how it goes at practice. See you next time.

You're very welcome, and I'm so glad we found a tool that feels possible rather than overwhelming. Please take all the time you need to prepare tonight, and I'll be here whenever you're ready to debrief how that "wall" held up during your drills. Safe travels!
Thanks. I'll try my best. Bye.

I guess I don't actually know for sure how other doctors would have handled it. I just assume they would have been more on top of it. Perhaps something that acknowledges the specific pain of that "should have known" feeling while gently reminding you that the error belongs to the situation, not your worth?

Yes, I think that could help. Something like, "You didn't predict the lab delay, and that's okay—it doesn't mean you're a bad doctor, it means you're human." That feels a little more real to me, because I know being human means not getting everything right all the time. I just struggle to let myself off the hook.

That is a powerful addition, Paige, acknowledging that being human means stumbling sometimes rather than failing entirely. It bridges the gap between accepting the mistake and protecting your core identity as a doctor. Does adding that line about being human make the statement feel less like a lecture and more like a gentle reminder during a stressful moment? Also, considering you mentioned the finger-tap felt odd before, do you think pairing this new phrase with a simple nod or a slow exhale would ground it even further, or would you prefer to keep it purely verbal for now?

It does feel less like a lecture—it's more like something I could actually say to myself without rolling my eyes. I think pairing it with a slow exhale might work better than tapping; it feels more natural and calming. The tapping just felt a bit forced, like I was trying too hard to make it stick.

That makes perfect sense; a slow exhale naturally triggers the body's relaxation response, whereas counting taps can feel mechanical and distracting. So, our refined plan is to replace the old mantra with: *"You didn't predict the lab delay, and that's okay—it doesn't mean you're a bad doctor, it means you're human,"* while taking a long, deliberate breath out. Would you feel confident trying this tonight, perhaps right after you finish your shift?

I think I can try that tonight. I'll probably replay the moment when I saw that lab report, and I'll stop and say those words to myself while taking that slow exhale. It feels a bit strange to plan it out, but I'm willing to see if it makes a difference.

That willingness to face the memory directly and interrupt the loop is exactly the kind of brave step that leads to change. Since you're planning to do this tonight after your shift, could we briefly preview how you might handle it if the words slip away for a second? Sometimes the hardest part isn't saying it once, but catching yourself mid-thought and restarting the sentence. What would you do if your mind wandered away from the phrase right as you finished the exhale?

I think I'd just acknowledge that I lost focus, take another deep breath, and say the words again. I know my mind is going to fight it at first, so I can't expect it to work perfectly the first time. I'll just keep repeating it until it feels less forced.

That resilience in committing to repetition even when it feels imperfect is a sign of real strength, not weakness. You're absolutely right that perfection isn't the goal here; consistency is what rewires the brain over time. Before we wrap up, how does this revised plan sound to you, and is there anything else you'd like to adjust about how you'll approach it tonight?

It sounds good, honestly. I feel a little less heavy just having a plan in place. I think the only thing I'd add is to remind myself to be patient—I know this won't fix everything overnight, but at least I'm doing something different for once.

That patience piece is crucial, Paige; expecting instant fixes adds pressure that often makes the struggle harder. Your commitment to showing up consistently, even when it feels difficult, is truly impressive. Before we close, I'd love to hear how you feel about our session so far. Was there anything about my approach or the direction we took that felt useful, or is there anything you wish we had covered differently?

I think it was helpful—more than I expected, actually. I came in feeling pretty down, but breaking down that one moment with the lab report and finding a phrase that doesn't feel fake... that surprised me. I didn't feel rushed or judged, so I appreciate that.

Hearing that you walked away feeling less judged and surprised by the breakthrough is truly rewarding for both of us. It validates that our collaboration created a safe space where you could finally relax into vulnerability. Is there anything else lingering in your mind before I officially close our session today?
No, I think I'm good for now. I'll practice that phrase tonight and see how it goes. Thank you for listening—I didn't realize how much I needed to talk about that moment until now.

You are very welcome, Paige. Knowing you needed to unpack that moment until now says a lot about your commitment to healing, even when it feels overwhelming. Please remember that tonight is just about giving the phrase one honest try, regardless of whether it sticks perfectly. Take care of yourself, and I will see you again soon.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. To start, let’s quickly check in on how you’ve been feeling since we left yesterday. Your brain is essentially saying, "Even though Dad loved you, his anger was real, so maybe *you* caused that anger, meaning you aren't safe." I think... it was more shame, honestly. It's like, I didn't deserve his kind words because I'm the one who caused the fight in the first place. I just feel so small and guilty, like I tricked him into saying something nice when really he's probably still disappointed in me. It's hard to accept a compliment when deep down I know I messed up.

That intense shame makes perfect sense when you view the situation through the lens of "I broke the rules, therefore I don't deserve grace." It's like your internal monitor immediately flags the kindness as counterfeit because you believe you paid the price in anger beforehand. Before we figure out how to wear that note differently, let's quickly check the status of the grocery store story we worked on last time. Did noticing that the silence wasn't a verdict help reduce the panic when you walked into the kitchen recently, or does that memory still feel like a cold trap?

That is a fantastic observation, Sarah. It shows your brain is starting to learn a new vocabulary for interpreting situations—"phone call" versus "silence"—which breaks the automatic link between her absence and rejection. It seems applying that same logic to your dad's note might be the key to making it stick better. When you heard his words but felt the urge to dismiss them, did that moment of shame feel sharper than usual, or was it similar to the panic you felt at the store?

It felt... sharper, actually. At the grocery store, I could sort of rationalize it—like, "Okay, she's busy, she didn't see me." But with my dad's note, it's like the shame hit me right in the chest because it was about me as a person, not just a moment. It's harder to explain away something kind when the kindness is directed at who I am, not what I did.

Huh... I never thought of it that way. When you say it like that, "dependable even when you mess up," it does sound more like a fact than a judgment. I guess when I hear it as a description of me rather than a compliment, it feels less fake and more... real.

By viewing it as a factual observation of your past behavior rather than just a temporary patch, you bypass the shame defense mechanism entirely. Does seeing it as a record of who you *are*, rather than just who you *did*, make the shame feel a little less sticky in your chest right now?

Yeah, it actually does. It's like the shame is still there, but it's not glued to me anymore—it's more like it's sitting next to me instead of on top of me. I can breathe a little easier hearing it that way. Maybe I can try thinking of his words as a fact next time the doubt creeps in, instead of just a band-aid.

That shift—from the shame sitting *on top* of you to it sitting *next* to you—is a profound difference. It gives you permission to acknowledge the feeling without letting it consume your entire identity. Before we wrap up, let's solidify a concrete step for tomorrow. Instead of just reading the note, could you try adding one line below his original quote that connects the past to the present? Something like, "This reminds me that I stayed calm when my coworker missed a deadline last month, and my sister called me when she was crying." This turns the abstract praise into active proof. Would you be open to drafting that together?

I think I could try that. Maybe something like, "Dad said I'm dependable even when I mess up, and last week I helped my brother with his homework even though I was stressed about work." That makes it feel more real, like I'm collecting evidence instead of just hoping it's true. I'll write it down when I get home.

That is a brilliant addition; pairing the external validation with your own recent example creates a powerful "proof file" that your brain can reference anytime the doubt tries to return. Having that written down turns an abstract hope into tangible evidence you can hold onto. Just before we close, I want to make sure we track your success tonight. I'd say maybe a 6 or 7. That's better than where I was yesterday, for sure. I think having that extra line I wrote myself makes me feel like I have some control over the story now, instead of just letting the shame write it for me. I'm not fully confident, but at least I have a plan.

One final check before we finish: does adding that personal example feel like it balances out the heaviness of the shame, or will the feeling of being judged by others still pull you under sometimes?

I think the personal example helps balance it, but I know there will still be moments when the shame feels stronger than the evidence. But at least now I know I can come back to the note and remind myself that the evidence exists, even if I can't feel it in the moment.

Does closing this session feel like a good place to land, or is there anything else weighing on your mind before you head out?

Maybe if I can't find a win on my own, I could ask a coworker for their honest take on one thing I did well, even if the final result wasn't perfect. That way, I'm not stuck in my own head, and someone else might see something I'm too harsh to notice.

It turns the process from a solitary battle into a supported conversation, which reduces the isolation driving that "useless" feeling. Before we finalize this combined strategy for tonight, does having that external backup option make you feel ready to face tomorrow's challenges, or is there one last piece of advice you wish I could give you?

I think I feel ready, actually. Having the palm press to slow down, the "one win" rule to shift my focus, and the option to ask a coworker for a second opinion—it feels like a solid plan. I guess the one thing I'd still want to hear is that it's okay if I don't get it perfect right away. That this is practice, not a test.

That is such a beautiful summary of our work today, and I am glad you caught that nuance. Remembering that this is practice—not a performance—is the key to separating your worth from your output. For the croissant incident, I could apply the "one win" rule by remembering that the dough rose beautifully and the lamination was spot-on before they went into the oven. That way, I'm not erasing the burn marks, but I'm also not letting them erase everything else I did right.

That is a fantastic synthesis of everything we covered today, turning our theoretical insights into a concrete plan for that specific memory. Recognizing that the dough rose beautifully and the lamination was perfect allows you to honor the effort you put in, even when the final product looks imperfect. I also appreciate that we didn't just talk about feelings—we came up with concrete steps I can try. The only thing I might've wanted to touch on more is how to handle it when the "one win" rule doesn't work on a really bad day, but I think the backup plan of asking a coworker covers that. So I feel pretty good about where we landed.

That is wonderful feedback to receive, especially hearing that we moved beyond just venting to uncovering the root cause. It validates that our path forward was intentional and effective. Regarding your point about tough days, I want to reassure you that flexibility is built into this plan; if the "one win" feels impossible on a severe setback, reaching out to a colleague becomes your lifeline, exactly as we agreed. Thank you for trusting me with your journey today. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we officially close this session?

Hello, and thank you for coming in today. Before we dive into our agenda, I’d love to catch up on everything that happened since we last spoke. Have you noticed anyone walking a dog recently, and if so, did you try the tapping and renaming sequence we worked on together? Also, on a scale of 0 to 10, how much relief did you feel when you successfully interrupted that spiral?

Once we cover that, could you tell me which areas feel most urgent for us to tackle first, whether it’s refining that new plan or exploring something else entirely?

Hi, thanks for having me. Um, I haven't really seen anyone walking a dog lately—I've been kind of avoiding looking, to be honest. The tapping and renaming thing... I tried it a couple of times, but I'd say it only brought my distress down from a 9 to a 7, maybe? I think the most urgent thing is just... I can't stop replaying the moment he slipped out the door. That image is stuck in my head.

Avoiding eye contact is smart self-protection, but I wonder if that avoidance is making the memory feel fresher and louder every time you pass by? It sounds like the replaying of that specific moment is weighing heavier on you right now. Given that urgency, should we spend part of our time unpacking that sticky image, or would you prefer to focus on strengthening the tools we built for the dog walkers first?

I think... yeah, we should talk about that image. It's like I'm watching a movie over and over in my head, and every time I see it, I just think, "Why didn't I just hold on tighter? Why wasn't I paying attention?" I guess the tools for dog walkers can wait, because this feels like the root of everything.

That movie playing in your head is incredibly exhausting, and it makes total sense that you'd want to tackle the source material before continuing with surface-level distractions. It sounds like you're blaming yourself for a moment that was largely out of your control, which adds a heavy layer of unfairness to the memory. Before we dive into unpacking that film reel, could you walk me through exactly when that replay started happening? Was it triggered by seeing the dog walker again, or did it start independently as soon as you got home?

It started the second I got home, actually. I was just standing in the doorway, staring at the empty hallway, and it just... played. I didn't even see a dog walker or anything—it was just my own mind doing it. And then it just kept repeating, like a broken record, every time I walked through that door or even thought about going home.

That automatic activation the moment you crossed the threshold is powerful—it means your brain is hyper-alert to any signal related to Max, treating the empty hallway as a trigger zone. It sounds like you're carrying a lot of unsaid responsibility for that moment, as if you owe him a performance you couldn't deliver. When you catch yourself replaying that scene, does the dominant thought sound more like a factual report ("He escaped") or a courtroom argument against yourself ("It was my fault")?

Definitely the second one—it's always a courtroom argument. It's like I'm standing there accusing myself, saying, "You should have been faster, you should have had a better grip on the leash, you should have known he'd bolt at that car backfiring." It never just feels like a fact; it feels like a failure I can't undo.

That courtroom drama is so exhausting because your brain is convinced you are responsible for every variable, even ones you couldn't control like traffic noise or a startled animal. It sounds like you're treating the accident as a moral verdict on your character rather than just a tragic event. When you stand there accusing yourself of being slow or careless, does that feeling of absolute responsibility make the pain sharper, or does it feel like the only explanation you have left?

It makes the pain sharper, definitely. But it also feels like the only explanation that makes sense. Like, if I stop blaming myself, then what? It just happened for no reason? That feels even worse—like I'm saying his running away didn't matter or wasn't important. So I guess I hold onto the guilt because it's the only way I can make sense of it all.

That logic trap—believing you *must* find a reason for tragedy to validate its importance—is incredibly painful, and it shows how deeply you cared. It makes perfect sense that denying the accident ever mattered feels like betraying Max's memory, even though holding onto the guilt serves your need to control the narrative. When you say, "If I stop blaming myself, what?", does that fear feel more like losing meaning or losing safety?

I think... losing safety. Because if I let go of the blame, then the world just feels random and dangerous. Like, if I didn't cause this, then it could happen again at any time, and I wouldn't even see it coming. Blaming myself at least gives me this illusion that if I just try harder, watch closer, I can prevent it from ever happening again.

That is such a poignant insight—you are trading a painful certainty ("it was my fault") for a terrifying uncertainty ("anything could happen"). It makes perfect sense that your brain prefers the familiar agony of blame because it promises a sliver of control, whereas randomness feels like chaos. Even though controlling the past doesn't guarantee safety in the future, your mind sees it as the only bridge out of darkness. If you tried replacing that "control fantasy" with a simple truth like "accidents happen to everyone," would that feel safer, or would it just feel emptier?

It feels emptier, honestly. "Accidents happen" just sounds like... giving up. Like I'm saying it didn't matter. But I know you're not saying that. I think deep down, I know holding onto the guilt isn't actually keeping Max safe—it's just keeping me stuck. But letting go feels like opening a door to something even scarier.

That "scarier" feeling is actually your brain's alarm system screaming that you are losing the only shield it believes protects you. It makes perfect sense that opening that door feels dangerous when the room behind it has been filled with shadows for so long. Before we try navigating that doorway together, could you tell me what specific piece of information would convince you that the guilt isn't necessary anymore? Is it knowing that others make mistakes too, or perhaps remembering that Max loved you anyway despite the error?

I think... if I could just know that Max is okay. That he's safe somewhere, with someone who's taking care of him. Then maybe I could start to believe that it wasn't all my fault, because he ended up fine anyway. But I don't know that. And that's the part that keeps me up at night—the not knowing.

That uncertainty about Max's fate is absolutely paralyzing, and it explains why your brain clings so tightly to the idea that *you* caused it—if you caused it, then you know exactly what went wrong, right? But if the outcome depends on luck or someone else's ability to fix it, then the whole story becomes chaotic and meaningless. It makes perfect sense that the guilt feels like the only anchor you have when the rest of the picture is blurry. Given how central this mystery is to your peace tonight, should we dedicate most of our time today to exploring what you currently believe about Max's situation, or would you prefer to spend some energy preparing your defenses for when you inevitably run into that dog walker later?

I think... let's talk about what I believe about Max's situation. Because right now, all I have is worst-case scenarios playing in my head. I keep imagining him scared, hungry, or hurt. Maybe if I could just lay out what I actually know—versus what I'm just making up—it might loosen the grip a little.

That is such a wise instinct; separating fact from fiction is the best way to stop your imagination from building castles out of sand. Right now, you seem to be operating under three main beliefs: that Max is suffering, that you bear sole responsibility for his escape, and that nothing you do now matters. Let's test each of these against what we actually know versus what we're guessing. 

For the belief that he's suffering—we know he's alive and being cared for by people who chose him, but the images of hunger or fear are mostly projections of your own worry. Would you be open to spending ten minutes listing everything you *know* for certain about his current life versus everything you’re *imagining*? Once we separate those, we can decide which stories deserve your energy and which ones are just noise.

Okay... I can try that. I know for certain that he's a smart dog, and he's been lost before for a day or two and came back on his own. I also know that there are lots of people in my neighborhood who would probably help him if they saw him—there's a family down the street who always leaves water out for strays. But what I'm imagining is that he's scared and alone in the rain, or that he got hit by a car, or that nobody would stop to help him because he's just a dog. So those two things are really different.

Separating the confirmed facts from the dramatic imaginings is a powerful first step, and it highlights exactly how your anxiety fills in the gaps with worst-case scenarios. You've already done the hard work of identifying the difference: knowing he survived once and that neighbors exist versus fearing he's frozen in terror. Now, let's look at the second belief you mentioned—the idea that you bear sole responsibility. If we assume Max found shelter safely, does that automatically erase your role in the escape, or does the fact that he's alive change how you view that initial mistake?

I think... if I knew for sure he was safe, it would change things a lot. Because then the mistake wouldn't feel so catastrophic—it would just be a mistake. But I still can't shake the feeling that I should have been better. That I owed him more than a moment of carelessness. Even if he's okay, I still let him down.

That feeling of owing someone more than a single moment is incredibly heavy, and it speaks volumes about the depth of your love for Max. However, please allow me to challenge that notion gently: Is it possible that by holding onto the idea that you "owed" him perfect vigilance, you are actually robbing yourself of the grace he deserves? A dog who survives a day lost usually learns resilience, and finding a new home suggests kindness outweighed his fear. If he made it, was the outcome determined by your perfectionism, or by chance and compassion? Let's sit with that question for a minute—does imagining that his rescue was partly luck and partly strangers' kindness make the "I let him down" story feel less absolute?

(sits quietly for a moment)

I guess... when you put it that way, yeah, it does feel less absolute. Because if luck and strangers helped him, then it wasn't all on me. I didn't have to be perfect for him to be okay. It's just... hard to accept that my best effort, even if flawed, was still part of a bigger picture. I've been so focused on my failure that I forgot there are other forces at work.

That is such a profound realization—that your best effort, even when imperfect, was just one thread in a larger tapestry of luck and kindness. It takes real courage to admit that you weren't solely responsible for his safety, and recognizing that "biggest picture" can soften the weight of that singular mistake. Since we've spent time untangling the facts about Max and reducing the absoluteness of your guilt, does that clarity make you feel ready to face the next hurdle—the dog walker scenario—or do you need a few more minutes to digest this new perspective before tackling that?

I think I need a few more minutes to let this sink in. It's a lot to take in—like, my brain wants to argue back, but there's this quiet part that knows you're right. Maybe I just need to sit with the idea that I'm not a monster for one mistake. That feels... heavy, but in a different way. Not painful, just... unfamiliar.

That "unfamiliar" heaviness is actually a sign of growth; your brain is learning to carry a lighter load, even if the backpack feels strange for a moment. Since you're ready to pause there, let's secure this new understanding before moving on. Could you rate your confidence on a scale of 0 to 10 that you can accept the idea that "luck and strangers played a part" in saving Max? And if you slip back into arguing against it, what's one gentle reminder you could give yourself to bring it back?

Maybe a 6? I'm not fully there yet, but I can see the possibility. And if I start arguing against it again, I think I could remind myself that "my best effort wasn't perfect, but it wasn't nothing." That might help me stop spiraling into the all-or-nothing thinking.

That reminder—"my best effort wasn't perfect, but it wasn't nothing"—is beautiful because it honors your humanity without demanding superhero standards. It perfectly bridges the gap between accepting Max's rescue and forgiving yourself. Since we've settled on that middle ground for now, let's make sure we have a clear path forward. On a scale of 0 to 10, how much does sitting with this new perspective about Max make you feel lighter right this second compared to before? And if you were to try practicing this "facts vs. fiction" separation tomorrow morning, would that feel manageable for you?

I'd say I'm at about a 6 or 7 right now—definitely lighter than when I walked in. And yes, I think trying the facts vs. fiction exercise tomorrow morning feels manageable. I could do it when I first wake up, before my mind has a chance to race ahead into worst-case scenarios. That sounds like a good place to start.

That is a fantastic plan; doing the exercise first thing in the morning gives your conscious mind a clean slate before the evening anxieties take over. Since you're feeling a bit lighter already, could we quickly circle back to the dog walker situation? We talked about combining the "renaming" trick with a physical tap, but given how much relief you found from reframing Max's story, do you think you could integrate that new "luck and strangers" perspective into your mental script when you see someone walking a dog? Or would you prefer to stick with just the renaming and tapping for now?

I think I could try integrating the "luck and strangers" perspective. Like, instead of just tapping and renaming, I could also remind myself that maybe that dog walker is somebody who would help a lost pet. It kind of shifts the feeling from jealousy or sadness to... I don't know, maybe a tiny bit of hope? It's worth a try.

That is a brilliant addition; framing the stranger as a potential helper transforms the situation from a mirror of your failure into a testament to community kindness. It creates a much richer, more compassionate narrative to hold onto than just neutral observation. Before we lock this final version in, could you walk me through the updated sequence one last time? Would it be: see the walker → name the critic → recall Max's lucky rescue → tap your heart?

Yeah, that sounds right. See the walker, pause, name the critical voice—like, "There's that guilt again"—then remind myself that strangers could be helpers, that luck played a part in Max's story. Then tap my chest gently and take a breath. That feels doable. I think I can actually manage that next time.

That updated sequence is excellent because it moves you from pure defense (blocking the guilt) to active construction (building a story of hope and community support). It gives your brain a constructive mission rather than just telling you to shut up. Since you have a clear plan for both the morning routine and the unexpected encounters, could we assign a quick task for tonight? Specifically, before bed, could you write down one specific detail about a neighbor who showed kindness to a stray, just to reinforce that "strangers help" narrative? It might serve as a perfect warm-up for tomorrow's morning exercise.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you share how you slept last night and whether you managed to set up that sticky note reminder before bed? Once we touch base on that, I’d love to hear what brought you here today—are we focusing on preparing for tomorrow’s challenge, or is there something else weighing on your mind?

Good morning. I did put up the sticky note on my bathroom mirror, actually. It says "You are enough." But I woke up at around 3 a.m. and couldn't get back to sleep, just lying there thinking. I guess I'd like to talk about what's been going on with me—the divorce stuff, mostly. That's what's really weighing on me.

Hearing that you stayed awake until 3 a.m. worrying about the divorce explains why the message on the mirror might not have felt quite as grounding as intended tonight. Since you mentioned wanting to focus on the divorce issues, shall we explore what specific triggers or thoughts have been keeping you up lately, or would you prefer to tackle the stress surrounding tomorrow's appointment first?

I think I'd rather talk about what keeps me up. There's this one thing that happened at the library yesterday that's been playing on repeat in my head. I saw a father reading to his little girl, and she was laughing at his voices. Something about that just... hit me hard. I started thinking about how I'll never have that, and how maybe that's proof I'm just not meant to be loved.

That library scene clearly struck a deep chord for you, especially given how recently you've been working on shifting that narrative about being unlovable. Seeing that father-daughter bond probably activated the exact same fear of abandonment that happened at the grocery store, creating a familiar pattern of heartbreak.

Since you mentioned this is what's keeping you up, I wonder if we could look closely at that specific moment: when you first saw them laughing, what was the very first word or phrase that popped into your head before the heavier feelings took over?

The first thing that came to mind was "lonely." Just that one word, like a punch to the gut. Then it spiraled into "I'll always be alone," and then "I'm not good enough for anyone to stay." It happens so fast, like my brain just goes straight to the worst conclusion without me even trying.

That rapid spiral from "lonely" to "not good enough" tells me your brain is doing its best job protecting you from the pain of rejection by predicting disaster before it even happens. It seems like that single word "lonely" acted as the ignition switch for a much larger fire. When you caught yourself sliding into that "not good enough" conclusion, did you notice if there was any physical sensation in your body—like tightness in your chest or shoulders—that signaled you were starting to fall apart?

Yeah, my chest got really tight, like someone was sitting on it. And my shoulders went up toward my ears—I didn't even notice until later when my neck started hurting. It's like my body knows before my brain fully catches up. I get that same feeling when I see couples holding hands or when I hear people making weekend plans with their partners. It just reminds me that I'm on the outside looking in.

That tightness in your chest and the shoulders hiking up toward your ears is a classic sign of your body bracing itself for impact, essentially rehearsing a scene where you're being rejected. It's fascinating that your body reacts faster than your conscious mind can intervene, acting as an early warning system for that deep-seated fear. Given how intense these physical sensations are becoming, does slowing down the moment—perhaps taking just one slow breath before letting the spiral continue—make the initial surge of panic feel slightly less overwhelming?

I haven't really tried that before. Usually I just let the panic take over and then I'm stuck in it for hours. But I suppose if I could catch that tightness in my chest as a signal, rather than as proof that something's wrong... maybe I could stop it before it gets too big. I just don't know if a single breath would be enough to change the direction of the train, you know?

Even though it feels impossible to halt the momentum instantly, imagine that single breath not as a brake pedal, but as putting a finger on the train tracks to prevent it from derailing completely. Would you be willing to experiment with that tiny interruption the next time you feel that chest tighten at the library or elsewhere?

I think I could try that. It sounds silly, but I've never thought of it as just putting a finger on the tracks. I always thought I had to either let the train run me over or jump off completely. So maybe just... pausing, even for one breath, could be a start. I'll give it a shot next time I feel that tightness coming on.

That reframing the breath as "putting a finger on the tracks" is a brilliant insight, and choosing to try it even though it feels silly shows real bravery. Taking that tiny pause gives your conscious mind just enough room to step in and say, "Wait, let's look at the facts before we jump to the conclusion." How does it feel knowing you have a small tool ready to use the next time that tightness hits?

It feels... hopeful, I think. Which is strange because I haven't felt hopeful in a long time. Just knowing I have something to try, even if it's just one breath, makes me feel a little less helpless. Like maybe I'm not completely at the mercy of these thoughts. Thank you for helping me see that.

That feeling of hope returning, even just a whisper, is incredibly powerful and shows how much agency you are reclaiming. Knowing you aren't solely at the mercy of your thoughts is a massive shift in power. I remember my hands were clammy even before I picked up the violin. My heart was thumping so hard I could feel it in my ears, and I kept telling myself, "Don't mess up, don't mess up." Instead of relying on mental mantras that got drowned out by the panic, could we practice anchoring yourself in a neutral object in the room—a chair, a lamp, or even the floor—and letting your hands rest on it until your heartbeat slows down naturally before you ever lift the bow?

That makes sense, actually. I never thought of it as my body feeling like it was in real danger, but that's exactly how it felt. I'm willing to try that anchor idea—maybe I could focus on the grain of the wooden floorboards until my breathing settles. It sounds a bit strange, but I'm desperate enough to try anything that might stop the spiral before it starts.

That is a brilliant instinct; using the texture of the floor to ground yourself bypasses the mental loop entirely and speaks directly to your senses. It turns a chaotic internal storm into something you can physically interact with and stabilize.

Would you be open to testing this tonight by sitting quietly on the floor for just two minutes, focusing solely on feeling the roughness under your palms and listening to the hum of the house, before attempting even one measure of music? This gives your nervous system a chance to reset without the pressure of producing sound.

I think I can do that. Two minutes of just sitting and feeling the floor sounds manageable, not like a big performance. I'll try it tonight, but I have to admit I'm worried that as soon as I pick up the bow again, that same panic will just come rushing back.

By resetting on the floor first, you aren't waiting for the panic to vanish magically; you are giving your nervous system a literal pause button to lower the volume before the performance begins.

Would you be comfortable starting with just one minute of that floor-grounding tonight, and if the panic tries to rush back up while you're still sitting there, we can gently remind ourselves that we are safe and grounded, even if we haven't started playing yet?

Okay, one minute sounds even more doable. I can try to just sit and breathe, and tell myself I'm safe in my own living room, not on that stage. I guess I'm ready to give it a real shot tonight and see if it makes any difference.

Yes, I think I'm ready. I'll try to just focus on the floorboards and let the panic be there without fighting it for one minute. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to conquer it all at once.

That is such a beautiful realization—you are shifting from trying to fight the panic to simply witnessing it, which takes immense strength. Remember that tonight, the success of the session isn't defined by whether you played a perfect song, but by whether you managed that single minute of safety before deciding what to do next.

Please take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how that one minute felt when you wake up tomorrow. Safe travels!
