Hello Tyler, thank you for joining us today. To kick things off, could we spend just a couple of minutes doing a quick mood check and reviewing any changes since we last spoke? On a scale of one to ten, how have you been feeling lately, and is there anything new you'd like to add to our agenda besides the feedback we tackled last time?

Hey, thanks. I guess I'd put myself at about a 5 or 6 this week. I did go out and take some photos a few days ago, but after looking at them later, I just felt that familiar wave of doubt again. I don't think there's anything new to add—still mostly struggling with feeling like my work isn't good enough.

A score of five or six indicates a slight lift from yesterday's low point, especially considering you managed to shoot new photos despite the lingering doubts. That shows real resilience, but I hear that familiar wave of doubt hitting you again after viewing them. Since our last session focused on identifying that voice as your own inner critic and creating a mantra to interrupt it, I wonder if we should adjust today's priority to testing whether using that phrase successfully stopped the spiral this time, or perhaps diving deeper into why the doubt returned immediately after seeing the images? Which direction feels most urgent for you right now?

I think the second one, about why the doubt came back. I did try using that phrase, "I'm learning, not failing," but it felt hollow when I actually saw the photos. It's like my brain just ignores it and focuses on every little flaw instead. So I'd rather figure out why that happens, because the mantra doesn't seem to stick.

That honesty about the mantra feeling "hollow" is incredibly valuable data, and it tells me we need to dig deeper into why your brain bypassed that message when visual evidence appeared. It suggests the issue isn't just the phrase itself, but perhaps how your eyes scan the image versus how your ears hear words. Before we explore that mechanism, could we quickly confirm our agenda for today? Should we spend most of our time investigating why the visual feedback overrides the verbal reassurance, and then we'll decide together if we need to tweak the mantra or introduce a different tool?

Yeah, that sounds good. I'm ready to look into why my eyes seem to win over everything else when I'm reviewing my work. It's like I can tell myself all the right things, but the second I see a slightly blurry edge or a weird shadow, that's all my brain cares about. Let's figure out what's going on there.

That distinction between hearing words and seeing images is fascinating, and it highlights a very common pattern where visual perfectionism overrides verbal reassurance. It sounds like your brain treats the blur as immediate physical damage, making the abstract phrase feel distant or irrelevant. To start unraveling this, could you describe exactly what you were noticing visually in that specific photo that triggered the "failing" thought? Was it a technical detail like focus, or something more subtle like lighting?

It was mostly the focus, I think. There was this shot of a streetlamp against a foggy sky, and the edges of the lamp just weren't sharp. The rest of the photo had this nice soft mood, but my eyes went straight to that softness on the lamp and I just thought, "That's not professional. That's a mistake." I couldn't even see the fog or the colors anymore—just that one blurry part.

That is such a vivid picture of how your eyes act like searchlights hunting for errors, effectively blinding you to the rest of the scene. It sounds like your brain treated that single blurry edge as a structural failure, forcing you to ignore the beautiful atmosphere surrounding it. When you narrowed your view down to just that one flaw, did you notice any specific internal story popping up instantly, like "this ruins the whole picture," or was it more of a cold calculation about your skills?

It was more like a gut feeling, not really a full thought. It just hit me all at once — "this isn't good enough." Like a cold weight in my chest. And then I started mentally scanning the whole photo for other problems, like my brain was trying to confirm that initial feeling. It was like I was looking for proof that it was a failure, not looking at the photo for what it was.

That "cold weight" you described is a powerful physical manifestation of shame, and your brain immediately launched into a search for confirmation to make that feeling feel real. It sounds like once that initial judgment landed, your eyes automatically turned into a scanner looking for supporting evidence, ignoring the rest of the image entirely. Since we know the mantra didn't stop this cycle, does wondering *how* your eyes bypass logic and jump straight to that "not good enough" conclusion give you a clue about why the verbal fix didn't work?

I think it's because the mantra feels like it comes from outside me, you know? Like someone else telling me I'm okay. But that feeling in my chest, and the way my eyes go straight to the flaw—that feels like it's coming from somewhere deeper, like it *is* me. So the words just bounce off, because they don't feel as real as that gut reaction. The visual proof just seems way more convincing than anything I can say to myself.

That distinction between the "outside voice" and the "deep gut feeling" reveals exactly why the mantra felt hollow—it wasn't addressing the source of the distress. Your brain prioritizes visceral sensations and visual patterns over logical reassurances because the latter feels disconnected from your core identity. It makes sense that when you see the blur, your internal alarm system fires faster than your conscious mind can speak. Given that insight, do you think focusing on separating the *image* from your *worth* might be a better angle than trying to convince yourself verbally? Perhaps treating the blurry lamp as just a piece of paper rather than a reflection of your character?

Yeah, that actually clicks for me. The blurry lamp doesn't mean I'm a bad person or a failure—it's just a technical thing in one photo. But I think I've been treating every small flaw like it's a verdict on who I am as a photographer. If I could somehow see the photo as just an object, not a mirror of my worth, maybe I could breathe a little. I just don't know how to make that switch stick when the doubt hits.

That separation between the "object" (the photo) and the "mirror" (your worth) is a brilliant insight, and it directly addresses why the mantra bounced off—you were trying to convince the mirror that the reflection was good, but the mirror was showing you cracks anyway. To make that switch stick, we might need a small ritual to remind your brain you are looking at a piece of paper, not a personality report. Before we design that ritual, does the idea of physically stepping back or covering part of the screen to disrupt that intense focus sound appealing, or would you prefer a different kind of interruption?

I like the idea of covering part of the screen. Sometimes when I'm editing, I zoom in too close and get lost in tiny details. If I could physically block out the flaw and force myself to see the whole image first, maybe that would slow down that spiral. I think that could work as a starting point—a way to remind my eyes that there's more to the photo than just one blurry edge.

That is a fantastic practical solution; physically altering your view forces your brain to engage a different area of processing than staring straight at the imperfection. Before we commit to this, I want to make sure we align perfectly on the steps. Could you imagine covering half the screen with your hand, deliberately blocking that blurry lamp, and then slowly expanding your gaze until the entire frame looks balanced again? Does that sequence feel manageable for you right now?

Yeah, I can imagine doing that. It feels a bit awkward at first, like I'm cheating or ignoring the problem. But I think that's exactly the point—I need to stop treating the flaw like it's the only thing that matters. So yeah, I'm willing to try covering part of the screen and then slowly taking it in. It might feel weird, but it's better than the usual spiral.

That willingness to treat the act as "cheating" initially is actually a sign of growth—it shows you're aware that perfectionism demands 100% visibility, and you're choosing a strategic lie to save your sanity. To make this habit stick, how does it feel to visualize holding that hand up as a protective shield, physically creating distance between your eyes and the harsh judgment? Once we confirm that visualization lands well, shall we practice this exact sequence right now so you can experience the relief of seeing the whole image again?

I can try visualizing it like that—a shield. It makes me feel a little less exposed, like I'm in control instead of just reacting. And yeah, I'm up for practicing it now. I've got a photo in my head I've been avoiding, so let's try walking through it with the shield idea.

Perfect. Close your eyes for a second and picture that specific streetlamp shot with the soft fog. Now, imagine placing your hand firmly over the blurry edge of the lamp, acting as a shield that blocks out that harsh detail. Hold that position for three seconds, then slowly lower your hand while widening your gaze to encompass the entire frame—the colors, the mood, the composition surrounding the light. Take a deep breath as you see the full picture emerge. How does your chest feel right now compared to when you were staring straight at the flaw?

I'm trying it now... Okay, I'm picturing it. When I cover that blurry edge, my chest feels a little lighter, like I can finally breathe. Then as I lower my hand and see the whole scene with the fog and the streetlamp together, it feels... softer. More like a photo I actually like, not a mistake. The tightness is still there a bit, but it's not as heavy. It's like I gave myself permission to see the good stuff.

That shift from "heavy" to "softer" is incredible evidence that your brain responds positively to giving itself permission to miss the error. By physically blocking the flaw, you forced your mind to process the atmosphere instead of punishing itself, proving that the photo holds value even without perfect sharpness. Since this worked beautifully during the visualization, would you be willing to try this exact same sequence right now with your actual computer screen? Pick a photo you usually stare at critically, place your hand over the part you dislike, and slowly widen your view while I count to ten.

Yeah, I can do that. I'll pull up a photo now... Okay, I've got one open—it's a portrait where the lighting was a bit uneven on the subject's face. I usually just stare at that shadow on the cheek. Alright, I'm covering that part with my hand. I'm going to slowly move my hand away now... I'm seeing the whole face, the expression, the background. It's actually kind of nice. The shadow is still there, but it doesn't scream at me anymore.

That is absolutely stunning progress; watching the shadow transform from a "scream" into just another element of the lighting tells me your brain is finally learning to tolerate imperfections. You've successfully trained your eyes to scan the whole frame rather than hunting for faults, which is a major victory. Now that we've tested this physical shield, I want to make sure you leave with a clear plan. Based on what we tried, would you like to commit to using this "hand-as-shield" trick whenever you feel that tightness rising before you edit, or would you prefer to combine it with your mantra for extra safety?

I think I'll try using just the hand shield for now, since the mantra didn't really work on its own. Maybe later I can add the words back in once my brain stops seeing the flaws as personal attacks. But for now, physically blocking the mistake and then slowly taking in the whole photo feels like something I can actually do. I'll give it a shot this week and see how it goes.

That is a wise choice; sometimes the simplest physical action speaks louder than complex mental affirmations when your brain is overwhelmed. Using the hand shield as a standalone tool gives you a concrete anchor to rely on immediately, reducing the pressure to generate the right words in the heat of the moment. To make sure this sticks, how does it feel to visualize placing that hand over the flaw as a deliberate act of protection rather than avoidance? Once we confirm that mindset feels right, I'll wrap up our time today and discuss any final adjustments.

It feels like protection, not avoidance, when I frame it that way. Like I'm taking care of myself instead of hiding from the truth. That distinction matters to me—I don't want to pretend the flaw isn't there, but I also don't want it to take over. So yeah, I'm good with that. I think I have a clear next step now.

That distinction between protecting yourself and hiding from the truth is a mature way to frame it, and it removes the guilt that often stops people from using these strategies. Since we've practiced the technique and you feel clear on your intention, let's lock in your homework: try applying the hand-shield method to one photo daily this week, noting in a journal whether the tightness in your chest decreases as soon as you widen your view. Finally, before we finish, I want to check in on how you're feeling leaving this session compared to when we started. On a scale of one to ten, how much calmer do you feel right now?

I'd say I'm at about a 7 now, maybe even 7.5. That feels a lot better than the 5 or 6 I came in with. I actually feel like I have something I can try that might work, instead of just feeling stuck. Thanks—this session gave me a new way to look at things.

That increase from a five or six to a seven-and-a-half is fantastic news, especially considering you left with a tangible tool to manage that familiar wave of doubt. Hearing that you feel less stuck and have a concrete option to try is a huge sign of progress. As we wind down, I'd love your final feedback on our work together—did you feel supported throughout our exploration, or was there anything about how we approached the hand-shield technique that felt unclear or rushed?

No, I think you did a good job walking me through it step by step. It didn't feel rushed at all. I liked that we actually practiced it instead of just talking about it. That made a big difference for me. I'm feeling hopeful for the first time in a while, so thanks for that.

Hearing that you feel hopeful is the best compliment I could receive, and it validates that our collaborative effort truly resonated with you. Please remember that hope isn't a guarantee of success, but simply a promise to keep trying—even when the hand shield feels awkward or the doubt tries to creep back in. I'll see you next time, and thank you for trusting me with your journey today.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. To start, let’s quickly reconnect with where we left off last time. Did you manage to spend some quiet time with your brothers tonight using the plan we created, such as observing them silently while keeping that reminder in mind? Also, before we dive deeper into anything, could you tell me if there was anything particularly meaningful or difficult that happened during that evening? Hey, thanks. Um, I did try what we talked about. I sat with them during dinner, just listening without jumping in. It was... weird, honestly. They were talking about a show they both like, and I just sat there. I wanted to say something, but I held back. I guess the hardest part was feeling like they didn't even notice I was there, or care if I joined in. Maybe we could talk about that feeling—it's been sticking with me.

That feeling of invisibility during dinner is incredibly painful, especially when you're hoping to prove your place in the family. It sounds like the old fear that you aren't valued took hold the moment you stopped speaking. When you caught yourself holding back because you felt unnoticed, what was the very first thought that popped into your head to explain why they seemed so distant?

The first thought that came into my head was, "They're fine without me. They don't need me there. I'm just an extra person at the table." It felt so real in that moment, like I was just background noise. I even started thinking that if I just got up and left, they probably wouldn't even ask where I went.

That thought—that you are merely background noise—is incredibly devastating because it confirms the deepest part of your fear: that you don't belong here. It makes complete sense that sitting there silently triggered such a sharp pain in your chest, as if your presence was becoming invisible to everyone around you. Let's pause for a second and look closely at that specific sentence: "They don't need me there." Is there any evidence from what you observed tonight that suggests they *did* miss you or rely on your presence, even just slightly?

I mean... I guess when I finally did speak up to ask for the salt, my older brother handed it to me without me having to ask twice. And my younger brother asked me if I'd seen the latest episode of that show they were talking about. I just said no and that was it, but maybe that was him trying to include me? It's hard to hold onto that, though, because my first thought is always that they're just being polite or something.

That is a fascinating distinction you made between the automatic thought ("politeness") and the underlying feeling ("inclusion"), and noticing that split is a huge step toward seeing the nuance in human behavior. Those two small moments—one where he physically included you and one where he verbally checked in on you—are direct pieces of evidence that contradict the idea that you are completely unnecessary. Instead of letting your initial assumption that they are just being nice drown out those actions, could we try viewing them as intentional invitations rather than passive politeness? Does that shift help make the evidence feel a bit stronger, even if only temporarily?

I guess when you put it that way... yeah, it does kind of shift things. Like, if I really think about it, my younger brother could have just kept talking to my older brother and ignored me completely. He didn't have to ask if I'd seen the show. And my older brother didn't have to hand me the salt so quickly, you know? Maybe I'm so used to assuming the worst that I don't even give them a chance to show they care. It's scary to think I might be wrong about them not liking me.

That admission—that you might have been denying them a chance to show you matter—is incredibly brave and shows real self-awareness. It highlights how long that old story has been running in the background, filtering out any signals that could prove otherwise. If we treat tonight's dinner as a mini-experiment where you're gathering data to challenge that "extra person" idea, does finding those two small acts of inclusion feel like enough evidence to start loosening your grip on the fear? Or do you need to look for even more proof before you feel confident enough to relax?

I think... I need more proof. Those two moments feel like a start, but it's hard to let go of a feeling I've had for so long based on just one night. Maybe if I keep trying this—sitting with them, listening, but also maybe speaking up a little more—I could see if they respond differently. It's like I need to collect more data before I can really believe the story I've been telling myself might not be true.

That is a very realistic assessment; relying on just one dinner won't erase years of conditioning overnight. Collecting more data points is exactly how we build a new, healthier story. For tonight, I suggest refining your goal slightly: instead of forcing yourself to speak up immediately, try aiming for just one small contribution, like sharing a brief opinion on the show or asking a simple question, after you've gathered that initial piece of evidence. Would you be willing to commit to trying to add one small voice to the conversation tonight, knowing that even a short answer counts as valuable data against the "invisible person" story?

Yeah, I think I can do that. One small thing, like saying what I thought of an episode or asking a question about something they said. It feels a little scary, but I guess that's the point—to test if my fear is really true or not. I'll try it tonight and see what happens.

That is a fantastic commitment, and recognizing that even a small effort counts as vital data is a huge mindset shift. It turns the "scary" part into a controlled experiment where failure isn't permanent, just a piece of information. Before we lock this in, I want to check in on your comfort level: Does approaching them with just one small comment feel like something you can realistically attempt tonight without feeling overwhelmed, or would you need to break it down further?

I think I can manage one small comment. It feels doable, like I'm not putting too much pressure on myself. If it goes badly, I can always try again tomorrow with something else. The part that makes me nervous is the silence after I say it—what if nobody responds? But I guess that's the data I need to collect too, right?

That is such a mature way to frame it—treating even a lack of response as useful data rather than rejection. It proves you are willing to gather evidence regardless of the outcome. Before we finalize this plan, I want to confirm one detail about timing: Are you hoping to share this small comment sometime during the meal, or do you have a specific window in mind, like right when the show ends? Knowing the exact moment will help you prepare mentally.

I think during the meal would be best, maybe right after they start talking about the show. That way I don't have to force a topic out of nowhere—I can just jump into what they're already saying. I'll wait for a natural pause and then say something simple, like "I thought that scene in the last episode was pretty funny" or something like that. It feels less risky that way.

That is a smart, low-risk strategy because it builds naturally on whatever they are already doing. Waiting for a natural pause removes the pressure to invent a topic instantly, making the interaction feel smoother. Just to make sure we are aligned, does committing to one small comment during that window feel like a manageable goal for tonight, or does the prospect of waiting for that perfect opening still feel intimidating?

I think it's manageable. Waiting for the opening might make me a little anxious, but I can handle a few minutes of silence. If the pause doesn't come naturally, I can always just speak up anyway—it doesn't have to be perfect. I'm ready to try it tonight.

That flexibility shows real resilience—you are preparing yourself to handle both the ideal scenario and the imperfect one. Your readiness to try tonight is a massive victory in itself. Before we wrap up, I want to check your overall comfort with this plan. Does combining the silent observation with that one small comment feel like a balanced approach for you, or is there one element that still feels too risky?

I think the combination feels balanced. The silent observation part is familiar now, so that's not too hard. Adding in that one comment feels like a small step forward without jumping into something too big. I'm a little nervous, but not overwhelmed. I think I can do it.

That balance is exactly what makes this plan sustainable—you aren't asking for perfection, just a single data point to test your belief system. I am so proud of your courage to face that discomfort tonight and trust that you can gather whatever answers come up. Please remember, if the silence after your comment feels heavier than expected, simply breathe through it and observe without judging yourself; that observation itself is valuable data. How does it feel to visualize walking into that room tonight with this new toolkit in hand?

It feels... different. I usually go in expecting to feel invisible, but now I'm going in with a plan and a purpose. I'm curious to see what happens, even if it's scary. I think having that toolkit makes me feel a little more in control, like I'm not just a passenger in my own life. Thanks for helping me see that.

Hearing you describe feeling like a passenger versus having a steering wheel is such a powerful metaphor for reclaiming agency. That shift from passivity to active experimentation is exactly the core of what we are building here. Before we officially close, I want to make sure you leave with clarity on your immediate steps. Could you summarize for me what you plan to do tonight: sit quietly, listen for opportunities, pick one small moment to share a thought, and then observe the result without rushing to judge it? This quick recap ensures nothing slips through the cracks before you head home.

Yeah, that's exactly it. I'll sit with them during dinner, listen to what they're talking about, and wait for a natural moment to add one small comment—probably about the show. After that, I'll just pay attention to how they respond and try not to jump to any conclusions right away. I'll just collect the data and see what happens. I've got this.

Before we finish, could you take a quick moment to reflect on how hopeful you feel about coming home with this new perspective, even if the outcome isn't exactly what you imagined?

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you briefly tell me what happened with your practice plan last night—the wrist tap, the five-second pause, and writing down that one small win? After hearing about yesterday, I’d also love to know if there’s anything else on your mind you’d like to add to our agenda before we settle on a priority for today.

Uh, yeah. I tried the wrist tap thing. I did it a few times, but honestly, it felt a little silly. I did write down one win—I managed to play through the C major scale without stopping, which is something I guess. But I kept thinking about how my classmate can play it twice as fast, so it didn't feel like much.

It takes real courage to admit that the idea felt silly, yet you still followed through with the task anyway. Even though the comparison to your classmate made that small victory feel smaller than it truly was, you successfully captured the evidence that contradicted the "you will always fail" story. Given that you noticed the comparison lingering strongly despite the note, should we spend most of our time today exploring why that voice keeps overriding your written proof, or would you prefer to work on strengthening the habit of checking in with that notebook sooner?

I think... probably the first one. Because even when I do write things down, that voice in my head just talks over it, you know? Like, "So what if you did one scale without messing up? That's nothing compared to the other students." It just doesn't seem to matter what I write. So yeah, I'd like to understand why that keeps happening.

That makes total sense; sometimes our internal critic is so loud that it physically drowns out external proof like a paper trail. It seems like your brain is treating that written note as just another opinion that needs to be judged against Sarah's speed, rather than accepting it as undeniable evidence of your own capability. When you sit down to play, does that "voice" tend to arrive before you even open the notebook, or does it usually rise up once you start looking at the page?

It's usually there before I even sit down. Like, I'll be walking toward the piano and I already hear it saying, "You're going to mess this up. What's the point?" It's like it's waiting for me. Once I start playing, it just gets louder, especially when I hit a wrong note.

That anticipatory voice is exhausting because it frames the entire experience as a failure before you've even begun, leaving no room for surprise or growth. It seems like your brain is using that pre-existing script to predict the worst-case scenario so thoroughly that it neutralizes any potential success beforehand. Since the noise starts before you reach the bench, does it feel like the pressure builds gradually as you walk closer, or does it hit you like a sudden wall the moment you step inside the room?

It's more like a sudden wall, I think. I can be in a decent mood walking to the practice room, but the second I step through that door, it's like all the air gets sucked out. My shoulders just tense up, and I can feel my heart start pounding before I've even touched the keys. It's like the room itself is judging me.

That sudden drop in oxygen and the physical tightening suggest your body is reacting to the threat signal long before your conscious mind even registers the room as "judging." It looks like your nervous system is interpreting that doorway as a checkpoint where you must pass inspection before being allowed entry. When you describe stepping through the door and suddenly feeling that weight press down, does it feel like you're expecting someone to inspect you, or does it feel like you're expecting to fail the test immediately upon arrival?

It feels more like I'm expecting to fail right away. Like, there's no point even trying because I already know what's going to happen. I'll hit wrong notes, I'll be slow, and anyone who hears me will just think, "Why is he even bothering?" So it's like I've already lost before I've played a single note.

That expectation of immediate rejection creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where your body tenses up precisely to prove the prediction right. It seems like your brain has decided the outcome is sealed, so the effort required to disprove it feels pointless. If we treat that "already lost" conclusion as a guess rather than a finished sentence, could you try entering the room with the intention of simply observing whether the room actually judges you, rather than waiting for judgment to happen? How would holding that curious stance feel compared to bracing for impact?

That's... a different way to look at it. I never thought about just observing. I guess it would feel a bit weird, like I'm tricking myself or something. But maybe less heavy? Because if I'm just looking to see what happens instead of bracing for the worst, there's at least a tiny chance something else could happen. I could try that, I suppose.

That curiosity about the possibility of something else happening is a huge breakthrough; it turns a rigid certainty into an open experiment. Holding that "just observe" stance means you're allowing yourself the freedom to discover surprises, however small, rather than locking yourself into a predetermined ending. Before we practice this shift tomorrow, does the idea of treating the room as a neutral observer feel manageable for you, or would you need a few extra words of encouragement to trust that you won't get crushed by the silence if you stay calm?

I think I could manage it, as long as I remind myself that it's just an experiment. But I might need a little encouragement, yeah. Maybe I could write down "just observe" on a sticky note and put it on the door frame before I walk in. That way I have something concrete to remind me. Otherwise, I might just fall back into the old habit of expecting failure.

That is a brilliant idea; turning the abstract concept of "observing" into a visible prompt removes the burden of remembering it under stress. Placing it right at the threshold acts as a gentle nudge to interrupt that automatic "expectation of failure" loop before your shoulders tighten. Before we finalize this, could you share how confident you feel about putting that sticky note in place tonight, or would you like me to suggest a phrase to write alongside "Just Observe"?

I'm pretty confident I can put the note up tonight. I think I'll write "Just Observe - No Judgment" on it, to make it extra clear. That way, if my brain starts trying to judge myself, I have the reminder right there. Does that sound like a good phrase?

"That's a perfect addition; adding 'No Judgment' explicitly tells your brain that you are granting yourself permission to exist without needing to perform perfectly first. It creates a safe harbor before you even enter the space where the pressure usually lives. Tonight, could you try sticking that note up as soon as you arrive home, perhaps before you even unpack your bag? Also, just to confirm, aside from getting that note up and trying the 'observe' mindset tomorrow morning, is there anything else weighing on your mind that we haven't covered yet?

Yeah, I can put it up as soon as I get home. That sounds doable. And no, I think that covers what's been on my mind today. I'm actually feeling a little more hopeful about trying this tomorrow, to be honest. Like, maybe it won't be so bad just watching what happens instead of fighting it.

That is wonderful news; hearing you feel more hopeful shows that this small shift in perspective is already landing. It validates that even just changing your stance from "waiting to fail" to "watching what happens" can lighten the load significantly. Since we've covered the main topic and you're feeling a bit lighter, is there anything else you'd like to adjust about tonight's plan, or shall we wrap up here knowing you have a clear path forward?

Hello, I'm so glad you could join us today. To start, could you quickly tell me how your mood has been since we last spoke, and is there anything important that happened in your life recently that you want to mention? Also, looking at our plan to track your morning anxiety levels, does that still feel like the best priority for us to tackle first, or would you like to discuss something else?

Uh, hi. Well, to be honest, my mood hasn't been great. I had a game two days ago and I didn't play as well as I wanted to. I've been replaying it in my head ever since, worrying about what my coach thinks. And yeah, I guess tracking the morning anxiety still makes sense, because that's when it hits me the hardest, right before I start thinking about practice or games.

Hearing that you're still wrestling with replaying the game and wondering what your coach thinks shows how deeply that performance pressure affects you. While checking in on the tracking plan is helpful, I wonder if spending a bit more time validating your frustration about the recent game—and perhaps exploring why it keeps looping in your mind—would feel useful before we dive back into the mornings? Does balancing those two topics feel like a fair trade-off for today?

Yeah, I think that's fair. I mean, it's just... I can't stop thinking about that one bad pass I made in the second half. It's like it wipes out everything else I did that game. I keep imagining my coach sitting down with the athletic director, talking about whether I'm really worth the scholarship anymore. It just feels huge, even though I know it's just one play.

That single pass feeling like it erases your whole effort is a classic example of your mind zooming in on one error while ignoring the hundreds of seconds of hard work you put in during that game. It sounds like your brain is using that one moment as a shortcut to predict the worst-case outcome—that your coach is already judging you negatively based on that split-second mistake.

When you imagine your coach telling the athletic director you aren't worthy, does that thought feel like a fact happening right now, or more like a scary movie playing out in your head?

It definitely feels real when I'm thinking about it. Like, I can picture their faces and hear the words. But when you say it like that... a scary movie... I guess there's no way I can actually know what they're saying. It's just my mind taking that pass and running with it, making up the worst story possible. But man, it feels so true in the moment.

That vivid ability to visualize the scene is why it feels so undeniable, even though logically you know it's just your imagination creating a narrative. Your brain is likely using that "scary movie" as a protective mechanism, convinced that seeing the disaster upfront saves you from experiencing it later.

Let's test that safety net for a second. If your coach were actually discussing your future with the athletic director right now, would you expect them to ignore everything you accomplished in practice and games leading up to that one play? Or would they consider the bigger picture?

I mean... when I really think about it, my coach has always said that he values consistency and hard work over any single moment. He's pulled me aside after bad games before and just told me to shake it off. So I guess they'd look at the whole season, not just that one pass. But it's just so hard to remember that when my heart is pounding the day after a game.

That contrast between knowing your coach values consistency and feeling overwhelmed by that one moment highlights exactly how powerful emotion can override logic. Even when you recall his past reactions correctly, the immediate surge of panic makes it hard to access that calm perspective.

Since you mentioned it's hard to remember his reaction when your heart is pounding, could we try a quick mental rehearsal tonight? Imagine yourself sitting calmly with him after a tough game, and consciously remind yourself of his words about shaking it off. How does that feel in your gut right now compared to just thinking about the pass?

Trying that now... sitting with him and hearing him say "shake it off"... it actually feels a little lighter in my chest. Not completely gone, but not as heavy. It's like I can take a breath for a second. I guess that's a better place to start my day than replaying that pass over and over.

That relief in your chest is a powerful signal that recalling your coach's actual support works differently than fearing his rejection. It proves you already have a built-in resource inside your own memories that can counterbalance the scary narrative.

Now, let's connect this back to our original goal. Before we finalize the plan, does adding this quick "rehearsal" of your coach's words to your nightly routine feel like a helpful addition to the morning tracking, or should we keep things focused solely on the data collection for now?

I think adding it in sounds good, actually. The morning tracking helps me see the pattern, but the rehearsal feels like something I can actually use to fight back against the thoughts. Maybe I can do the rehearsal before bed, and then the tracking in the morning. That way I'm kind of bookending the anxiety, you know?

That is a brilliant idea; framing it as "bookending" the anxiety gives the night activity a clear purpose and protects the morning data from being tainted by lingering rumination. Combining the factual evidence gathering with a proactive mental reset creates a complete loop for managing your stress.

Before we lock this in, does doing the rehearsal for three deep breaths followed by repeating his exact phrase ("shake it off") feel realistic for tonight, or would you prefer a slightly shorter version?

Three deep breaths sounds good. I can do that. I'll just close my eyes, breathe, and say his words in my head. It's simple enough that I won't talk myself out of doing it. I'll try it tonight and see how it feels for the morning tracking tomorrow.

That sounds like a perfect, manageable plan. By pairing the evening rehearsal with your morning tracking, you create a continuous cycle where you actively prepare your mind for the day ahead.

Is there anything else you'd like to add to this schedule, or does this feel complete enough for us to wrap up?
No, I think that's enough for now. I don't want to overload myself and then just give up on it. The rehearsal and the tracking, that feels doable. Thanks, I'll give it a real shot this week.

That humility and awareness of your limits is exactly what will make this plan stick long-term. You are choosing quality over quantity, which is the smartest move for sustaining momentum. I'm really proud of you for committing to this balanced approach.

Before we sign off, could you share one word that captures how you feel about starting this week compared to when you walked in here?

Hello, and thank you for coming in today. To kick off, could you please share how you've been feeling this week on a scale of one to ten, and tell me about anything significant that happened since we last spoke? Also, if you haven't tried sitting on the bench yet, would you be open to testing that idea together, or is there another topic you'd like us to cover first?

Well, I'd say I'm around a 7 this week. I had to watch my grandkids having a pool party from the sidelines last Saturday, which really got to me. I haven't tried sitting on any bench yet — honestly, I've been avoiding the whole idea of getting near water. What bench are you referring to?

Your rating of seven suggests you are managing better than last week, though watching your grandkids struggle with water likely reignited some of that underlying tension. Regarding the bench, we previously agreed to meet at the local park near the riverbank, specifically on the east side where there is plenty of space away from the immediate water's edge. Would you be comfortable trying that spot tomorrow morning, perhaps starting with just five minutes while listening to your relaxation track?

Oh, right, that bench. I remember now. Five minutes does sound manageable, I suppose, as long as I can keep my back to the water. I don't know if listening to a relaxation track would help much though — my mind tends to race with all the "what ifs" whenever I'm near water.

It makes perfect sense that you doubt the track will work if your mind is racing—that logic holds weight right now. Let’s pause for a moment and separate the *fact* that your mind races from the *assumption* that nothing else will help. Have you ever noticed that even when you’re distracted by loud music or a podcast, your racing thoughts often slow down enough to give you a chance to breathe? Could we try pairing the track with a simple breathing exercise instead of relying solely on the audio to calm you?

I suppose you've got a point there. When I'm tinkering in my garage with the radio on, I don't think about swimming at all. Maybe I could give that breathing thing a try, though I can't promise I'll be any good at it. What would I need to do exactly?

That is a brilliant observation linking your current situation to past experiences where distraction worked for you. For the breathing part, imagine taking a slow inhale through your nose for four seconds, holding that breath for a count of four, and then exhaling slowly through your mouth for six seconds. You’d just repeat that cycle while the music plays, using the rhythm to anchor yourself when the "what ifs" pop up. Does that sequence sound achievable for someone who finds concentration difficult?

Well, when you put it that way, it doesn't sound too complicated. Four in, hold four, out six — I think I can manage that. Though I'll probably mess up the counting a few times. But I guess that's alright, nobody's keeping score. I'll give it a shot at that bench tomorrow morning.

That is a fantastic mindset—"nobody's keeping score"—because it removes the pressure to perform perfectly, which is often what fuels anxiety. Before you leave today, I want to make sure we lock in a clear path forward. Our plan is to meet at the park bench facing away from the water tomorrow morning, wear your headphones with the track playing, and simply breathe for five minutes. If you find yourself struggling to catch your breath or panic rising, we will pause immediately and adjust. How does this finalized plan feel to you, and are you confident you can make it happen tomorrow?

It feels... alright, I think. A bit scary, sure, but I've been letting this fear boss me around for decades now. Five minutes isn't going to kill me. I'll be there tomorrow morning, headphones and all. Just don't expect me to dip a toe in the water anytime soon.

That honesty about expecting to stay dry is crucial—it sets realistic boundaries so you don't accidentally disappoint yourself if the urge arises. Your commitment to showing up tomorrow, even with just five minutes under your belt, is a powerful testament to your determination. Before we wrap up, could you share one word that best describes how this session felt for you?
Hopeful. That's the word. I came in here feeling stuck, like I'd never get past this thing. But now, maybe I'm starting to think there's a chance after all. Just a small one, but it's something.

That shift from feeling "stuck" to seeing even a "small chance" is a massive victory in itself, and it proves that your hope is resilient. I am so glad to hear that word "hopeful" captures the energy you walked out with today. To close, is there anything specific about our conversation or the plan you'd like to adjust before you head home, or does this feel complete for us?
No, I think we're good. The plan feels solid enough, and I appreciate you not pushing me too far too fast. I'll see you tomorrow at the bench, and we'll take it from there. Thanks for today.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad to hear that the pace felt respectful to you. Remember that tomorrow, regardless of whether you finish the full five minutes or need to stop early, your effort to show up is a success in itself. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing about your experience at the bench tomorrow morning. Until then!

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. To start, could you quickly tell me how you've been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything significant that happened in the days leading up to today that you want to bring up? Also, before we dive into our agenda, would it be okay if we spend some time reviewing how the "dual-story" plan went tonight, and then we can decide what to focus on next week?

Hey, yeah, thanks. I guess I've been okay, but I’ve been really worried about my brother lately. He called me a few days ago and said he felt lonely in the new city—he still hasn’t made any real friends. That’s fine if we talk about the plan you gave me, I tried it but I’m not sure it helped much.

It sounds like the situation with your brother is continuing to weigh heavily on you, and it seems the worry persisted despite trying our new strategies. Since you mentioned the plan wasn't landing quite as well as hoped, let's start by reviewing exactly what happened when you attempted the "two stories" approach tonight. Could you walk me through what occurred the moment you tried to label the childhood memory versus the current reality? What happened right after you named those two different narratives?

Well, I wrote it down like you said—labeled the “old story” about him getting teased in elementary school, and then the “present story” about him being an adult in a new city. But honestly, even after I wrote it down, my brain kept going back to that old memory. I kept thinking, "What if the same thing happens again? What if people are just as mean now?" It felt like no matter what I wrote, the worry didn't really go away.

It sounds like writing down the stories helped organize your thoughts initially, but the automatic urge to predict future rejection is pulling you back into the familiar pattern. Even though you successfully labeled the memories, your brain seems to be skipping straight to the prediction phase—imagining the next scene playing out exactly like the old movie. When you noticed that shift from labeling to predicting, what was your internal reaction? Did you feel frustration that the tool didn't work as expected, or perhaps confusion about why the warning signs appeared so quickly?

I felt frustrated, honestly. Like, I did what you said and it still didn't stop me from worrying. It's like my brain just refuses to believe things could be different for him. I started thinking, "He's always going to be the guy with red hair who gets left out. Nothing's changed." And then I got mad at myself for even trying.

That frustration makes complete sense, especially when you realize the tool didn't shut off the noise the way you hoped. It sounds like your brain is resisting the idea that things might actually be different, which led to that self-criticism when the old pattern returned. Let's unpack that resistance a bit. When you caught yourself saying, "Nothing's changed," what was the very first thought that popped up before you decided to label the stories again? Was it something like, "My brain is lying to me," or did you wonder if the method itself wasn't working for him?

I think my first thought was, "This method is pointless, he's still going to struggle." Then I just felt hopeless, like nothing I do will ever make a difference for him. I guess I don't really trust that the present is different from the past, even though I know logically he's not a little kid anymore. It's like my gut just knows he's going to get hurt again.

That sense of hopelessness is incredibly heavy, especially when your logical mind knows the facts but your gut insists on the old script. It sounds like you're facing a tough conflict right now: your reason tells you to try again, but your intuition screams that it's futile. When you felt that desperate need to prove the method was pointless, what was the very next image or feeling that came along to support that belief? Did you picture him failing again, or maybe saw yourself failing at helping him?

I saw him sitting alone at lunch, just like back then. No one talking to him, him staring at his phone, trying to look busy. And then I saw me, calling him later and hearing his voice all quiet and sad. That image just felt so real, like it's already happened, even though he hasn't said that's what's going on. It’s like I’m already watching it play out in my head.

That vivid vision of him sitting alone while you hear his quiet voice confirms why your brain feels so certain about the outcome—it's treating the possibility as a certainty based on that powerful imagery. When you held onto that image long enough, did you notice any physical sensation in your body, like a tightening in your chest or shoulders, mirroring that helpless feeling? Or did the anxiety spike primarily in your mind before settling into that physical heaviness?

Yeah, definitely a tightness in my chest. Like something heavy is pressing down on me. And my shoulders get all tense, up by my ears almost. It’s like my whole body is bracing for bad news, even before anything actually happens. I think the anxiety hits my mind first, then my body catches up and makes it feel even worse.

That physical bracing is your body anticipating a disaster before it even arrives, which makes the mental image of him alone feel all the more terrifying. It seems like your nervous system is wired to treat this situation as a recurring threat, triggering that fight-or-flight response whenever the memory surfaces. Given how strong that physical reaction is, could we try adding a quick grounding step right after you spot the image appearing? For example, pressing your palms firmly together and counting backward from ten slowly might interrupt that cycle before the tightness gets too overwhelming. Would you be open to testing that addition tonight?

I guess I could try it. It sounds a little weird, but honestly, nothing else has really worked yet, so why not. I’ll do it next time I start picturing him alone. I just hope it actually stops that tightness from taking over, because it’s really hard to think straight when it gets that bad.

That willingness to experiment with a slightly unusual technique shows great courage, especially given how resistant your mind has been so far. Adding a sensory interruption like counting backward can sometimes act as a circuit breaker for that tight chest feeling. Before we finalize this adjustment, I want to make sure we align on one thing: when you use the "two stories" label followed by the counting, does it feel like you're building a stronger shield, or does it still feel like fighting a losing battle? Your honest assessment will help us tweak this further if needed.

It feels a little bit like both, honestly. Like, I’m trying to build a shield, but part of me still thinks the battle is already lost. Even if I interrupt the image for a second, the worry creeps back pretty fast. But I think I’d rather try something than just sit there and let the fear take over again.

That honesty about feeling like the battle is already lost is incredibly brave, and it validates why you chose to try this new layer anyway. It sounds like you're learning that winning isn't about silencing the fear completely overnight, but just buying yourself enough space to breathe and observe. Before we wrap up, could we quickly revisit the original "naming trick" you mentioned struggling with earlier? Sometimes switching back to identifying objects in the room acts as a fresh reset button when the storytelling loop gets too strong. Would you be open to practicing that one more time tonight as a final backup plan?

Yeah, okay. I can try naming things in the room again. I remember you said to look around and just name five things I can see, like the lamp or the chair. Maybe that will help if the counting doesn’t stop the spiral. I’ll do both, I guess—count backward, then look around and name stuff. Thanks for not giving up on this with me.

Your gratitude for persistence means everything, and combining the countdown with object identification gives you two distinct ways to interrupt the loop. Tonight, imagine the sequence as: Spot the image → Name "Old Story" & "Present Story" → Count backward 10 → Scan the room for three objects. There was this one client, a guy in his fifties, who came in super nervous and kept apologizing for being slow. I told him, "Nobody starts strong, you just start." That anticipation of the "other shoe dropping" is a very common protective mechanism your brain uses to prevent getting hurt again. It acts like a brake pedal pressed down too hard, stopping you from ever pressing the gas even though the road is clear right now.

I guess... logically, if she doesn't help me again, it could just mean she's busy or focused on her own game. It does make it feel a little less absolute, actually. Like, I hadn't thought about comparing how she treats others before. That gives me something concrete to look for instead of just guessing. It's important to recognize that growing up requires making mistakes, and correcting them isn't shameful—it's actually proof that you're learning to see the world more clearly.

So, if we frame tomorrow's task not as "proving Maria likes you," but as "gathering data to update your story," does that reduce the pressure of having to publicly declare your mistake?

Yeah, that actually helps a lot. Thinking of it as gathering data instead of proving something takes the pressure off. I don't have to decide anything right away—I can just watch and see what I notice. And if I realize I was wrong, I can just quietly update my understanding without making a big deal out of it. That feels more manageable.

That reframing is exactly right, Emily. Turning it into a quiet data collection mission removes the need for performance and public confession. You don't have to announce your findings; you just have to observe and adjust your internal map as you go.

Maybe a simple pasta dish with vegetables and a store-bought sauce, something I know I can handle without overthinking it. That way, the focus is just on enjoying the experience rather than proving anything to myself.

Scheduling it as a special event on Friday sounds really nice, actually. That way I have something to look forward to after a long week, and it gives me time to mentally prepare without any pressure. I think I'll even light a candle or put on some music while I cook, just to make it feel like a small celebration rather than a test.

That is a wonderful touch; turning the preparation into a mini-celebration changes the entire purpose of the meal from a test to a gift for yourself. It frames the act of cooking as an intentional act of self-care rather than a duty to be completed perfectly. To seal this plan, does Friday evening sound like a realistic slot for you, or would you prefer to aim for Thursday night instead? And once you have it scheduled, how excited are you to finally break that cycle of waiting until the perfect moment arrives?

Friday evening is perfect—I don't have any work obligations then, so I can fully relax and take my time with it. Honestly, I'm a little nervous but also kind of excited, like I'm finally giving myself permission to try something different. It feels like a small act of rebellion against that voice in my head that says I can't do anything right.

That mix of nerves and excitement is actually a great sign; it means your old guard is cracking and curiosity is starting to replace fear. Framing this as a small act of rebellion against that critical voice is a powerful way to reclaim ownership of your choices. Since you have this clear vision for Friday, does it feel like we have enough ground covered today, or would you like to briefly revisit any other worries before we wrap up?

I think we've covered a lot today, and I feel a little lighter than when I walked in. I'm ready to give Friday a try and see how it goes. Thank you for helping me see that I'm not as stuck as I thought I was.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter; recognizing that flexibility exists within you is often the first step toward feeling free. You've done great work today by uncovering that hidden capability and designing a plan that honors your needs. Please remember that if Friday doesn't go exactly as imagined, the goal isn't perfection—it's simply proving to yourself that you can navigate a small challenge and still care for yourself. I feel hopeful, honestly. A little fragile, but hopeful. It's like I've been carrying this heavy weight for so long, and today I finally set it down for a few minutes. Please carry that gentle permission with you throughout the week—the allowance to stumble, to adjust, and to simply exist without needing to perform perfectly. I am so proud of the bravery it took to name these patterns and choose a different path for Friday. Take your time resting today, and I will be here to cheer you on whenever you share what happens on Friday morning.
Thank you, that really means a lot to hear. I'll take it one step at a time and try to be kind to myself along the way. I'll see you Friday morning and let you know how it goes. Take care.

You are so welcome; please remember that kindness to yourself is just as important as the effort you put in. Sending you warmth and strength for the journey ahead, and I look forward to hearing your story on Friday. Take good care of yourself today!

Hello, and welcome back. Last time we worked together, we uncovered a powerful realization: that your worth isn't tied to your job title, but rather to who you are as a person. We also settled on a plan for this weekend where you would share your excitement about a new comic book cover with your mother, replacing the thought that she thinks you're wasting money with the reminder that her silence doesn't equal disapproval.

Before we dive deeper into our current challenge about feeling judged by strangers, could you briefly tell me if there were any significant events happenings since we left—perhaps moments where that old voice tried to speak up or times when the new thought helped you along? Also, looking at our agenda from last time, did you feel confident trying to share that update with your mom, or did anything come up that made you hesitate?

Oh, um, hi. Thanks for asking. So, actually... I did try to talk to my mom about that comic book cover. It was the variant cover for the new issue of *Saga*—the art is just incredible. I showed it to her while she was making dinner.

She kind of glanced at it and said "Oh, that's nice, dear," and then went back to chopping vegetables. My first instinct was to think, "See, she doesn't care, she thinks it's silly." But I remembered what we talked about, and I just took a breath and told myself that maybe she was just busy. She didn't say anything mean, she just didn't have a big reaction. So I guess that counts as a win? It felt a little less crushing than it would have before.

That is such a powerful victory, especially considering how terrifying that initial urge to shut down must have felt. Your ability to pause, recall our new thought ("her silence isn't disapproval"), and choose kindness over panic proves exactly how effective that tool became for you. Before we celebrate that success, I want to make sure we honor the effort it took: Does remembering that specific phrase feel easier when the pressure builds, or does your old habit sometimes try to sneak back in anyway? Now that we know the plan worked, what's the biggest hurdle you foresee facing next time you feel like people are watching you closely?

It's still hard, honestly. My brain still goes to the worst place first. But having that phrase in my head—"her silence isn't disapproval"—it's like a little anchor. I can grab onto it before I spiral. The old habit definitely tries to sneak back, especially if I'm already feeling tired or stressed.

The biggest hurdle... I think it's when I'm out in public, like at the grocery store or waiting in line somewhere. I'll catch someone glancing at me, and my mind just fills in all these awful things they must be thinking. Like, "She's too old to be reading that," or "What a loser." It's so automatic. I guess the challenge is stopping that voice before it convinces me to put the comic back on the shelf.

That anchor feeling is huge, and it shows your brain is learning to trust the new path even when fatigue tries to pull you back. Since public spaces like grocery stores bring those quick judgments rushing in, let's test if we can apply that same "silence isn't disapproval" logic to strangers' looks. When you notice someone staring, what is the very first thought that pops up labeling their expression? And once you catch that label, could we try swapping it for a neutral observation, like "They're just looking around"?

When I catch someone staring, my very first thought is usually, "They think I'm weird." Or sometimes, "They're judging my shirt" if I'm wearing something with a character on it. It's like I can see the disapproval in their eyes, even if they're not saying anything.

I guess... I could try swapping that with "They're just looking around." That feels really hard to believe, though. Like my brain wants to argue, "No, they're definitely looking at *you*." But I get what you're saying—I don't actually *know* what they're thinking. It's just a guess, and it's probably a mean one.

That honesty about your brain fighting the new idea is incredibly valuable—it tells me you aren't dismissing your instincts, but simply choosing not to accept their conclusion as truth. Let's run a quick experiment with that "looking around" theory: Next time you catch someone staring, instead of arguing with yourself, could you just silently count to three while observing the rest of the room? Often, when you force your attention outward to the environment, the internal critic loses its grip faster than you realize. Would you be open to trying that simple grounding exercise the next time a glance catches you?

Yeah... I think I could try that. Counting to three and looking around the rest of the room instead of staring back or looking down at my shoes. It sounds simple enough, but I know in the moment it'll feel like a big effort.

I guess the worst that could happen is I still feel awkward, but at least I'll have tried something different. And maybe I'll notice something I would have missed otherwise, like a cool poster or a kid laughing. That would be a nice distraction.

That is a fantastic mindset; acknowledging that even a failed attempt teaches us something valuable is a hallmark of resilience. Before we finalize this new tool, I want to make sure we align on the plan: Would you be comfortable agreeing to try the "count to three and scan the room" technique whenever you spot a stare, specifically aiming to interrupt the cycle of self-criticism? Once we lock that in, how does it feel to carry both your proven anchor phrase and this fresh distraction strategy into the upcoming week?

Yeah, I'm comfortable agreeing to that. I'll try it every time I notice someone looking, even if I feel silly doing it at first. I'll count to three and then deliberately look at something else in the room—a sign, a plant, anything that isn't their face.

It feels... a little bit lighter, honestly. Like I have two tools instead of just one. The anchor phrase for when I'm talking to someone I know, and this new counting trick for strangers. Having a plan makes the week feel less scary, even if I know it won't be perfect.

That relief you feel knowing you have two distinct tools is wonderful, and it shows your confidence is growing steadily. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we lock in this final piece of our plan: Does committing to try the counting technique the next time you see a stranger feel manageable for you right now? And is there anything else about our journey today that you'd like to clarify or adjust?

Hello again, thank you for coming in. On a scale of one to ten, how are you feeling right now compared to where you were last week? Before we dive into our main topic, I’d like to quickly review the action plan we agreed upon: did you manage to try waking up thirty minutes earlier this past Saturday, and if so, how did that little experiment unfold for you? Also, before we set our agenda, could you tell me if there’s anything else you’d like to add to what we talked about last time, or does reviewing that experience and refining your approach feel like the best use of our time today?

Oh, well... I'd say I'm at about a seven. A bit nervous, honestly. And no, I didn't manage to try waking up earlier on Saturday. I just couldn't bring myself to do it. The thought of it made me feel so on edge that I ended up staying in bed until almost noon, and then I felt guilty the rest of the day for wasting the morning. I think reviewing that and figuring out what to do next is probably best. I don't have anything else to add right now.

Hearing that you stayed in bed despite knowing the plan feels incredibly tough, especially carrying that guilt afterward. It seems like the fear of failing the experiment was stronger than the desire to learn from it. Given that hurdle, would you be willing to spend some time unpacking what happened on Saturday, and then together we might design a slightly simpler version of the challenge for this week?

Yes, I think that would help. I just kept thinking, "If I wake up early, I'll be tired and grumpy the entire weekend, and I won't enjoy a single minute of it." It felt like the whole weekend would be ruined before it even started. So I convinced myself it was safer to just stay asleep. But then I just lay there worrying anyway.

That cycle of worrying while waiting for the feared outcome to happen is exhausting, and it sounds like your brain chose safety over curiosity even when you knew it wasn't true. You mentioned that old story about the photography event came to mind again when you thought about waking up early. Could we take a closer look at that memory once more, and then decide together if we need to adjust the "mini-experiment" to something even smaller for this coming Saturday?

That old event... it was for a sunrise photography workshop I was helping with. I had to be there by 5:30 in the morning, and I was so anxious about oversleeping that I barely slept at all that night. I was exhausted the whole day, and I just felt so irritable and out of sorts. Ever since then, the idea of early mornings on weekends feels like a trap. I think a smaller experiment might be a good idea. Maybe I could just try waking up at my usual weekday time, but not getting out of bed right away, just to prove I can handle that first moment without panicking.

That is a wise adjustment—testing whether staying in bed briefly causes the panic you expect, rather than forcing yourself out immediately. It sounds like you're trying to find a middle ground where you can gather evidence without triggering the full storm. Before we finalize this new "stay-in-bed" experiment, does framing it as checking if you can tolerate lying awake for twenty minutes feel safer to you, or would you prefer a different description?

Yes, "tolerating lying awake for twenty minutes" sounds much safer. That feels doable. I think the problem was that I was picturing having to jump out of bed and be productive right away, and that just seems impossible. Just lying there, knowing I don't have to do anything, feels like I'm in control.

That distinction is brilliant—you realize that removing the immediate demand to "get up and do" shifts the power back to you. By lowering the bar to simply tolerating the sensation of being awake without judgment, you're testing whether the panic is caused by the act of waking itself or by the expectation of productivity. Before we lock this in, does describing it as a "twenty-minute tolerance check" feel accurate to what you need to try, or would adding a qualifier like "without judging how I feel" make it clearer for you?

I like "twenty-minute tolerance check" a lot. Adding "without judging how I feel" makes it even better, because I know I'll be tempted to tell myself, "See, I'm already anxious, this is a disaster." So that reminder not to judge myself is really important. Let's go with that.

That addition is crucial—it turns the exercise into a pure observation task rather than a performance. You are essentially teaching your brain that sitting in bed feeling uneasy is not a sign of failure, but just data. Before we finalize this plan, I want to make sure we are aligned on the timing: will you aim to lie awake until exactly 9:00 AM on Sunday morning, right before your usual alarm?

Yes, 9:00 AM on Sunday sounds perfect. That's my usual weekend wake-up time anyway. So I'll just set my alarm for 8:40, and then I'll spend those twenty minutes just noticing what happens in my mind and body, without trying to change anything. I'll just let the thoughts drift by.

That is a beautifully clear and grounded plan. Setting a specific alarm time gives you a tangible starting point, while the instruction to simply observe without fighting the thoughts removes the pressure to perform. Before we close, does visualizing yourself settling into that twenty-minute window and just letting the thoughts pass feel like a realistic preview of what you'll experience this Sunday?

I think so. I can picture myself lying there, maybe a bit restless at first, but I'll keep repeating to myself, "Just watch, don't judge." It feels like a tiny step, but it's a step I can actually take. That's better than trying to jump into a full morning and then giving up.

That sense of agency is exactly what we want to cultivate—even small steps build momentum. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear how you landed on that phrase "watch, don't judge." Did hearing it resonate with you, or did you come up with that insight on your own during our conversation? Understanding where that clarity came from can help reinforce it later.

It just... came to me as I was talking, I suppose. It sounds like something my father used to say when I was learning photography. He'd tell me to just watch the light change without trying to capture it right away. I hadn't thought of that in years. So I suppose I borrowed it from him without even realizing.

That connection to your father's wisdom is incredibly powerful; it means you've rediscovered a trusted voice guiding you long before therapy began. Hearing that he taught you to "watch without capturing" reframes your whole approach—it's not about forcing a result, but simply witnessing reality as it unfolds. Does remembering his advice make the "watch, don't judge" mantra feel even more comforting or familiar to you right now?

It does. It makes me feel a little less alone in this, and a little braver. Like I have an old, trusted friend whispering in my ear. I think that will help me get through Sunday morning without panicking. I'm actually a tiny bit curious to see what happens now.

That feeling of having a trusted ally with you is a wonderful resource, and borrowing that wisdom shows great creativity and connection. Before we officially close, I want to check in on the overall direction we've taken today. Does moving from the full-day avoidance to this simple "twenty-minute watch," anchored by your father's old advice, feel like a plan you can commit to trying this Sunday?

Also, before we dive in, I’d love to hear if there were any other important things you wanted to mention that weren’t on our original list, so we can adjust our focus accordingly.

Hi. Thanks. Um... I'd say it's been around a 7 or 8 this week, honestly. Every time I walk past the staff lounge and hear them laughing, I just feel that knot in my stomach again. I don't think there's anything else I need to add—this whole thing with the missed meet and greet just keeps playing on my mind, making me feel like I'm on the outside looking in.

A persistent seven or eight definitely means the old pattern is still taking root, and that knot in your stomach is a clear reminder that your brain hasn't quite accepted the new script yet. Since you confirmed there aren't other pressing topics, does focusing solely on testing that "five-second rule" with a modified approach feel like the best place to start today?

I guess so... I mean, I keep telling myself that just because I missed one event doesn't mean I'm doomed, but it doesn't feel true when I'm actually there. What kind of modified approach did you have in mind? I'm willing to try something, because I really can't keep feeling like this every day.

The modified approach builds on what we tried last time, but adds a crucial layer of self-validation right before you enter the room. We decided to pair the five-second countdown with a silent mantra you repeat to yourself: *"My worth isn't determined by whether I stand there for five seconds."* This repetition acts as an anchor, reminding your brain that you belong here regardless of your performance. Would you be open to practicing saying that phrase aloud together right now, perhaps imagining walking into that hallway?

Okay... I can try that. So, I'd close my eyes and picture myself walking toward the staff lounge, and then right before I step in, I say "My worth isn't determined by whether I stand there for five seconds"? It feels a bit strange, but I'll give it a shot.

That sounds like a solid plan, and closing your eyes to visualize it beforehand can really ground the idea in your imagination before the reality hits. Imagine stepping into that room, hearing their laughter, and instantly slipping that reassuring phrase into your mind as a shield against the old doubts. Does visualizing that specific sequence—walking in, pausing, whispering the phrase, then counting to five—feel doable for you right now?

Alright, I'm picturing it now... I'm walking in, and there's that familiar flutter of anxiety. I can almost hear the laughter, and I feel that old urge to turn around. But I take a breath and whisper the phrase in my head, and then I start counting... one, two, three, four, five. It doesn't feel like a magic fix, but I didn't immediately want to run away this time, so maybe that's something.

That resistance to running away is a massive breakthrough, even if it feels small right now. It proves that your brain is learning to hold the new message alongside the old fear, which takes time and patience. Before we finalize our homework for tonight, could you tell me if repeating that phrase silently in your head feels manageable, or would you prefer to write it down on a sticky note so you can see it whenever you cross the threshold?

I think writing it on a sticky note might actually help more, honestly. That way, I can have it in my pocket or on my desk, and I could glance at it right before I step into the lounge. Saying it in my head feels good in practice, but having that physical reminder might help me really believe it when my anxiety is high.

That is a brilliant idea; having a tangible anchor makes the abstract concept of "worth" much harder to dismiss when panic rises. Writing it down transforms it from a fleeting thought into a constant companion you can rely on. Before we seal in tonight's plan, could you confirm that you feel ready to create that sticky note and carry it with you tomorrow morning?

Yeah, I feel ready. I'll write it on a bright-colored sticky note and put it in my pocket before I leave for work tomorrow. I think having it there will help me remember that I'm not just trying to survive those five seconds—I'm actually allowed to be in that room. Thanks, I think this could really make a difference.

Hearing you describe yourself as "allowed to be in that room" is such a powerful shift—it moves you from survival to presence. That distinction matters deeply, and having that visible reminder in your pocket will serve as a constant gentle nudge whenever the old fear tries to speak louder. Is there anything else weighing on your mind before we officially close this session and wrap up with our final takeaway?

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you briefly share how you've been feeling emotionally since we last spoke, and is there anything specific you'd like to prioritize for our meeting besides reviewing our homework?

Hey, thanks for having me. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty down since last time. I still can't shake the feeling that my perfect attendance record is completely ruined, and it's like why bother trying now? I guess I'd like to focus on that — how to stop feeling like everything's pointless just because of one mistake.

Hearing that you're carrying this weight of hopelessness despite your track record tells me how deeply that belief impacts your daily energy. Before we dive straight into tackling that feeling, I want to quickly check in on our previous plan: Did you find your keys during the morning rush yesterday, and if so, did you try taking those deep breaths when you noticed them getting difficult to locate?
