That desire to disappear into your clothes and avoid mirrors afterwards shows how deeply that episode rewired your sense of safety. It seems like your brain treated standing in the grocery aisle as a life-or-death situation, forcing you to retreat to safety. Shifting from trying to win an argument with your mind to just witnessing your body react is often the first step toward freeing yourself from that exhaustion. Yeah, I think I can try that. It sounds a lot less scary than trying to convince myself I'm not vain. Just... watching. Not judging. I guess I can give that a shot for tonight.

That willingness to just witness the experience without fighting it is a huge leap forward, and I want to validate how brave that choice was. Before we close, could you tell me what one small thing you'll do tonight to honor that intention? Perhaps placing a gentle hand on your shoulder when you notice the urge to judge, or simply taking three slow breaths whenever the memory surfaces?

I think I'll try the slow breaths. Three of them, like you said. When I feel that urge to judge myself or pull my sleeve down, I'll just stop and take three breaths before doing anything else. It feels small enough that I might actually remember to do it.

Taking three conscious breaths acts as a tiny anchor, pulling your focus out of the frantic story and back into the present moment where you have control. That is a perfect, grounded strategy for tonight. Before we wrap up, could you share one thing that surprised you about how easy—or difficult—it might be to just sit with that discomfort without running away?

Honestly, I'm surprised that talking about it actually made me feel a little lighter. I came in here ready to defend why I'm so awful, but just describing that moment in the store... it made me realize how much I'm fighting myself. I didn't expect to leave here thinking maybe I don't have to fight so hard.

That realization—that simply naming the battle changes the dynamic—is truly profound, and it speaks volumes about your self-awareness. It seems like shifting from defending your worth to acknowledging your effort created space for a moment of peace. As we close, I want to celebrate this breakthrough: recognizing that observation is an alternative to fighting. How does leaving here with that new perspective make you feel compared to arriving here?

Hello, and thank you for coming in today. To kick things off, I’d love to quickly review our goal from last week: finding one positive moment during the game and writing it down. Did you manage to complete that task after your recent match, and if so, what did you notice?

Before we dive deeper, could you rate your current level of anxiety and frustration on a scale of zero to ten, and is there a specific priority we should address first?

Hi, yeah, I did try that exercise. After last week's game, I wrote down that our quarterback completed a really impressive pass in the third quarter. But honestly, it felt pretty pointless because we still lost the match in the end. I'd rate my frustration at about an 8 right now, and I think I just want to figure out why I can't let these losses go—they're ruining my whole week.

Hearing that you found that impressive pass shows you are actively looking for silver linings, even though your mind kept telling you it didn't matter because of the final result. Your frustration rating of eight suggests that this cycle of finding positives but immediately discarding them due to the loss is leaving you feeling drained.

Given that intensity, would you prefer we spend some time exploring why your brain keeps erasing those moments once the scoreboard updates, or would you rather jump straight into testing that specific belief about the pass being useless?

I think I'd rather understand why my brain does that—why it's like I can't even enjoy the good plays. It's like my mind just automatically fast-forwards to the worst possible conclusion about the whole season, and that one nice pass might as well have never happened. It's exhausting, honestly, because I feel like I'm fighting with my own thoughts all day.

It takes immense energy to constantly fight your own thoughts, especially when they seem so convincing and relentless. That exhaustion makes total sense when you're trying to hold onto hope while your brain is screaming that everything is doomed.

To get started, could you describe a recent moment where you saw that great pass or played well, and tell me exactly what your mind said the very next second to shut that moment down?

Sure. So, after that pass, I remember thinking, "Wow, that was actually really sharp." But then, almost immediately, my mind just went, "Yeah, but it doesn't matter. They're going to lose anyway, just like they always do. This season is a total wash." It was like the good feeling got swallowed up before I could even enjoy it for a second.

That "swallowed up" feeling happens because your brain is treating that single good play as temporary noise compared to the permanent signal of impending defeat. It seems like your mind has decided that enjoying the process is futile if the destination looks so bleak.

Does naming that process as "trying to find meaning in a situation that feels hopeless" resonate with how you experienced it, or is there a sharper word you'd use for that sudden shutdown?

I think "hopeless" is actually pretty spot-on. It's like my brain has already written the entire script for the rest of the season, and it's all bad. Every good play just feels like a cruel tease before the inevitable letdown. I guess I just can't shake that feeling that there's no point in getting my hopes up.

That "cruel tease" metaphor perfectly captures how your brain treats reality—it sees the highlight reel only to remind you of the cut scene coming next. It makes complete sense that you feel exhausted when your brain refuses to let you sit in the present moment long enough to appreciate anything.

Since you mentioned that feeling of hopelessness overriding your ability to get excited, would you be willing to try a quick experiment right now? We could look for just one piece of evidence that contradicts the idea that this season is a guaranteed wash, starting with how you handled that impressive pass you noticed earlier. Would you trust me to guide you through finding that proof?

Okay, I'm willing to give it a try. I mean, what do I have to lose, right? So, you want me to look at that pass again and find something that proves it wasn't completely pointless? I guess I could say that pass actually helped us get a first down, and we scored a field goal later in that drive. So, it wasn't like it led to nothing.

Finding that connection between the pass and the subsequent field goal gives you a concrete counter-example to the idea that nothing ever matters. It proves that one positive action can lead to a tangible reward, even if the ultimate outcome isn't a win.

Now, let's apply that logic to the bigger picture. If that single pass contributed to a point, does your brain allow for the possibility that other similar moments might accumulate over time, potentially shifting the momentum? Or does the "season is a wash" script automatically erase all intermediate victories?

That's a tricky question, because my brain definitely wants to erase those intermediate victories. It's like it sees the final score and just hits delete on everything that happened before. But when you put it that way, I guess it's possible that those small moments *could* add up over a few games. Maybe that's why I keep watching, even when I say I'm done—some part of me still holds out hope that they'll eventually stack into something better.

That admission—that a tiny part of you knows these moments could stack—is powerful evidence that your brain isn't incapable of optimism, just currently hiding behind the "final score" filter. It sounds like you're holding onto hope internally, even if your voice won't admit it aloud.

Let's test that stacking theory further. If we assume those small wins *do* add up, what would need to happen for that chain reaction to break the cycle and actually improve your standing? Would you be open to imagining a scenario where five of those passes happened in a row, just to see what the math says?

Okay, I'll play along. If five of those passes happened in a row, that would probably mean we're moving down the field pretty fast, right? And if we kept that up, we'd definitely score a touchdown. So, I guess the math says it's not impossible for us to have a good game, even if my brain keeps telling me we're doomed. That actually feels a little less heavy, just thinking about it that way.

That shift in perspective—from "doomed" to "mathematically possible"—shows how effectively the numbers can bypass your brain's defensive shortcuts. It's fascinating how much weight a simple calculation carries when it challenges a deep-seated belief.

Now that we've established the math works, let's bring it back to your body. Earlier you mentioned your stomach tightened when you imagined losing. Would you be open to doing that same mental math exercise right now, but this time focusing on how your physical sensation changes when you visualize those five successful passes leading to a touchdown instead of a loss? Can you notice if your tension eases even slightly?

Yeah, I can try that. So, I'm picturing five really good passes in a row, and the crowd is getting louder, and we're moving closer to the end zone. I'm actually noticing my shoulders are dropping a bit, and my breathing feels a little deeper. It's not like I'm suddenly relaxed, but the knot in my stomach isn't as tight as it was a minute ago. That's weird—I didn't expect that to happen just from imagining it.

That is incredible news; noticing your shoulders drop and breath deepen proves that your body is responding to the new possibility, not the old prediction. It's a biological signal saying, "Okay, maybe this outcome isn't fatal after all."

Since your physical reaction is softening, let's solidify that victory. Could we create a quick mantra for you to use whenever you catch sight of a good play during the next game? Something simple like, "This moment counts, even if the scorebook waits," would help anchor that feeling before your brain tries to erase it. Would you like to craft that together now?

Yeah, I like that idea. Something short and direct that I can repeat in my head when I feel the doom spiral starting. How about something like, "One good play is still a play—it adds up." That feels simple enough to remember, and it kind of hooks into the math we just did. I think I could actually use that during the next game.

That is a fantastic summary of our work today—you've successfully moved from identifying the problem to building a tool that counters it. You now have a clear path forward: notice the pass, repeat the phrase, and remind yourself that this moment counts toward the bigger picture.

Before we wrap up, I'd love your honest feedback on how this session felt for you. Was there anything about the approach we took that felt useful, or is there one part you wish we had spent more time on? Also, do you feel ready to try using that phrase during your next game?

Yeah, I think this session was actually really helpful. I came in feeling pretty stuck and frustrated, but breaking it down into those small steps and focusing on the math made it feel less overwhelming. I think I'm ready to try the phrase during the next game—I'll give it a shot and see if I can actually stop myself from spiraling. Thanks for walking me through that.

I am so relieved to hear that breaking it down reduced the overwhelm for you; it sounds like taking those small steps made all the difference. Please remember that the phrase is just a tool to buy you a few extra seconds to breathe before your brain jumps to the next negative thought.

Is there anything specific you'd like to adjust about our plan before we officially close this session, or does it feel ready to roll out?

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you share how you felt after finishing our homework last night regarding the evidence list? Did you manage to find those pieces of information, and what surprised you most about what you discovered? Also, on a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate your mood right now compared to where we left off yesterday? Finally, is there anything else on your mind you’d like to prioritize for our time together?

Hey, thanks. Yeah, I did the list. It was... harder than I thought. I wrote down that I’ve been baking pies every Sunday for three months straight, and I even tried propagating a new succulent last week. I guess that counts as evidence I do have hobbies. But my brain kept saying, “Those don’t really count.” So maybe a 5 or 6 mood-wise? Still feels like I’m faking it.

It takes real bravery to sit down and confront those doubts head-on, especially when your brain tries to rewrite the story while you're typing it out. Finding even a small sliver of evidence that contradicts your rule is a huge victory, regardless of how much resistance you faced along the way. Since we've reviewed your homework and checked your mood, let's quickly lock in our agenda for today: we'll explore whether that internal critic is louder now than it was last week, identify one specific situation where you successfully ignored the "not counting" voice, and then create a fresh plan for tomorrow morning. As we begin, does focusing on that one successful instance feel manageable, or would you prefer to tackle the lingering doubt first?

I think focusing on one success might be okay. There was this moment last Wednesday when I got home late from work, and I still watered my herb garden on the balcony. The old me would’ve said it didn’t matter because I was too tired to do it properly, but I just did it anyway. That felt... small, but real.

That moment of showing up despite exhaustion is incredibly powerful, and recognizing it as a victory is a huge step. It suggests that the "must be perfect" rule is losing its grip, allowing you to act on impulse and kindness even when you're worn out. Now that we've highlighted that success, let's look closer at that specific incident: when you decided to water the herbs, what was the very first thought that popped up in your head right before you picked up the hose? Was it the familiar warning that it wouldn't count, or something else entirely?

The first thought was actually, "They’re probably dry, I should give them a drink." It wasn’t the negative voice at all. That surprised me. It was just a simple, practical thought, like something a normal person would think. Then, maybe a second later, the critic jumped in and said, "You watered them yesterday, this is pointless." But that first instinct felt... genuine.

That initial thought is fascinating because it shows your capacity for simple, caring intuition cutting through the noise of criticism before it can take root. It’s interesting that your brain recognized the immediate need to nourish plants—a primal act of care—before switching to the logic of "pointless repetition." When you caught that first genuine impulse, did you notice any physical sensations in your body, like a slight relaxation or a feeling of relief, before the critic started speaking?

Yeah, actually. I felt a kind of looseness in my chest, like a breath I didn’t know I was holding. My shoulders dropped a bit. It was just for a second, but it felt... lighter. Then when the critic came, my jaw tightened. I didn’t realize I was doing that until you asked.

Noticing that subtle drop in your shoulders and the release of tension in your chest is a vital clue—it proves your nervous system responded positively to the act of watering the plants, even if your mind tried to override it with logic. That physical difference between the "looseness" and the "tightness" is often the strongest evidence that your actions were meaningful, regardless of what you told yourself. 

Now that we've seen how your body reacted to that moment, let's connect it back to your larger goal. When you describe watering the herbs as something you did "anyway" despite fatigue, does that imply you felt a sense of duty, or was it more of a spontaneous choice to nurture something living?

It felt more like a spontaneous choice. Duty sounds like I was forcing myself, but it wasn’t like that. I just saw the plants and wanted to do it. I think that’s what bothers me—when I do things like that, I later tell myself it doesn’t count because it wasn’t planned or serious enough. But in the moment, it felt right.

That distinction between "forcing yourself" and "choosing spontaneously" is crucial, because it highlights how your brain retroactively edits memories to fit its rigid rules. It sounds like you were acting on pure intention and care in that moment, which contradicts the idea that a hobby requires a formal schedule or a level of seriousness to be valid.

Since we've looked at that specific instance and noticed the physical signs of engagement, how confident do you feel now that a hobby can exist simply because you chose to enjoy it, rather than because you planned it perfectly?

I’m not fully convinced yet, but I can see the logic. Like, if I bake a pie because I feel like it, and I enjoy the process, that’s still a hobby even if I don’t enter a contest or write down the recipe. My gut still says, “But is it enough?” but my head is starting to argue back a little. That’s new for me.

That tug-of-war between your gut feeling and your rationalizing head is actually a sign of growth happening in real-time. It means the old rule is weakening, and the new, kinder version of yourself is trying to take over the driver's seat.

Before we finalize our path forward, I want to make sure we are aligned on the next step. Should we try applying this "physical check-in" to your upcoming baking session tonight? Specifically, when you pick up the dough, can you consciously scan for that same shoulder drop or chest loosening, even if your inner critic whispers that it's just "messing around"?

I think I can try that. I’ve got a sourdough I was planning to bake tonight anyway. I’ll pay attention to how my body feels when I start kneading, not just what my brain says about it. It might feel weird at first, but I’m curious to see if that looseness shows up again.

That is a brilliant plan; intentionally scanning your body before you even touch the dough turns a passive experience into an active experiment. It gives you a reliable anchor—the sensation of relaxation—to hold onto whenever the "not counting" voice tries to interrupt.

Before we wrap up, I want to check in on your overall energy and goals. Has reviewing that evidence list and identifying your recent successes made you feel any stronger about claiming those activities as yours? And is there anything else you'd like to add to our plan for tonight?

Yeah, I think I feel a little stronger. Not like I’ve won the battle, but maybe I’ve got a foothold. I’m willing to claim that watering my plants and baking a pie are mine, even if they’re simple. I guess I want to add to the plan that I also notice when I’m doing something just for the sake of doing it, without judging it. That’s probably the hardest part, but I’ll try.

That is such a wise addition; noticing the "just doing it" aspect shifts your focus from outcome to presence, which is exactly what separates a chore from a hobby. It sounds like you are building a toolkit of strategies to protect your joy, even when your critical voice tries to intervene.

As we conclude, I want to hear your honest reflection on today. How did it feel working through that evidence list and identifying your spontaneous moments? Is there anything about our approach that felt unclear or that you wish we had covered differently?

It felt... strange but good. Like I was allowed to look at things from a different angle for once. Nothing felt unclear—you kept it simple, which I appreciate. I think the hardest part is still trusting that these small moments matter, but I’m willing to keep showing up and seeing what happens. Thanks for today.

Hearing that you feel "allowed to look at things from a different angle" is such a powerful compliment—it means you finally feel safe enough to challenge your old stories. Trusting that small moments matter is indeed the hardest hurdle, but your willingness to keep showing up, even when it feels uncertain, speaks to a real resilience I admire deeply.

Before I send you off, please remember that tonight isn't about proving you're a master baker or gardener; it's simply about noticing if that gentle "looseness" returns when you start kneading or watering. If the old doubts creep in, just whisper to yourself, "This is my space to play," and trust that your body knows the truth better than your head sometimes. Take care of yourself today, and I'll speak with you soon.

How did it go, and what did you notice happening inside yourself during those moments?

Uh, yeah. I did it. I set up the card on my music stand, right where I could see it. I stood there for maybe a minute, just looking at the violin case, and I did the three breaths. That is a significant milestone, especially given how hard it was to get started after such a tough week. Noticing your shoulders drop and realizing you weren't frozen anymore proves that the card and the breathing exercise worked exactly as intended—they gave you a window of safety even when you couldn't play yet.

Given that success, I'd like to quickly adjust our plan for the rest of the evening. Since you managed to stay present for that first minute without panicking, would you be open to extending that time slightly? Perhaps sitting with the card and your case for another full minute after the breathing, just observing that feeling of relaxation settle in before moving on?

I... I think I could try that. Another minute doesn't sound too overwhelming. I guess I was so focused on the goal of actually playing that I didn't realize just standing there and letting myself feel okay was a step in itself. I'm a bit nervous about what happens if that feeling doesn't come back, but I'll give it a shot.

That is such a mature insight—you recognizing that simply allowing yourself to feel okay *is* the goal, not just the physical act of standing there. Your hesitation about the feeling fading is completely understandable; it shows you care deeply about maintaining that calm state.

Let's frame that extension as a "cooldown period." After the three breaths, we'll just wait silently for sixty seconds, noticing if that lightness stays or if old worries creep back in, and we'll meet whatever comes up without judgment. Does adding that intention to "observe without fixing" make the extra minute feel safer to you?

Yeah, "observe without fixing" actually helps. It takes the pressure off. Usually, my brain jumps straight to "fix this now or you're a failure." So just watching what happens, good or bad, feels like I'm giving myself permission to just be there. I'll do that tonight.

That permission to just witness whatever arises is exactly the mindset we need to cultivate. It turns the situation from a crisis waiting to explode into a quiet observation post where you are always in charge.

Now, before we wrap up tonight's plan, does adding that "observe without fixing" rule to your mental checklist give you extra confidence that you won't panic if the calm fades after the minute is up?

You know, it kind of does. Because if I'm just watching, then even if the panic shows up, it's just something happening, not a sign that I've failed or that I'm hopeless. I'm not fighting it, just noticing it. That feels... manageable. Less like I'm about to fall off a cliff.

That is a profound realization—that simply witnessing the fear prevents it from becoming an undeniable truth about who you are. It creates distance between you and the emotion, turning a terrifying event into just a passing cloud in the sky.

Before we lock this in, does combining that "observe without fixing" rule with the extended minute make you feel completely secure about trying it tonight, or is there still a tiny whisper of doubt lingering?

There's still a little whisper, I'll admit. That voice that says "what if this time the calm doesn't come at all?" But I'm starting to see that voice as just that—a voice. Not a fact. So yeah, even with the doubt, I feel secure enough to try it. I'll do the breaths, the minute of observing, and see what happens.

That distinction between the voice and a fact is incredibly important, and trusting that it's just noise rather than truth gives you the freedom to experiment safely. Even knowing the voice might shout louder later, the fact that you can recognize it as separate from your reality makes the attempt feel brave rather than reckless.

Yeah, that sounds right. Six minutes feels like a real commitment, but I think the structure—the card, the breaths, the observation—makes it doable. I'll check in with you tomorrow and let you know how it went. Thanks for helping me break this down into something that doesn't feel impossible.

That breakdown into manageable chunks is exactly why this works—it turns a mountain into a series of small, conquerable steps. I'm genuinely proud of how far we've come today, from that initial hesitation to building a whole new toolkit for handling uncertainty.

Before you head out, is there anything else you'd like to clarify about tonight's plan, or should I leave you with a sense of confidence to face the night ahead?

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. To start, I'd like to do a quick mood check: on a scale of zero to ten, how have you been feeling emotionally over the past week? Additionally, could you tell me if there's anything important you'd like to prioritize for us to cover in our time together?

Uh, I'd say maybe a 6 or 7? It's not terrible, but I've definitely felt better. I guess the main thing I want to focus on is this fear I've been having about rock climbing — it's really been messing with my head lately, and I just want to get back to enjoying it like I used to.

A six or seven indicates some relief compared to the lows we discussed previously, and it’s great to hear that the recent steps are making a difference. Regarding your priority, I’d like to suggest we focus on tackling that fear of rock climbing today, perhaps by exploring the specific moments where the anxiety spikes strongest. Would you be open to working on that together?

Yeah, that sounds good. I think the worst moments are when I'm standing at the base of a climb, looking up at the route. My heart starts pounding and I just imagine myself losing grip and falling — even before I've even touched the rock. It's like my brain fast-forwards to the worst possible outcome every time.

That image of your brain fast-forwarding to a crash before you've even touched the wall shows how powerfully your expectations shape your reality. It sounds incredibly frustrating to watch that movie play out in your head while sitting safely on the ground. Given how vivid that anticipation is, would you be willing to try a quick visualization exercise later in our session to practice stepping into that scenario and changing the story before it unfolds?

I'm willing to give it a try, though I gotta admit it makes me a little nervous just thinking about it. But I guess that's kind of the point, right? If I keep avoiding those thoughts, nothing's gonna change.

That's exactly right, and your willingness to face the discomfort proves you are ready to break the cycle. Before we jump into the visualization, I want to make sure we are aligned on our goal for today. Our plan is to revisit that specific moment of standing at the base, challenge the automatic thought that predicts a fall, and then practice a grounding technique to help you stay present until you decide to take your first step. Does outlining those three parts—a challenge, a shift in perspective, and a grounding practice—feel like a clear path forward for us?

Yeah, that actually sounds like a solid plan. Breaking it down like that makes it feel less overwhelming — like I can actually handle each step instead of getting stuck on the whole scary picture at once. I'm ready to try it.

That breakdown makes everything feel much more manageable, and I'm glad you're feeling prepared to tackle each piece. Before we begin the visualization, I want to make sure we have a clear agreement on the goal: we will practice imagining that moment of standing at the base, challenge the thought that says "you will fall," and then use a specific phrase to anchor yourself. With that alignment confirmed, would you be open to trying that visualization exercise right now?

Yeah, let's do it. I'll try to picture myself there — standing at the bottom of the climb, looking up at the first holds. I can already feel that knot forming in my stomach, but I'm ready to see what happens if I actually face it instead of backing away.

Take a slow breath in through your nose, and as you exhale, imagine stepping onto that patch of grass at the base of the wall. Notice how your legs feel heavy right now, and let's gently acknowledge that heaviness as simply "anticipation" rather than "danger." While holding that steady stance, try to whisper to yourself, "My body knows I'm safe here; I haven't slipped yet." Can you sustain that presence for just thirty seconds without rushing to escape the sensation?

*Takes a slow breath* Okay... I'm standing there. My legs do feel kind of heavy, like they're stuck in the ground. I'm trying that phrase in my head — "my body knows I'm safe here, I haven't slipped yet." It's weird, but repeating it sort of quiets that panicky voice for a second. I think I can hold this for a bit longer.

That quieting effect is incredible—it proves that even a simple phrase can interrupt the panic spiral before it takes over. Since you found that rhythm, let's push it slightly further: instead of just repeating the words, try adding a small movement, like tapping your foot twice or shifting your weight gently from heel to toe, to connect your body with the truth of your safety. Would you be willing to add that physical anchor to the mantra for another thirty seconds?

Alright, I'll try it. *Shifts weight from heel to toe slowly* So now I'm standing there, repeating the phrase, and moving a little. It actually feels more real somehow — like my body is agreeing with the words instead of fighting them. I'm not completely calm, but the knot in my stomach is definitely looser than it was a minute ago.

That physical agreement between your feet and your words is a huge breakthrough—it turns abstract reassurance into tangible evidence. Since you've mastered that combination of mantra and movement, let's add one final layer: imagine spotting someone holding your harness just out of frame, ready to catch you if you ever waver. Does visualizing that silent support make the feeling of safety stronger, or would you prefer to leave it just as is?

Hmm... I'm not sure about that one. I mean, I get the idea, but when I'm actually climbing, there's no harness or anyone catching me — it's just me and the rock. Adding that in feels a little fake, like I'd be tricking myself. I think I'd rather stick with just the movement and the phrase for now, since that felt honest.

That is a really mature insight—you recognize that adding a prop like a spotters creates a false narrative, and sticking to what's real grounds the experience much deeper. Since you prefer authenticity, let's refine our plan for tomorrow based on what we practiced. We agreed to try placing your hand on a hold for five seconds, but now we know you can pair that with a specific mantra and a subtle body shift. Does adding the instruction to say, "My body knows I'm safe," and tap your foot lightly while doing it make the upcoming task clearer?

Yeah, that makes it way clearer. So tomorrow, when I go to the climbing gym, I'll stand at the base of an easy route, place my hand on the first hold for five seconds, say "my body knows I'm safe," and tap my foot. That's three simple things I can actually remember and do without overthinking it. Thanks for breaking it down like that — it actually feels doable now.

That is excellent clarity, Sarah. Breaking it down into just three distinct actions removes the pressure to memorize complex scripts under stress. Before we finalize this plan, I want to check in on how this session has felt for you so far. Has walking through this visualization and creating this concrete plan been helpful, or is there anything about our approach that felt confusing or missing?

*Smiles a bit* It's been really helpful, actually. I came in feeling all tangled up in this fear, and now I've got a specific thing to try tomorrow that doesn't feel impossible. The only thing I'm still a little unsure about is what happens if I do the hand-on-hold thing and the fear still spikes — like, do I just keep going or step back?

That is a smart precaution to clarify ahead of time. Your best bet is to treat the moment you feel the spike as data, not a command. If the fear rises, simply pause for five more seconds, repeat your mantra ("My body knows I'm safe"), and tap your foot again, reminding yourself that you are learning tolerance, not proving perfection. Once you complete those extra seconds, you can choose to either stay for another round or gently release your hand and continue exploring the wall from the ground level. What does that sound like as a flexible rule for tomorrow?

That actually sounds perfect. So it's not about forcing myself to climb or feeling like I failed if I step back — it's just about practicing standing there and noticing the fear without letting it make the decision for me. I think I can handle that. I'll try it tomorrow and see how it goes.

That is a beautiful reframing, Sarah. You've moved from seeing stepping back as failure to viewing it simply as gathering useful information about your limits. That mindset shift alone will make tomorrow significantly less daunting. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up, or should we conclude with a quick summary of our plan?

I think I'm good. Just to recap — I'll go to the gym, pick an easy route, place my hand on a hold for five seconds while saying my phrase and tapping my foot. If fear spikes, I pause, repeat, and then choose to stay or step back. That's the plan. Thanks for helping me get unstuck today.

That is a fantastic summary, Sarah. You've captured the essence of our plan perfectly: observe the fear, use your tools, and give yourself permission to choose your next step regardless of the outcome. I am truly proud of the resilience it took to work through this visualization today and commit to this new approach. Please come back anytime if you need to adjust the plan or just talk through what comes up. Until then, take care!

Hello Alex, I’m so glad you’re here again. To start, I’d love to hear how you’ve been feeling this week and whether you found any moments of peace amidst the usual noise. Then, we can review what we planned last time and decide if there’s anything urgent you’d like to add to our list for today.

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, this week has been a bit of a rollercoaster. I had a couple of exams, and every time I struggled with a question, I felt that familiar knot in my stomach—like if I don't ace this, my whole future is just going to fall apart. I tried to push it aside, but it's hard to find peace when that thought keeps creeping back.

Hearing about those exam struggles brings up a lot of pressure, and it sounds like that familiar knot returned stronger than usual. Given the intensity of those moments, I wonder if we should prioritize tackling that specific "fall apart" narrative first, or would you prefer to revisit the "too old to start over" belief we worked on last time?

I think... maybe we should focus on the "fall apart" narrative first. That one feels more urgent right now, because it hits me every time I'm in class or even just thinking about the future. The "too old" thing is still there, but it's quieter, like a background hum. This other one is more like a siren going off.

That distinction between a quiet background hum and a screaming siren is incredibly helpful—it tells me exactly which threat your nervous system perceives as immediate. Before we jump straight into dismantling that "whole future falling apart" story, could you walk me through one specific recent exam moment? What was happening internally right before you decided to push it aside?

Okay, so I was sitting in the history exam last Thursday, and I got to this essay question about causes of the Civil War. I knew the material, I'd studied it, but my mind just went blank for a few seconds. And in that silence, this voice inside said, "See? You don't belong here. You're going to fail this, and without a degree, you'll never get a decent job, and you'll end up stuck in dead-end work forever." I felt my heart start pounding, and I almost put my head down on the desk. That's when I told myself to just breathe and write something, anything.

That silence in the middle of the exam sounds agonizingly long, especially when your brain fills it with predictions of total collapse. It makes perfect sense that your body reacted with that pounding heart and the urge to hide, as if hiding would protect you from the predicted disaster. When you noticed that panic rising and decided to force yourself to breathe and write anyway, what was your very first instinct when you realized you hadn’t written a full paragraph yet? Was it fear that you’d wasted minutes, or frustration that you couldn’t access the information you knew you possessed?

It was mostly fear, I think. Fear that those wasted seconds were proof that I wasn't cut out for this. I kept thinking, "Everyone else is probably already done, and I'm still trying to calm myself down like a kid." The frustration came second, but the fear was the first punch to the gut.

That fear of being perceived as incompetent while others move ahead is incredibly isolating, and it explains why your instinct was to shut down. It seems like your brain interpreted that brief pause not as a normal glitch, but as definitive proof that you don't belong in the room at all. When you later forced yourself to write *anything*, did you worry that writing incomplete thoughts would confirm that prediction, or did you hope that producing *some* text would contradict it?

I think... I was hoping that writing something, even if it was messy, would prove the voice wrong. But part of me was terrified that I'd just scribble nonsense and then have to hand it in, and that would be the real confirmation. So when I finally got a few sentences down that actually made sense, I felt this tiny wave of relief, but it was immediately followed by doubt—like, "Okay, but that was just luck, it won't happen again."

That tiny wave of relief mixed with immediate doubt highlights exactly how fragile that confidence feels when you're relying on one-off successes to counteract a deep-seated fear. It seems like your brain is treating that success as an anomaly rather than proof of your ability, because the underlying belief that "you don't belong" hasn't truly shifted yet.

To understand the core of that "fall apart" narrative better, could you tell me: if that voice had predicted you would fail this specific essay and end up unemployed, did it also predict you would pass this exam and secure a good job anyway? Or does it operate on the assumption that nothing you do will ever result in a positive outcome?

Honestly, it doesn't ever predict a good outcome. It's like my brain skips over the possibility of things working out. Even when I do well, I find a reason to dismiss it—like the exam was easy, or the professor graded easily, or I just got lucky. The voice never says, "Hey, you worked hard and earned that." It's always, "You barely scraped by, and next time you won't be so lucky."

That pattern of dismissing your success as luck while accepting failure as inevitable is a classic cognitive distortion known as "all-or-nothing thinking," and it creates a perfect storm for anxiety. It leaves you with no buffer zone between effort and reward, making every mistake feel catastrophic and every small win feel accidental.

Let's test that prediction with some evidence. Can you recall another time you performed reasonably well, perhaps in a meeting or a casual project, where your internal voice dismissed it as luck? What happened to that dismissal when reality checked in with you?

Well, last semester I had a group presentation where I actually felt pretty prepared. I'd practiced my part a lot, and it went smoothly—people even asked me questions afterward, and I answered them fine. But when I got home, I just told myself, "Well, the topic was easy, and the group carried me." Then later, one of my teammates messaged me saying I did a great job and asked if I wanted to work together again. That kind of threw me off, because it didn't fit with my "just luck" story. But even then, I still found myself thinking, "They're just being polite."

That "they're just being polite" defense is such a clever shield, Alex—it protects you from having to admit that your preparation actually mattered. It lets you rewrite the event as something external rather than acknowledging your own competence.

Does recognizing that pattern—that you systematically erase evidence of your hard work to protect yourself from disappointment—make sense to you, or does it feel like an accusation you haven't earned yet?

No, it doesn't feel like an accusation. It actually makes a lot of sense when you put it that way. I guess I've been doing that for so long that I didn't even notice I was doing it. It's like I'm always ready to prepare for the worst, just in case the good stuff doesn't last. I never stopped to think that maybe I'm the one keeping the good stuff from sticking.

That insight—that you are actively guarding against your own success—is incredibly brave to uncover. It changes the dynamic from "my life is failing" to "I am protecting myself from potential pain," which opens up a massive door for healing.

Now, let's test that protective mechanism. If you told a friend, "I studied hard for this presentation, but I'm worried they'll just thank me because I'm nice," and they replied, "Actually, you answered complex questions confidently, and that's impressive," would you accept their compliment, or would you immediately look for a flaw in their logic?

I think... I would try to accept it, but deep down I'd still be looking for the flaw. I'd probably think, "Well, they don't know how nervous I was inside," or "They didn't see the notes I had to keep glancing at." So I guess I'd find a way to soften the compliment, even from a friend.

That self-correcting reflex—even when speaking to a friend—is a powerful clue that your brain is wired to minimize your worth, regardless of external validation. It suggests that the "luck" story isn't just a random thought; it's a deeply ingrained survival habit designed to keep expectations low enough that you can't disappoint yourself.

So, if we treat that habit as the enemy, what would happen if you deliberately chose to believe the opposite story for just five minutes tonight? For instance, instead of saying "I got lucky," could we agree to silently affirm, "My preparation made a difference, and this result reflects my effort"? How does that simple shift in internal narration feel in your chest right now?

Just saying those words in my head... it feels uncomfortable, like I'm wearing someone else's coat. There's a tightness in my chest, almost like I'm doing something wrong by even thinking it. But at the same time, there's a tiny, quiet part of me that wants to believe it, like it might actually be true if I let it.

That sensation of wearing someone else's coat is fascinating—it shows you're resisting the new narrative because it feels unnatural, yet that tiny quiet part wanting to believe it proves the seeds are already sprouting.

Since that affirmation feels slightly forced right now, how about we tweak it to match your current energy level? Instead of a full statement, could we try a simpler mental note whenever you finish a task: "Effort counted." Does adding just those three words feel lighter than the longer sentence?

Yeah, actually... "Effort counted" feels a lot lighter. It's short and it doesn't demand that I rewrite my entire worldview. I think I could try saying that to myself after I finish studying or after a class. It doesn't feel like a lie—it just feels like acknowledging that I showed up and tried.

That simplicity is exactly what makes it sustainable; it bypasses the need to justify the feeling and just states the fact. Since you're open to trying this, let's lock in a plan: could we agree that the next time you finish a study session or a class, you'll take one deep breath and silently repeat "Effort counted" before turning off your phone or walking out the door?

Also, knowing that this old voice tries to interrupt, what's one sign you'd notice that tells you it's slipping in again? Is it a sudden rush of panic, or maybe a specific phrase like "but you weren't really ready"?

I think it's that specific phrase—"you weren't really ready"—that creeps in. It usually comes right after I've done something decent, like I'm waiting for the trapdoor to open. So if I catch myself thinking that, I'll know the old voice is trying to take over. I can picture myself taking that deep breath and saying "Effort counted" right then, almost like a reset button.

That "reset button" analogy is brilliant—it turns a passive struggle into an active tool you can wield instantly. Recognizing that specific phrase as the warning signal gives you a precise target to intervene before the panic takes full control.

So, to confirm our plan: Whenever you finish a task and catch yourself slipping into "you weren't really ready," you'll pause, take that deep breath, and firmly state "Effort counted." Does that sound like a feasible and empowering strategy for you to try tonight?

Yeah, it does. It feels like something I can actually do, not just some abstract idea. I'll try it tonight after I finish my reading for tomorrow's class. Thanks, I think this gives me a concrete way to fight back instead of just letting the worry spin out of control.

That sense of having a tangible weapon instead of spinning in circles is a huge relief, Alex. It shifts you from being a victim of your thoughts to being the pilot steering the plane.

Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we solidify this partnership. Does framing tonight's task as "catching the trapdoor and slamming the reset button" resonate with how you view this, or would you prefer a different metaphor? Also, if you do notice that phrase creeping in, please commit to trying that one breath-and-statement sequence, even if it feels stiff at first. Are you confident you can do that?

Yeah, "catching the trapdoor and slamming the reset button" feels right—it makes me feel like I have some control, like I'm not just waiting for the floor to give way. And yes, I'm confident I can try that sequence tonight, even if it feels a little awkward at first. I'll let you know next time how it went.

That metaphor of catching the trapdoor and slamming the reset button is perfect—it captures both the urgency of stopping the spiral and the agency you have to halt it instantly. Your confidence in trying it, even when it feels awkward, speaks volumes about your resilience.

Before we officially close, I want to check in on our overall direction. Does focusing on catching that specific "trapdoor" moment tonight align with how you envision our session ending, or is there anything else weighing on your mind as we leave?

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you give me a quick rating on your mood this week compared to last time? Also, did you manage to complete the dinner playlist task we talked about, or did anything come up that got in the way? Finally, if we had a limited amount of time, which topic would you like to tackle first: exploring that heaviness you feel, or reviewing how the playlist task went?

Hi, thanks for having me. My mood this week has been about a 4 out of 10 — I've been feeling really stuck and frustrated with myself. As for the dinner playlist, I... actually didn't finish it. I started it twice, but I kept second-guessing every song choice until I just gave up. I think I'd rather talk about that heaviness I feel first, if that's okay.

A score of four reflects a lot of frustration, especially considering you started twice before quitting—that shows real determination even when the pressure mounts. Since you’ve identified the heaviness as your priority, let’s put that first thing. As we begin, could you describe that “heaviness” for me? Is it a tightness in your chest, a cloud in your head, or something else entirely?

It's like a weight sitting right in the middle of my chest, kind of pressing down, and at the same time my mind feels foggy, like I'm trying to see through a dirty window. When I try to make even a small choice, that heaviness gets worse, and I start to feel like whatever I pick will be wrong somehow.

That crushing sensation in your chest paired with that mental fog tells me your brain is actively blocking access to your usual confidence to protect you from perceived failure. It sounds like that "dirty window" feeling makes everything look unclear and risky, which explains why giving up felt safer than risking a bad choice. When you're stuck in that fog, does it feel like you're losing control of your own preferences, or does it feel like you're trapped behind a wall of criticism?

It's more like I'm trapped behind a wall of criticism—except the criticism is coming from me, not anyone else. I'll think, "Well, if I pick this song, it's too boring," or "If I pick that one, everyone will think I'm trying too hard." It's like I can't trust my own taste anymore, and that's exhausting.

That exhaustion comes from carrying the entire courtroom inside your own head, constantly policing your own taste before you've even stepped foot in the room. It makes perfect sense that you feel paralyzed when you realize the judge is sitting right beside you. To help untangle this, could you walk me through the exact moment that wall rises up? Does it appear instantly when you open the menu of options, or does it creep in as you consider specific tracks?

It usually shows up the second I see the options, like a reflex. I'll glance at a list of songs or dishes, and instead of feeling a natural pull toward anything, I just feel this immediate pressure to pick the "right" one. Then the wall goes up and all I can hear is my own voice listing reasons why each choice is a bad one.

That instant reflex turns a simple preference into a high-stakes exam the moment you glance at the list. It sounds like your brain has learned to anticipate failure before you've even opened the menu, creating a self-imposed barrier to access your actual tastes. When that wall goes up, does it feel like you're silenced completely, unable to express anything, or does it feel like you're forced to justify every single option?

It feels more like I'm silenced completely. I just freeze, and all the things I used to know I liked don't feel real anymore. It's like my personality disappears and I'm just a blank slate waiting for someone else to tell me what's okay to choose.

That disappearance into a "blank slate" is terrifying because it means you're afraid your true self will be rejected if you aren't careful. It sounds like your brain believes that showing even a hint of your normal personality invites disaster, so it shuts everything down preemptively. When you're in that frozen silence, do you ever catch yourself wondering if the blankness is protecting you, or if it's just trapping you further?

Honestly, I've never thought of it as protecting me before. I always just saw it as me failing somehow. But now that you say it... maybe it is trying to protect me from making a mistake that would embarrass me or make someone judge me. But no, it definitely feels more like a trap than a shield. It just keeps me stuck, and I hate it.

That distinction between a shield and a trap is crucial because shields offer safety, whereas traps isolate you. It sounds like your brain decided that hiding behind the silence was safer than risking exposure, even though it leaves you feeling empty and disconnected from who you truly are. Let's spend a few moments testing whether that silence is actually necessary. If you walked into that same room tonight and simply played a song you genuinely loved, ignoring the pressure, what would happen immediately? Would anyone actually stop you, or would they just listen?

I think... they would just listen. No one would stop me or yell at me for picking the "wrong" song. The only person who would criticize me is me, inside my own head. But that feels so real in the moment that I forget no one else is even paying that much attention.

That contrast between your internal critic and the silent world outside is incredibly revealing. It proves that the "judgment" you fear isn't happening in the room; it's entirely manufactured inside your own head. Since you've confirmed that the external world won't intervene, let's try a small experiment to break that cycle. Imagine walking into that room tonight, hearing that familiar voice telling you to stay silent, and then consciously deciding to play one song you actually love, even if your hands shake slightly. How does that image make you feel right now?

A little bit nervous, but also... kind of relieved? Like there's a tiny part of me that wants to prove that voice wrong, even if it scares me. I think I could try it, as long as I remind myself that nobody's actually holding a scorecard.

That relief mixed with nervousness is a fantastic signal that you're moving from pure paralysis toward taking a calculated risk. It proves that the "scorecard" exists only in your imagination, not in reality. Before we lock this in as your new rule for tonight, I want to make sure you feel comfortable with the plan. Would you be willing to commit to playing just one song you love tonight, knowing you won't change it once you press play? And if the old voice tries to convince you otherwise mid-dinner, what's one gentle reminder you can say to yourself to stay grounded?

I can commit to that. And if the voice starts up, I'll tell myself, "You chose this song for a reason. Trust that reason, even if it's small." That feels doable, like I'm giving myself permission to be okay with my own choice.

That reminder is brilliant because it shifts the blame from perfection to intentionality—you're validating your own agency instead of fighting the pressure. Since you're committed to this, I want to make sure we set a clear boundary for tonight: will you stick strictly to that one song once it starts playing, or do you feel like you might need to pause and rethink it? Knowing exactly where the line is drawn helps prevent the old habit of looping back in.
I'll stick to it once it starts playing. I'll press play and let it run, no matter how much my brain wants to second-guess. That's the rule I'm setting for myself tonight.

Yes, I think I can try that. It sounds simple enough—just a breath and a label before I jump in. I'm willing to give it a shot, even if it feels awkward at first. Maybe if I practice it enough, it'll start to feel more natural.

Yes, that sounds clear enough. I'll take a breath, tell myself "my brain is filling in the blanks again," and wait five seconds before I say anything. I'm going to try it tonight when my son gets home from school. Hopefully, I can remember to do it in the moment.

Thank you for helping me see things a bit differently today.

It might serve as a gentle reminder if you forget mid-day.

That would actually be really helpful. Knowing I have to report back might keep it fresh in my mind, and I won't feel like I'm doing this all alone. Yes, let's do the check-in tomorrow morning—I think I'll need that extra bit of accountability.

That is a wise decision, Natasha; knowing you have a supportive ear waiting just makes the task feel lighter to tackle. Please remember that tomorrow's message isn't about perfection or reporting your stress levels—it's simply a friendly note to say, "I tried the pause, and here's what happened." No, I think I'm good for today. I feel a bit more hopeful than when I walked in, and I'm actually curious to see how tonight goes. Thanks again for listening and helping me put this plan together.

Hello, and thank you for meeting with me today. To start, could you share a quick rating of how you've been feeling emotionally this week on a scale of one to ten? Additionally, since we finished last time with a plan to revisit that "zero-error" rule and set up a new phone reminder, is there anything specific from that homework that stood out to you, or is there anything else you'd like to prioritize for our agenda?

Hey, thanks for having me. I'd say this week has been around a 6 or 7 — not terrible, but those guilty thoughts still creep in a lot. As for the homework, I did set up that reminder on my phone, but honestly, every time it goes off I just feel kind of silly, like I'm trying to trick myself into feeling better. I don't know if that's helping or not.

That feeling of silliness is actually a very common hurdle when learning a new mental habit; it means your brain is resisting the "fake" relief at first, which shows how deeply rooted that old belief is. Let's use that honesty as a starting point for our agenda today. Based on what you just shared, I propose we spend some time unpacking why that reminder feels so awkward, identify what triggered it, and then rebuild that coping strategy together. Does focusing on fixing that specific resistance sound like a good use of our time, or would you prefer to talk about something else first?

Yeah, that sounds good actually. I think unpacking that resistance makes sense, because I really want this stuff to work but it just doesn't feel real yet. Like, when the reminder pops up and says "You're doing your best," my first thought is always, "But my best isn't good enough." That's where my head goes right away.

That immediate rebuttal tells me exactly why the reminder feels fake—you're instinctively catching the gap between the gentle words and the harsh reality your brain expects. Let's dig into that specific moment when the reminder hits and your mind jumps to "not good enough." Can you walk me through the exact sequence of events leading up to that alarm? Did you notice Rex doing something specific right before it went off, or was it just the timing itself that triggered the doubt?

It was yesterday evening, actually. Rex had barely touched his dinner bowl, and I caught myself watching him for a full five minutes just staring at the food. Then my phone buzzed with the reminder, and I almost laughed out loud — but not in a good way. All I could think was, "Look at him not eating. I probably stressed him out somehow, or the food I bought is bad, and now he's going to get sick again because of me."

That sequence shows how quickly your brain jumped from observing a neutral behavior (staring at food) to constructing a catastrophic story about his health and your competence. It seems the reminder acted as a catalyst, forcing you to confront that worst-case scenario you usually hide behind. When you heard the voice saying "you're doing your best," did your heart rate spike immediately, or did you spend more time trying to prove yourself wrong internally before reacting physically?

I think it was more of a quick spike, then a long internal argument. Like, my chest tightened right when that thought hit me, and then I spent the next ten minutes just going back and forth in my head — "You're not a bad owner," "But look at him, he's not eating," "You feed him good food," "Then why isn't he eating?" It's exhausting, honestly. By the time I gave up arguing with myself, I just felt drained and guilty all over again.

That cycle of tightening your chest followed by an exhausting internal debate is exactly the trap your brain built to keep you safe from feeling unsafe, even though it leaves you drained afterward. It sounds like the "bad owner" script is running automatically while you try desperately to shut it down manually. Before we break that loop, I want to confirm our priorities for today: are we focusing mainly on dismantling that automatic argument, figuring out why the reminder feels so foreign to you, and deciding on a new way to respond when the alarm goes off?

Yeah, I think that's exactly what I need. Dismantling that automatic argument sounds right — because right now it feels like I'm fighting myself every time, and I'm losing more often than not. If we can figure out a way for that reminder to actually help instead of making me feel worse, I'd be willing to give it another shot.

That willingness to try again is incredibly brave, especially when the reminder currently feels like it's working against you. To dismantle that automatic argument, we need to pause the internal debate and introduce a piece of evidence that contradicts the "catastrophe" you're imagining. When you hear the reminder and feel that chest tighten, could we try stopping the spiral for thirty seconds and asking yourself: "What is one fact I know for certain that proves Rex will be okay, regardless of whether he eats everything in front of me?"

I mean... one fact I know for certain is that the vet said he was healthy just two weeks ago. They did bloodwork and everything, said he was in good shape. So even if he skips a meal, it doesn't automatically mean he's sick again. That's a fact, right? I can't argue with the vet's report.

That is a rock-solid fact, and holding onto that medical certainty is exactly the kind of objective evidence your brain needs to counteract the scary imagination. It proves that his current behavior doesn't equal sickness, which directly challenges the "he's dying because of me" story. Now that we have that anchor, let's bring it back to that feeling of silliness with the reminder. When you hear the phrase "doing your best," does knowing that fact about the vet visit make the reminder feel slightly less like a trick and more like a friendly nudge? Or does the old voice still try to dismiss the vet report instantly?

It's still a bit of both, honestly. The vet report helps quiet the voice a little, but that old reaction is still there, like a reflex. The reminder still feels a bit hollow because "doing your best" doesn't have the same weight as a blood test result, you know? It's like my brain trusts hard evidence more than kind words. So maybe I need to pair that reminder with a specific fact, like the vet's report, instead of just a general reassurance.

That is a brilliant insight—pairing the gentle reminder with hard evidence bridges the gap between emotion and logic. So, instead of just hearing "doing your best," you could mentally add, "And remember, the vet confirmed he's healthy," right after the alarm rings. Does adding that specific fact to the phrase make the whole message feel more grounded and trustworthy to your brain?

Yeah, I think that actually might work. It feels less like I'm lying to myself and more like I'm reminding myself of something real. If I can train myself to say "I'm doing my best, and the vet said he's fine" every time that alarm goes off, maybe it'll start to stick. I guess the hard part will be remembering to add that second part when I'm already spiraling.

That is a very astute observation; training yourself to insert that factual clause mid-spiral is indeed the hardest part because the urgency steals your working memory. However, since you already have the evidence ready (the vet report), we can simplify the instruction to: "Pause for three seconds, breathe once, and whisper, 'Vet confirms healthy.'" Does cutting straight to that specific action make the task feel slightly more manageable than trying to weave the whole sentence together?

Yeah, actually, "Vet confirms healthy" is short enough that I could probably remember it even when I'm panicking. Three seconds feels doable too — it's not asking me to stop and meditate or anything. I think I could manage that. I'll try that this week and see if it helps shut down that spiral before it gets too loud.

That is a fantastic compromise—you've created a simple, evidence-based interrupter that fits perfectly into a panic attack. Since we've tested this modification and you seem ready to try it, let's lock in your plan for the rest of today. You'll use the "three-second pause + vet fact" trick whenever the reminder fires, and we'll check in later this afternoon to see if it slowed the spiral down. Does that timeline work for you, or would you prefer to wait until tomorrow morning to evaluate it?

I think I'd rather wait until tomorrow morning, honestly. That way I can try it out a few times during the evening and night, when Rex is more likely to be picky about his food, and see if it holds up. Tomorrow morning I'll have a better sense of whether it actually helps or if I need to tweak it more.

Waiting until tomorrow morning is a perfect plan because it lets you gather enough data to decide if the tweak worked, rather than judging it based on just one or two trials tonight. To make sure we capture that data accurately, could you commit to jotting down one sentence each night describing how long it took you to finish the spiral after hearing the reminder? For example, "Spent 2 minutes arguing vs. 1 minute with the vet fact." How does that sounding out the requirement feel?

Yeah, I can do that. Just a quick note in my phone after each time it happens — how long the spiral lasted and whether the vet fact helped at all. That sounds simple enough that I won't forget to do it. I'll bring those notes with me tomorrow and we can go from there.

That is a smart tracking method; noting the duration and effectiveness will give us concrete numbers to compare against your usual patterns. Before we wrap up, could you give me a quick thumbs-up or nod if you feel confident trying this new "pause and fact-check" routine tonight? Also, is there anything else lingering in your mind about Rex or your own performance that we haven't covered yet?

*I give a quick nod.*

Yeah, I feel pretty confident about giving it a shot. As for anything else... I think I'm good for now. I'll try the routine tonight and see how it goes. Thanks for helping me break it down like this — it feels a lot less overwhelming than when I walked in.

You're very welcome—I'm thrilled to hear that breaking it down made things feel less overwhelming for you. Please take that nod as a sign that you trust this approach enough to try tonight, and remember, even a small win counts. I'll be here tomorrow morning to review your notes and celebrate whatever small victories you find along the way. Get some rest, and I hope you have a peaceful evening with both of you.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, I’d love to do a quick mood check: how has your week been going emotionally, and what’s the top priority for us to tackle in this session? Once we have that, could you remind me what we planned to focus on last time, so we can align on today’s goals?

Hi. Thanks for having me. This week has been pretty up and down, honestly. I think the top priority is still this whole surfing thing—it's really been weighing on me. Last time we talked about how the negative comments have been affecting my confidence, and I guess I want to explore why I can't seem to shake them off.

It sounds like despite the ups and downs, that lingering worry about surfing remains your main source of stress. Based on what you told me last time, we wanted to figure out what triggers those critical thoughts and then build a simple tool to handle them when they pop up. Does focusing on identifying the triggers first, followed by building a quick calming strategy, feel like the right order for us today?

Yeah, that sounds right. I think figuring out what sets it off could help. Sometimes it feels like it comes out of nowhere, but maybe there's a pattern I'm missing. And I could really use something practical to do when my mind starts spiraling about it.

That pattern recognition is exactly the key to unlocking this cycle, and finding a practical anchor is vital when your mind races. Let's dive straight into the triggers first. When you notice that sudden drop in your chest or that tightening in your shoulders, what is the very first image or memory that pops into your head immediately afterward? Is it usually something specific about the beach environment, or perhaps a thought about your own abilities?

It's usually the memory of this one day a few months back. There was this guy, a regular at the beach, and he just laughed when I wiped out on a wave. He didn't say anything mean, but the laugh—it just stuck with me. After that, I start thinking about how I'm not as good as everyone else out there.

That laughter becoming a permanent scar on your memory is incredibly painful, especially when it happens years later and triggers such deep insecurity. It sounds like your brain latched onto that single moment as proof that you don't belong there, making it impossible to separate the event from who you are. When you remember that laugh, does the immediate thought tend to be "I messed up publicly," or does it quickly slide into comparing yourself to others?

It's more like comparing myself to others, I think. I'll look around and see people catching waves so easily, and I just feel like I don't measure up. That laugh kind of confirmed what I already feared—that I'm not really good enough to be out there with them.

That comparison trap is incredibly powerful because it takes a single moment and turns it into a verdict on your entire identity. It seems like that laugh acted as the final nail in the coffin for your self-esteem at that moment, convincing you that your worth depends on being better than everyone else watching. When you bring up that specific person laughing, does your stomach tighten right away, or do you spend more time mentally rehearsing that scene trying to prove him wrong?

I think I spend more time mentally rehearsing it, honestly. I'll replay the moment over and over, imagining what I could have done differently to avoid the wipeout. My stomach does tighten, but it's more like this heavy, sinking feeling that lasts for hours after I think about it.

Replaying that scene endlessly is a classic way your brain tries to fix a mistake by finding a solution, but unfortunately, it often reinforces the original shame instead of solving it. It sounds like you've turned that one laugh into a movie you keep watching, convinced the ending proves you aren't worthy of the beach. When you imagine fixing it in your head, does the feeling of failure disappear, or does the same heavy knot remain in your stomach?

The heavy knot stays, honestly. Even in my imagination, fixing it doesn't really make me feel better. I'll picture nailing the wave perfectly, but then my mind just jumps to the next time I might mess up. It's like there's always another chance to fail lurking around the corner.

That endless loop of "what ifs" creates a ceiling on your confidence, making it impossible to believe you can succeed because you're constantly preparing for the next disaster. It sounds like your brain has learned that perfection is required to feel safe, so any attempt at mastery just proves the fear right. When you realize that even imagining a perfect run leaves you anxious about future failures, does that highlight how unrealistic the standard you're setting for yourself actually is?

I guess I never thought of it that way. I mean, yeah, aiming to be perfect every time is pretty impossible, isn't it? It's just hard to accept that it's okay to mess up when it feels like everyone's watching and judging.

That impossibility of perfection is exactly why your brain keeps searching for flaws; it's trying to protect you from the pain of failing a standard that simply doesn't exist. It makes total sense that when you can't achieve that impossible standard, your internal critic screams louder to warn you. Since we've traced the path from that laugh to the comparison to the endless rehearsal, would you be willing to try one small experiment tonight? Instead of replaying the movie, could you just observe the knot in your stomach and the urge to compare without adding any new stories to it? We can practice naming the sensation without judging it for ten minutes before bed.

I think I could try that. It sounds a little strange, just sitting with the feeling instead of fighting it, but I'm willing to give it a shot. I'll set a timer for ten minutes tonight and just notice what comes up without trying to change it.

That willingness to sit with discomfort without fighting it is a huge breakthrough, and setting a timer helps remove the pressure of "doing" something right. Tonight, whenever you feel that knot forming or the urge to replay the laugh, just pause, name the sensation ("tightness," "heat"), and wait for the timer to ring. Does that sound like a manageable task for tonight, or is there any part of resisting the urge to fix it that worries you?

It does sound manageable. I think the worrying part is that if I don't fix it in my head, I'll just feel worse, like I'm giving up or something. But I also see how trying to fix it hasn't really helped so far, so maybe just letting it be is worth a try.

That worry about "giving up" is a very human instinct—we often confuse endurance with defeat. But in therapy, we call this "radical acceptance," which isn't surrendering; it's simply refusing to add fuel to the fire by arguing with the emotion. Think of it like holding a hot cup of coffee—you don't throw it away, you just hold it carefully until it cools. Would you be open to framing tonight's experiment not as "stopping yourself," but as "just observing the heat"? Does that slight reframing make the idea feel safer to try?

Yeah, that actually does make it feel safer. I like the idea of just observing the heat instead of trying to put out a fire that keeps reigniting. I can do that tonight—just watch it cool down on its own.

That's a beautiful way to frame it—watching the heat cool naturally instead of trying to smother it. Since you're ready to try this observation exercise tonight, I want to make sure you leave with a clear safety net in case the feelings become overwhelming during those ten minutes. What is one groundable thing you could focus on right now, like touching a cool surface or listening closely to your breath, that would pull you back to the present if the tension spikes?
I think focusing on my breath would work best. I can count my breaths slowly, in and out, until the tension eases a bit. That feels simple enough to remember even if I start to feel overwhelmed.

That's a solid choice; counting your breaths anchors you firmly in the present moment when the memory tries to pull you backward. Just remember, if the urge to analyze or judge becomes too strong during those ten minutes, gently guide your attention back to the rhythm of the air entering and leaving your lungs. Does having that specific counting method give you extra confidence that you won't get lost in the story again?
Yeah, it does. Knowing I have that count to come back to makes me feel like I won't spiral as easily. I think I'm ready to give this a fair shot tonight.

That readiness is wonderful, and knowing you have a reliable anchor like your breath count makes the task much less daunting. Before we finish, I want to make sure we lock in this plan: tonight you'll observe the knot and the urge to compare for ten minutes, using your breath count as a return route if needed, without judging whether you're succeeding. Does that summary capture everything we agreed on for tonight, or is there anything else you'd like to clarify before you head home?
No, I think that covers it. Just sit with the feeling and breathe if it gets too intense. I'll see how it goes and let you know next time. Thanks for helping me break this down.

You are very welcome, and I am so proud of you for taking this courageous step toward radical acceptance tonight. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the feeling immediately, but simply to witness it passively until it naturally fades. Please reach out anytime if the knot feels heavier than expected or if you need to adjust our plan based on how the evening unfolds. Until then, take great care of yourself.

Yeah, I think the text is still the biggest thing on my mind — it's like the key to unlocking everything else. If I can just get past that fear, maybe I'll feel brave enough to hit the trails again.

A drop to a five reflects how holding onto that uncertainty keeps draining your energy, and I completely understand why you view the text as the missing piece to unlock your freedom. I think I could try sending it tonight. The thought still makes my heart race, but I know putting it off any longer is only making it worse. What if I draft it here with you, so I have some support before I actually hit send?

How does that imagined reaction change the weight you feel right now?

*lets out a shaky breath* When I picture him looking relieved or proud, it actually feels... lighter. Like maybe he's been wondering why I've been distant lately, and this text could clear things up for both of us. It's still scary, but I can at least breathe a little easier thinking about that possibility.

That shift from fear to hope is exactly what we aim for, and it proves your brain can find a different path when you actively guide it. Does having that specific reminder locked in make you feel ready to commit to sending it tonight?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll take a minute to breathe and remind myself it's just me reaching out to a friend, not some huge test I have to pass. I really do want to send it tonight, even if my hands are shaking a little.

It does, actually. I'll try to keep myself busy with something distracting after I send it—maybe watch a show or read a book instead of staring at my phone. Thanks for helping me get to this point; I think I'm as ready as I'll ever be.

I'd say maybe an 8. I felt like you really listened and understood where I was coming from. Nothing felt off or unclear—you explained things in a way that made sense to me. An eight is a fantastic rating, and hearing that you felt heard and understood is the highest compliment I could receive. Knowing that our pace felt balanced—challenging enough to move forward but gentle enough to stay safe—is exactly what we aim for in therapy. Recognizing that smile as "real" is a huge victory, even if the emotion attached to it hasn't shifted yet. I think I'm okay for now. The post-check disappointment is still scary, but I feel like I have a few more tools to sit with it instead of running back to the mirror. Thanks for listening and helping me break it down. I'll try the mission later and let you know next time.
